Note that we can write a corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:
![](images/f9/f91ceb948ae8dadf7a0ce4750d28e6550a996ce7adeb13e63d6622d5a273625b.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124614 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" "question-55574236-41f2-5d82-abc0-f140064784e6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/id #uuid "718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-135486" :question/problem "Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.7 \\ 0.9 & 0.3\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.35 \\ 0.25 & 0.65\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.7 \\ 0.9 & 0.3\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.1+0.9=1 \\ 0.7+0.3=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $V$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.35 \\ 0.25 & 0.65\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $W$  *not* a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries):

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$

- Vector $v$ is *not* a stochastic vector since it contains negative entries.

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.25 \\ 0.55 & 0.75\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $V$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.25 \\ 0.55 & 0.75\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.45+0.55=1 \\ 0.25+0.75=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $W$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$V$ only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121211 :answer-field/correct 17592186121213 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/id #uuid "7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/math-academy-id "q-135564" :question/problem "There are three supermarket chains in a particular city: chain $A,$ chain $B,$ and chain $C.$ A study has shown that, each month

That is, $70%$ of flour $A$ customers switch to flour $B$ each month, and $60%$ of flour $B$ customers change to flour $A.$

Currently, $6\,000$ customers use flour $A,$ while $4\,000$ customers use flour $B.$ How many customers will use flour $A$ in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change." :question/worked-solution "From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of flour is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6\,000 \\ 4\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(10\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{10\,000}[\begin{aligned}6\,000 \\ 4\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.42 \\ 0.58\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one month, $42%$ of customers will use flour $A.$ Computing $42%$ of $10\,000,$ we obtain

$$
10\,000\cdot 0.42=4\,200.
$$

Therefore, $4\,200$ customers will use flour $A$ in one month." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c2b5c355-cad0-5348-8dff-54a6b032b4f8"] Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

- it is a square matrix

- the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$

- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

A square matrix with these properties is called a **stochastic matrix**.

Now suppose that, at the time of the study, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside. We can represent this **initial state** using a so-called **stochastic vector** $\mathbf x_0,$ given by

![](images/35/35a20015fc0e96a78ebf1ea2b8fa49721343279a39a35206d41c5ade0ac78ba8.svg)

Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals $1.$ Note that each column of $P$ is a stochastic vector.

Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

- To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product $P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}$
![](images/93/93e30410bcea9b657efe84dc9c32e5f8b3fd3cff159c41f0196547ac5119c766.svg)

 respectively, where

To find the state vector corresponding to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

A sequence of stochastic vectors $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ related to a stochastic matrix $P$ in this way is called a **Markov chain**." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124711 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184142 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" "question-97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" "question-a7374391-644b-5fe8-92d1-774c6f2685b8" "question-dbced5cb-cb8f-554f-bc5c-eb4739e6f20e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184226 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4643f6f8-6def-57fc-9f05-9106c1781f57" "question-2e61a3ba-7f7b-576c-9651-31afc3ef6f71" "question-9ecd9133-5002-52de-bbff-55ef2618e8b0" "question-f8787df3-5e2e-5b10-9759-f8010831da06" "question-bb1f9724-9227-5181-ae8d-25a299447d4f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/id #uuid "24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-274506" :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

If $v$ lies in the first quadrant, then $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡v=1-{sin}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡v & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{11}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})+(-\frac{2}{3})(\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}}{18}-\frac{10}{18} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}-10}{18}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/id #uuid "82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer/id #uuid "d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{55}-10}{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" :question/id #uuid "97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-119317" :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$

$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, find the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{3}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the fourth quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a\sqrt{3}-b\sqrt{7}}{8},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡v=1-{sin}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡v & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ab314b19-c35e-5b2b-9cf9-5dbd3ed37713" "answer-field-24922baa-2702-5f4a-9cd9-809ee303d03c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ab314b19-c35e-5b2b-9cf9-5dbd3ed37713" :answer-field/id #uuid "ab314b19-c35e-5b2b-9cf9-5dbd3ed37713" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-3fa37d87-2d10-5b67-a6d0-78d0e0a5a54d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3fa37d87-2d10-5b67-a6d0-78d0e0a5a54d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fa37d87-2d10-5b67-a6d0-78d0e0a5a54d" :answer/id #uuid "3fa37d87-2d10-5b67-a6d0-78d0e0a5a54d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-24922baa-2702-5f4a-9cd9-809ee303d03c" :answer-field/id #uuid "24922baa-2702-5f4a-9cd9-809ee303d03c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-df83a4e1-66ba-5873-97da-2d74aacdb5f5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-df83a4e1-66ba-5873-97da-2d74aacdb5f5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-df83a4e1-66ba-5873-97da-2d74aacdb5f5" :answer/id #uuid "df83a4e1-66ba-5873-97da-2d74aacdb5f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "15" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185347 :tutorial/content "We can compute trigonometric ratios using the sum and difference formulas for sine together with the Pythagorean identity.

Let's suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin v = \dfrac{3}{5}, \qquad \cos v = \dfrac{4}{5}, \qquad \sin u = -\dfrac{12}{13}.
$$

How can we find the value of $\sin\left(u - v\right)$ given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant? 

First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\sin(u-v) = \sin u \cos v- \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{v}$, $\cos{v}$, and $\sin{u}.$ To find the missing value of $\cos{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \cos^2 u = 1- \sin^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(-\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{12}^{2}}{{13}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{169}{169}-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{25}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{169}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have 

$$
\cos u= -\dfrac{5}{13}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{12}{13})(\frac{4}{5})-(-\frac{5}{13})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{48}{65}+\frac{15}{65} \\  & =-\frac{33}{65}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184422 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186156933 :answer-field/choices 17592186156934] [:db/retract 17592186156933 :answer-field/choices 17592186156935] [:db/retract 17592186156933 :answer-field/choices 17592186156936] [:db/retract 17592186156933 :answer-field/choices 17592186156937] [:db/retract 17592186156933 :answer-field/choices 17592186156938] [:db/retract 17592186156969 :answer-field/choices 17592186156970] [:db/retract 17592186156969 :answer-field/choices 17592186156971] [:db/retract 17592186156969 :answer-field/choices 17592186156972] [:db/retract 17592186156969 :answer-field/choices 17592186156973] [:db/retract 17592186156969 :answer-field/choices 17592186156974] {:db/id 17592186157376 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9d49aabd-7000-5cc9-aab2-77d9e81c75f5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158002 :question/problem "In a particular park, the smallest tree is $6$ meters tall, and the tallest tree $10$ meters tall. Assuming that the height of the trees is uniformly distributed, what is the mean height of the trees in this park?" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the height of a randomly chosen tree. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U[6,10],$ and we wish to compute $\text{E}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[6,10],$ we have the following expected value:

$$

$$

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{-15+5}{2}=-5
$$

:question/problem "When a new app was first launched, it had $60$ downloads. An exponential model estimates that at the end of each day after launch, the number of downloads increased by $120%$ of the number of downloads at the end of the previous day.

Which of the following equations best represents this model, where $D$ is the estimated number of downloads $t$ days after the app was launched, and $t\le 7?$" :question/worked-solution "The number of downloads $D(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $120%.$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=60$ is the total number of downloads initially

- $r=1.2$ is the growth rate ($120%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in days) after launch

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
D=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $D(t)$ is

$$
D=60\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
D(t)=60\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c306525f-8dcb-5d5f-ac56-1625bc0e3733"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id In this fraction, the numerator represents the width and the denominator represents the length.

We can make a denominator of $18$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9$:

$$
\frac{1\times 9}{2\times 9}=\frac{9}{18}
$$

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "Either the positive or negative of the expression inside the absolute value must be equal to the right-hand side of the equation.

So, we set up the two corresponding equations and solve them independently:

- If $|9-y|=9-y,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|9-y| & =4 \\ 9-y & =4 \\ -y & =-5 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|9-y|=-(9-y),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|9-y| & =4 \\ -(9-y) & =4 \\ -9+y & =4 \\ y & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{3}\,\, & \le \,\,3 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-3)\cdot 3 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,-9\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ (\cancel{-}3)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ 3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{3y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{\cancel{3}y}{\cancel{3}} & \ge -9 \\ y & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y\ge -9.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4e4a26f0-ed0b-57e8-a627-d6b00292461a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {"source" ":org/Math-Academy" "forms" [{:db/id 17592186179739 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2310204a-fdf5-57d1-9e96-98189fedc070"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2310204a-fdf5-57d1-9e96-98189fedc070" :question/id #uuid "2310204a-fdf5-57d1-9e96-98189fedc070" :question/math-academy-id "q-125490" :question/problem "![](images/9f/9f94742a7f37fd7f6a1c789401a2e323fec80aca584774453cba03cf69f28ade.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above, and let $C$ be the path along the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$

III. ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$  works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/f4/f4e8c62562ee1657e41bb36a21c901dc95935558641f724f934a4c58706f4a64.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that if we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/40/40b100dd4bc71b95f5ad99eb0cec8ed87133211bb371b22deccb851f79c695b3.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-53503a6a-a2ae-508c-9eef-c15dd0d61993"] :db/ensure Consider the vector field $F(x,y)$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the semiellipse is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$

III. ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/1d/1d91a85ccbb948e070db738373ffc5032f4e91a0ba8e04cd14e79276b0e798f8.png)

So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- Statement III is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/a8/a8e0bffd04fb7b765d3c654f62b1958ab55a42f0d26cbc9f2b2e31f7d8e6f775.png)

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be155506-4e79-5a1a-866f-997f1cb30ccc"] :db/ensure "002b6494-db6e-5c52-baa6-f8349498d2c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-331789" :question/problem "Consider a function $r(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{r(t)\}=R(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{3t}r(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{3t}r(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,r(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{3t}r(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{3t}\,r(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-3)t}\,r(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $R(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,r(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-3)t}\,r(t)\,\text{d}t=R(s-3),
$$

where 

$$
s-3>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+3.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2cf6229-1b40-568c-b2ae-1e954c9aa404" "answer-field-02bc9620-90dd-5010-be23-891afbacbab1" {:db/id 17592186368088 :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}$ for $s>1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}\} \\  & =L\{7{t}^{2}\}+L\{5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}\} \\  & =7L\{{t}^{2}\}+5L\{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}} \\ L\{{t}^{4}\} & =\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}\}=\frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =7L\{{t}^{2}\}+5L\{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}\} \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{120}{(s-1)^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-c46cfffe-18b2-5eac-8e1f-91eedc4c8269" :activity/id #uuid "c46cfffe-18b2-5eac-8e1f-91eedc4c8269" :activity/title "The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186050615 :activity/course 17592186046660 :activity/steps ["step-f579c56e-583e-5d0a-8431-cb59e1d5eecc" "step-4352ef4f-23b6-5c61-ac25-56e4098a43c6" "step-34e3daa2-8ba3-59ec-8c00-c52a7eef4a03"] :activity/first-step "step-f579c56e-583e-5d0a-8431-cb59e1d5eecc" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-f579c56e-583e-5d0a-8431-cb59e1d5eecc" :step/id #uuid "f579c56e-583e-5d0a-8431-cb59e1d5eecc" :step/content "question-002b6494-db6e-5c52-baa6-f8349498d2c1" :step/next "step-4352ef4f-23b6-5c61-ac25-56e4098a43c6" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-4352ef4f-23b6-5c61-ac25-56e4098a43c6" :step/id #uuid "4352ef4f-23b6-5c61-ac25-56e4098a43c6" :step/content "question-bf25d1c4-52d6-5c8a-89b9-2f0b3253eb28" :step/next "step-34e3daa2-8ba3-59ec-8c00-c52a7eef4a03" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-34e3daa2-8ba3-59ec-8c00-c52a7eef4a03" :step/id #uuid "34e3daa2-8ba3-59ec-8c00-c52a7eef4a03" :step/content 17592186368088 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186161210 :answer-field/choices 17592186161211] [:db/retract 17592186161210 :answer-field/choices 17592186161212] [:db/retract 17592186161210 :answer-field/choices 17592186161213] [:db/retract 17592186161210 :answer-field/choices 17592186161214] [:db/retract 17592186161210 :answer-field/choices 17592186161215] {:db/id 17592186162005 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e2384f15-0b1d-5ffb-9cdd-5f07e0af2003" "question-f4e82a18-a51f-5302-8e3f-b37a2f43e1e2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161797 :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/09/09d935cd479371e7cde4e52b2073cb23343a5137f311803c8da5879a59896fb4.svg)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,2,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

![](images/51/51694be12d594a39b6a07f48b37aedb47323fc5537a60f5d6a766576103d48f6.svg)

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 + 2y_2^2 - y_3^2.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e2384f15-0b1d-5ffb-9cdd-5f07e0af2003" :question/id #uuid "e2384f15-0b1d-5ffb-9cdd-5f07e0af2003" :question/math-academy-id "q-140988" :question/problem "Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -5) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -5)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,2,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
5{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{3}^{2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-15\lambda +50 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,5\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

17592186163229 :tutorial/content "Consider a quadratic form 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. As we know, any symmetric matrix can be orthogonally diagonalized as follows:

$$
D = P^T \! AP,
$$

where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix and $D$ is a diagonal matrix that contains eigenvalues of $A$ on the main diagonal. 

Now, substituting the change of variable $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}$ into our quadratic form, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}\,AP)y \\  & ={y}^{T}\,Dy,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives us a canonical form. 

As a result, using the orthogonal diagonalization of $A,$ we can find the canonical form of $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}.$

For example, let's find the canonical form of 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+4x_1x_2+x_2^2.
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/43/43e0dc28161c0564a75f6ea2dc7f0e09ad74dffae05b864e13c61330221f2983.svg)

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we compute the slope $m$ of the line as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{3-(-3)}{1-4} \\  & =\frac{6}{-3} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$

$$

As we found previously, the slope is $m=-2.$

Substituting $m=-2$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-2x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+b \\ -3 & =-2(4)+b \\ -3 & =-8+b \\ 5 & =b \\ b & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-2x+5.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2793c581-3bd2-5896-8ef5-e95aced92eee" "answer-field-8958b128-5689-552d-8a7a-ed52385902c0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2793c581-3bd2-5896-8ef5-e95aced92eee" :answer-field/id #uuid "2793c581-3bd2-5896-8ef5-e95aced92eee" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8e4ffc75-7371-5c2d-b74f-e086c2d908f3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8e4ffc75-7371-5c2d-b74f-e086c2d908f3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e4ffc75-7371-5c2d-b74f-e086c2d908f3" :answer/id #uuid "8e4ffc75-7371-5c2d-b74f-e086c2d908f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8958b128-5689-552d-8a7a-ed52385902c0" :answer-field/id #uuid "8958b128-5689-552d-8a7a-ed52385902c0" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-35ec4058-3033-5189-b180-d21d1d98d10d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-35ec4058-3033-5189-b180-d21d1d98d10d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35ec4058-3033-5189-b180-d21d1d98d10d" :answer/id #uuid "35ec4058-3033-5189-b180-d21d1d98d10d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2x+5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068926 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41" :question/id #uuid "2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41" :question/math-academy-id "q-167103" :question/problem "Calculate the $x$-intercept of the line $\overset{↔}{AB}.$

}_{e}^{3e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{e}^{3e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=e,$ and the upper bound is $b=3e.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3e-e}{n}=\frac{2e}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{e}^{3e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(e+i\cdot \frac{2e}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(e+\frac{2ie}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{2ie}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186393254 :answer/value "{lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{2ie}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186393252 :answer/value "{lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{4ie}{n})\cdot \frac{4e}{n}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186393256 :answer/value "{lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fea7dc0c-332b-5e65-b34c-aa74602e656a" :question/id #uuid "fea7dc0c-332b-5e65-b34c-aa74602e656a" :question/math-academy-id "q-113885" :question/problem "What is ${\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

:question/math-academy-id "q-114899" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].$" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{1}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{1}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=4{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=4{x}^{3}$ and $b=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0a33f6fd-b93c-5b4f-b219-979a3489cf29"] :db/ensure III. $[-2,2)$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124285 :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=|x-2|-2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

I. $x \in (-\infty, 2]$

II. $x \in (0, \infty)$

III. $x \in (-1,4]$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's graph the given function. The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-2|-2$ can be obtained in the following way:  

1\. Take the curve $y=|x|.$

2\. Translate it by $2$ units to the right,  to get $y= |x-2|.$

3\. Finally, translate $y= |x-2|$ by $2$ units down to get $f(x)=|x-2|-2.$

![](images/60/60c2601abfd3c4034991408f47b75c8cf70a1bccb72f73b2f9624a52d0ed7b42.png)

Now, remember that a function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in(-\infty,2].$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/45/45b0cdd26280d9379a449af41edbc9e69dd9d76f3b4116d938fbe708c21f6f29.png)

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in(0,\infty)$ and $x \in (-1,4].$ On these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/55/55b8483c59362d3a59dfd269db74f2c5f17a97cee1f25c896ece16890d80bd42.png)

  

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc" :question/id #uuid "0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-108578" :question/problem "![](images/44/448ae88055ea0da5dd44fb3db608b5ac71dbd3709c88edd41440c15124d74eae.png)

From the above, we see that:

- For graphs I, III, and IV, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line. Therefore, graphs I, III, and IV show one-to-one functions. As a result, those functions are invertible.

"question-dd52658d-d0dc-5c1e-b084-552fde414f6a" :question/id #uuid "dd52658d-d0dc-5c1e-b084-552fde414f6a" :question/math-academy-id "q-130775" :question/problem "Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

"Find the product ${E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{E}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{1}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{1}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{1}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116496 :tutorial/content "Each elementary matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as ![](images/01/0144b651cc6eff46265156e1491f58aacfc167da6dce571dbf4a92c9d94e7177.svg)
To find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/fb/fbb291c4f2d7ccc79939cf9368579b07f6649709f123fb70a1383deefaec6fc1.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to the entire row (not only the left part):

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,{I}_{2}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[{I}_{2}\,|\,{E}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
![](images/1e/1e71a52dda452f98fa77c01117f40d055fa0661100a0e4ffc25147d9baefc0af.svg)

Given the triangle above, find the length of $\overset{―}{BC}$ rounded to one decimal place." :question/worked-solution "For an angle $\theta $ in a right triangle, the trigonometric ratios are as follows:

- $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}$

First, note that we are given the length of the hypotenuse $\overset{―}{AB}$ and wish to find the length of the leg $\overset{―}{BC}$ adjacent to the given angle $∠B.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse is *cosine*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(m∠B) & =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}) & =\frac{BC}{12} \\ BC & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}).\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}) \\  & =12(0.788\,01…) \\  & =9.456\,12… \\  & ≈9.5,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1b7b0522-84f1-5956-962e-86aea240df5c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1b7b0522-84f1-5956-962e-86aea240df5c" :answer-field/id #uuid "1b7b0522-84f1-5956-962e-86aea240df5c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5a69af37-0c06-5df1-aa78-ca7c1546903d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-26256598-94e5-56e9-a905-4f642b7536ae" "answer-36140525-504a-5b6d-8a94-c1d35b940038" "answer-51d7af68-0a6e-5e14-8481-2347a142bf70" "answer-5a69af37-0c06-5df1-aa78-ca7c1546903d" "answer-093e66c5-68b2-5de8-be74-d3e1b20f43d4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-26256598-94e5-56e9-a905-4f642b7536ae" :answer/id #uuid "26256598-94e5-56e9-a905-4f642b7536ae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-36140525-504a-5b6d-8a94-c1d35b940038" :answer/id #uuid "36140525-504a-5b6d-8a94-c1d35b940038" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-51d7af68-0a6e-5e14-8481-2347a142bf70" :answer/id #uuid "51d7af68-0a6e-5e14-8481-2347a142bf70" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8.9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a69af37-0c06-5df1-aa78-ca7c1546903d" :answer/id #uuid "5a69af37-0c06-5df1-aa78-ca7c1546903d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-093e66c5-68b2-5de8-be74-d3e1b20f43d4" :answer/id #uuid "093e66c5-68b2-5de8-be74-d3e1b20f43d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-db59e458-8e99-5a95-814f-8adc8a6a9836" :question/id #uuid "db59e458-8e99-5a95-814f-8adc8a6a9836" :question/math-academy-id "q-122353" :question/problem "![](images/77/77242f149dc99e0641e6e095d02aeeb1fffdf764ee664cfcc02e659f9d0e03b0.png)

Given the triangle above, find the length of $\overset{―}{AC}$ rounded to one decimal place." :question/worked-solution "For an angle $\theta $ in a right triangle, the trigonometric ratios are as follows:

- $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}$

First, note that we are given the length of the adjacent leg $\overset{―}{AB}$ and wish to find the length of the leg $\overset{―}{AC}$ hypotenuse to the given angle $∠A.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse is *cosine*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(m∠C) & =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({22}^{∘}) & =\frac{7}{AC} \\ AC\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({22}^{∘}) & =7 \\ AC & =\frac{7}{\operatorname{cos}⁡({22}^{∘})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =\frac{7}{\operatorname{cos}⁡({22}^{∘})} \\  & =\frac{7}{(0.927\,18…)} \\  & =7.549\,74… \\  & ≈7.5,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dee662f8-4fb6-5dbb-876b-c57ec504e694"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-dee662f8-4fb6-5dbb-876b-c57ec504e694" :answer-field/id #uuid "dee662f8-4fb6-5dbb-876b-c57ec504e694" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a27513fc-52d7-5aae-8114-61b988f68c53" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a4475272-1254-5374-b9a5-1ae13bf40580" "answer-a27513fc-52d7-5aae-8114-61b988f68c53" "answer-b7f65878-4423-5003-bb30-a8b179c3fc21" "answer-f715c199-77ad-5e4d-b6a4-19176a3b13e6" "answer-720d9d1c-5ab9-50e9-b083-1d77e7c43301"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4475272-1254-5374-b9a5-1ae13bf40580" :answer/id #uuid "a4475272-1254-5374-b9a5-1ae13bf40580" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7.4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a27513fc-52d7-5aae-8114-61b988f68c53" :answer/id #uuid "a27513fc-52d7-5aae-8114-61b988f68c53" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b7f65878-4423-5003-bb30-a8b179c3fc21" :answer/id #uuid "b7f65878-4423-5003-bb30-a8b179c3fc21" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f715c199-77ad-5e4d-b6a4-19176a3b13e6" :answer/id #uuid "f715c199-77ad-5e4d-b6a4-19176a3b13e6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-720d9d1c-5ab9-50e9-b083-1d77e7c43301" :answer/id #uuid "720d9d1c-5ab9-50e9-b083-1d77e7c43301" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078725 :question/problem "A triangle $△LMN$ has $m∠L={90}^{∘},$ $m∠N={37}^{∘},$ and $LM=8.$ Find the length of $\overset{―}{LN}$ rounded to the nearest integer." :question/worked-solution "For an angle $\theta $ in a right triangle, the trigonometric ratios are as follows:

Notice that we are given the length of the leg $\overset{―}{LM}$ opposite to the given angle $∠N$ and wish to find the length of the leg $\overset{―}{LN}$ adjacent$∠N.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite leg to the adjacent leg is *tangent*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠N) & =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘}) & =\frac{8}{LN} \\ LN\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘}) & =8 \\ LN & =\frac{8}{\operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =\frac{8}{\operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘})} \\  & =\frac{8}{(0.753\,55…)} \\  & =10.616\,35… \\  & ≈11,\end{aligned}
$$

"question-6acce05c-927e-54a3-ab7e-dea3332ed930" :question/id #uuid "6acce05c-927e-54a3-ab7e-dea3332ed930" :question/math-academy-id "q-342257" :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-5x, & x\in [-2,0) \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}, & x\in [0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-2,2).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-2,2).$ Its graph is shown below.

![](images/64/64b557365c3642ae7a4206794080804bf2bbccb07230dfa46a4f415570f85329.png)

- Statement II is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is $\text{true}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}-5x=-5(-2)=10
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}(2)^{2}=10.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{true}$ since statements I, II, and III are all true.

**Note:** The $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R$ has the graph shown below.

F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}1, & x\in [0,1) \\ x, & x\in [-1,0)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-1,1).$ 
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-1,1)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-1,1)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement II is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-1,1).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is $\text{false}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}x=-1
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}1=1.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}F(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{false}$ since statements I and III are false.

**Note:** The $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R$ has the graph shown below.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}+1} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}+1}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}-1} & = \\ \frac{(1-\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{3}-1)}{(\sqrt{3}+1)(\sqrt{3}-1)} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}-1-(\sqrt{3})^{2}+\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-(1)^{2}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}-1-3+\sqrt{3}}{3-1} & = \\ \frac{2\sqrt{3}-4}{2} & = \\ \frac{2(\sqrt{3}-2)}{2} & = \\ \sqrt{3}-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186052449 :answer-field/correct "answer-48563d18-51b3-56ca-8174-bcd3d2395f03" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc408780-d5be-5c9c-a818-aa55dd20d3a7" "answer-1f951e3d-f904-57c0-a208-d0aa3eba31c4" "answer-d62ec90e-b49c-5418-9264-c77f8cc9f9fb" "answer-2420e859-faac-5e9c-aad9-2c3cc3554c7d" "answer-48563d18-51b3-56ca-8174-bcd3d2395f03"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc408780-d5be-5c9c-a818-aa55dd20d3a7" :answer/id #uuid "bc408780-d5be-5c9c-a818-aa55dd20d3a7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}+5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f951e3d-f904-57c0-a208-d0aa3eba31c4" :answer/id #uuid "1f951e3d-f904-57c0-a208-d0aa3eba31c4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}+5}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d62ec90e-b49c-5418-9264-c77f8cc9f9fb" :answer/id #uuid "d62ec90e-b49c-5418-9264-c77f8cc9f9fb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2420e859-faac-5e9c-aad9-2c3cc3554c7d" :answer/id #uuid "2420e859-faac-5e9c-aad9-2c3cc3554c7d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48563d18-51b3-56ca-8174-bcd3d2395f03" :answer/id #uuid "48563d18-51b3-56ca-8174-bcd3d2395f03" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2be8c3b4-39c9-5644-83d2-b15c8e4f70a2" :question/id #uuid "2be8c3b4-39c9-5644-83d2-b15c8e4f70a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-293483" :question/problem "Rationalize the denominator of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{3}}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the denominator's conjugate is $\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{3}.$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $2.2.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =50,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.1+4\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5+0.4+0.3+0.8 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.2)-{2}^{2} \\  & =(0.5+0.8+0.9+3.2)-4 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2,\frac{1.4}{50}) \\  & ∼N(2,0.028).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2) & ≈P(Z>\frac{2.2-2}{\sqrt{0.028}}) \\  & =P(Z>1.20) \\  & =1-Φ(1.20).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2)=1-Φ(1.20).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186061068 :answer-field/correct "answer-4390c73f-e235-5d8c-b21e-b2ce65a311eb" :answer-field/choices Find the line of the form $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, what will be the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft}?$

*Hint: You can use the fact that*

$$
({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}84.75 & -13 \\ -13 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{X}^{T}y=[\begin{aligned}33 \\ 217\end{aligned}],
$$

*where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector.*" :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 1 & 6.5 \\ 1 & 6.5 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8 \\ 10 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

 

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =[\begin{aligned}84.75 & -13 \\ -13 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}33 \\ 217\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-24.25 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=-24.25+5x.$ 

Finally, to predict the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft},$  we substitute $x=6.45$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-24.25+5(6.45) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, according to the model,  the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft}$ will be $8$  points per game." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/problem "A physics experiment consists of a small object moving along a straight line. The following table contains data collected on the distance traveled by the object (in inches) during the first five seconds. 

| Time $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$5$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Distance $(y)$ | $8.6$ | $13.1$ | $24.6$ | $28.1$ | $38.6$ |

Find the line of the form $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, what distance will the object cover after $6$ seconds, assuming the trend continues? 

*Hint: You can use the fact that*

$$
({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{X}^{T}y=[\begin{aligned}113 \\ 414\end{aligned}],
$$

*where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector.*" :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8.6 \\ 13.1 \\ 24.6 \\ 28.1 \\ 38.6\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}113 \\ 414\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 7.5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=0.1+7.5x.$

Finally, to predict the distance the object will cover after $6$ seconds, we substitute $x=6$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.1+7.5(6) \\  & =45.1\end{aligned}
$$

So, according to the model, the object will cover a distance of $45.1$ inches in $6$ seconds.  

**Note**: Since we're extrapolating ($x=6$ is not within the range of the original set of $x$-values), our result *may* be unreliable." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7cbcd786-caa3-5353-bd0b-1dabaa09f399"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7cbcd786-caa3-5353-bd0b-1dabaa09f399" :answer-field/id #uuid "7cbcd786-caa3-5353-bd0b-1dabaa09f399" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d868415f-f29e-51af-aefa-fa2b3c4c46cd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0231280f-3c96-52d4-bb02-f31de91a72d7" "answer-d868415f-f29e-51af-aefa-fa2b3c4c46cd" "answer-2e066363-c73f-5f32-81f2-579f95f3d955" "answer-e78f56b5-9629-515c-a62c-674b58e812ce" "answer-54b64262-45e4-5112-8f5a-007f27ab1984"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0231280f-3c96-52d4-bb02-f31de91a72d7" :answer/id #uuid "0231280f-3c96-52d4-bb02-f31de91a72d7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$44.7$ inches" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d868415f-f29e-51af-aefa-fa2b3c4c46cd" :answer/id #uuid "d868415f-f29e-51af-aefa-fa2b3c4c46cd" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$45.1$  inches" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e066363-c73f-5f32-81f2-579f95f3d955" :answer/id #uuid "2e066363-c73f-5f32-81f2-579f95f3d955" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$45.8$  inches" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e78f56b5-9629-515c-a62c-674b58e812ce" :answer/id #uuid "e78f56b5-9629-515c-a62c-674b58e812ce" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$46.2$  inches" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-54b64262-45e4-5112-8f5a-007f27ab1984" :answer/id #uuid "54b64262-45e4-5112-8f5a-007f27ab1984" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$46.9$ inches" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135062 :tutorial/content "Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1}=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1}=15\end{aligned}
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

![](images/8b/8bacbea6990395351aecca8befe779358d57d50f8c14f865d73c2107688fa728.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0.1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134029 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078415 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078416 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3d4bf850-5813-5f60-9b39-8cfc55a16cca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/id #uuid "d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/math-academy-id "q-7002" :question/problem "For the function $f(x)$ defined by $f(x)=2x-3,$ find ${f}^{-1}(x).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y=2x-3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x=2y-3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-3 \\ x+3 & =2y \\ \frac{x+3}{2} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x)$:

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+3}{2}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2df6be3a-0f6d-5096-bf4e-b8bfa2d2b0ec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: Use elementary row operations to make the entries above and below ${a}_{33}$ equal to zero.*" :question/worked-solution "Let's make entries above and below ${a}_{33}=-1$ equal to zero using elementary row operations.

Since adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another row (column) in a matrix does not change the value of its determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 & -2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{3} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{3} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+3{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & -7 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 7 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{6}{7}$ and $y=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{6}{7},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}.
$$

Knowing that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we can calculate $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta :$

$$

The point $P(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6},\frac{5}{6})$ lies on the unit circle, as shown. What is $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ?$ Do not round your answer.

$\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "![](images/48/489a919487ffe7051a27f736ff8ca210e4c246bceac42055e31f5150bc4e094b.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{6}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{6}.
$$

Knowing that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we can calculate $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta :$

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{5}{6})}=\frac{6}{5}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1767cf0-549a-5130-876d-9403ed25774d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1767cf0-549a-5130-876d-9403ed25774d" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1767cf0-549a-5130-876d-9403ed25774d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d65c081f-46e7-50d2-b0af-c99aac626906" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d65c081f-46e7-50d2-b0af-c99aac626906"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d65c081f-46e7-50d2-b0af-c99aac626906" :answer/id #uuid "d65c081f-46e7-50d2-b0af-c99aac626906" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5237ac2b-249d-5de5-a0f0-312a03200ea8" :question/id #uuid "5237ac2b-249d-5de5-a0f0-312a03200ea8" :question/math-academy-id "q-267419" :question/problem "![](images/a8/a8fc1b09d51bf0d7ac526a917b2341015b787b3098627bedd25e1638ecf041cc.png)

"question-a3aefa5f-7730-50af-bdda-78228d7a1e41" :question/id #uuid "a3aefa5f-7730-50af-bdda-78228d7a1e41" :question/math-academy-id "q-143572" :question/problem "In a hardware store, there are three boxes containing light bulbs. Box $A$ contains $15$ bulbs, of which $2$ are defective. Box $B$ contains $10$ bulbs, of which $1$ is defective. And box $C$ contains $10$ light bulbs, of which $2$ are defective. A box is selected at random, and a bulb is randomly selected from the box. Find the probability that the bulb is defective." :question/worked-solution "Let $D$ be the event of selecting a defective bulb, and 

- let $A$ be the event that the bulb is from box $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the bulb is from box $B$

- let $C$ be the event that the bulb is from box $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space. 

To calculate the probability of selecting a defective bulb at random from one of the three boxes, we can use the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D\cap A)+P(D\cap B)+P(D\cap C) \\  & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since a box is selected at random, we have

$$
P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Since there are $2$ defective bulbs out of $15$  in box $A,$ $1$ defective bulb out of $10$ in box $B,$ and $2$  defective bulbs out of $10$ bulbs in box $C,$ we have 

$$
P(D|A)=\frac{2}{15},\,P(D|B)=\frac{1}{10},\,P(D|C)=\frac{2}{10}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability, the probability of selecting a defective bulb at random from one of the three boxes is 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C) \\  & =(\frac{2}{15})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{10})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{2}{10})(\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{45}+\frac{1}{30}+\frac{2}{30} \\  & =\frac{13}{90}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be770eee-142d-5138-82b0-d774ea34700b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id dairy cow?" :question/worked-solution "Let $D$ be the event that a selected cow is a dairy cow, and 

- let $A$ be the event that the cow is from ranch $A$,

- let $B$ be the event that the cow is from ranch $B$,

- let $C$ be the event that the cow is from ranch $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space.

To calculate the probability that the randomly selected cow is a dairy cow, we use the law of total probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D\cap A)+P(D\cap B)+P(D\cap C) \\  & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation. 

- Since $34%$ of all the rancher's cows are on ranch $A$, $36%$ are on ranch $B,$ and $30%$ are on ranch $C,$ we have

$$
P(A)=0.34,\,P(B)=0.36,\,P(C)=0.3.
$$

- Since $25%$ of all cows on ranch $A$ and $20%$ of all cows on ranch $B$ are dairy cows, we have 

$$
P(D|A)=0.25,\,P(D|B)=0.2.
$$

- Since the probability that a randomly selected cow from any of the three ranches is  a dairy cow is $37%,$ we have

$$
P(D)=0.37.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(D|C),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C) \\ 0.37 & =(0.25)(0.34)+(0.2)(0.36)+P(D|C)(0.3) \\ 0.37 & =0.085+0.072+0.3P(D|C) \\ 0.3P(D|C) & =0.213 \\ P(D|C) & =0.71\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected cow from ranch $C$ is a dairy cow is $71%.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{3})$ means the same thing as ${}_{7}{C}_{3}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=7$ and $r=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{7}{C}_{3} & =\frac{7!}{(7-3)!3!} \\  & =\frac{7!}{4!3!} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot 6\cdot 5\cdot \cancel{4!}}{\cancel{4!}3!} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot 6\cdot 5}{6} \\  & =35.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b1a5a15e-ede3-5556-ae58-86c4c81f9d96"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b1a5a15e-ede3-5556-ae58-86c4c81f9d96" :answer-field/id #uuid "b1a5a15e-ede3-5556-ae58-86c4c81f9d96" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ddae95b6-690f-5af4-a9a8-b1a950ef1aa3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-05bc4eb8-604f-53ae-8cad-cebb805ad20d" "answer-65546efd-9ca8-5f2d-8c2c-136dd631ea88" "answer-28eaf4dc-a8b0-5796-9977-06739a824eef" "answer-ddae95b6-690f-5af4-a9a8-b1a950ef1aa3" "answer-a49f8fb6-757b-5132-94c8-92eac2ab0522"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05bc4eb8-604f-53ae-8cad-cebb805ad20d" :answer/id #uuid "05bc4eb8-604f-53ae-8cad-cebb805ad20d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "110" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-65546efd-9ca8-5f2d-8c2c-136dd631ea88" :answer/id #uuid "65546efd-9ca8-5f2d-8c2c-136dd631ea88" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "180" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28eaf4dc-a8b0-5796-9977-06739a824eef" :answer/id #uuid "28eaf4dc-a8b0-5796-9977-06739a824eef" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "210" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ddae95b6-690f-5af4-a9a8-b1a950ef1aa3" :answer/id #uuid "ddae95b6-690f-5af4-a9a8-b1a950ef1aa3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "35" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a49f8fb6-757b-5132-94c8-92eac2ab0522" :answer/id #uuid "a49f8fb6-757b-5132-94c8-92eac2ab0522" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "420" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186354383 :question/problem "Evaluate $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{0}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{0})$ means the same thing as ${}_{25}{C}_{0}.$

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=25$ and $r=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{25}{C}_{0} & =\frac{25!}{(25-0)!0!} \\  & =\frac{25!}{25!0!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{25!}}{\cancel{25!}\cdot 1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-bb459970-a15b-5219-80ad-e6f542ce56c5" :activity/id #uuid "bb459970-a15b-5219-80ad-e6f542ce56c5" :activity/title "Combinations" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186049434 :activity/course 17592186046647 :activity/steps ["step-314e0b58-65bb-533e-b437-e2dbd19da869" "step-4e72fa17-5558-5e4e-ace4-52051946e318" "step-dffa73c5-7ead-5048-bee5-5764f9977efe"] :activity/first-step "step-314e0b58-65bb-533e-b437-e2dbd19da869" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-314e0b58-65bb-533e-b437-e2dbd19da869" :step/id #uuid "314e0b58-65bb-533e-b437-e2dbd19da869" :step/content "question-31fc7ad4-02c1-5d63-bb54-860ef7ba25ac" :step/next "step-4e72fa17-5558-5e4e-ace4-52051946e318" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-4e72fa17-5558-5e4e-ace4-52051946e318" :step/id #uuid "4e72fa17-5558-5e4e-ace4-52051946e318" :step/content 17592186332935 :step/next "step-dffa73c5-7ead-5048-bee5-5764f9977efe" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-dffa73c5-7ead-5048-bee5-5764f9977efe" :step/id #uuid "dffa73c5-7ead-5048-bee5-5764f9977efe" :step/content 17592186354383 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124591 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" "question-6c7a58a4-6c9f-528f-bd18-00fe71c43a41" "question-31d0899c-0442-5601-b2c5-58d91ebde08a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" :question/id #uuid "60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" :question/math-academy-id "q-107105" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3,$ and its subset $B=\{a{t}^{3}+b{t}^{2}+ct\,|\,a,b,c\in Q\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{3}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{1}t$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{3}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}t$ are two polynomials from $B,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{3}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{1}t)+({a}_{2}{t}^{3}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}t) \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{3}+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}){t}^{2}+({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})t,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $B$ since ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},\,{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}$ are in $Q.$ So, $B$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(t)={t}^{2}$ and $k=\sqrt{2},$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =\sqrt{2}{t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B,$ because $\sqrt{2}\notin Q.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f070b514-e12a-594a-9f0a-12adec04946c"] :db/ensure
