$$
y=-2x+5.
$$

At the $x$-intercept, the $y$-coordinate is equal to $0.$ So, we can substitute $y=0$ into the equation and then solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ 0 & =-2x+5 \\ 2x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $x=\frac{5}{2}.$ The coordinates of the $x$-intercept are $(\frac{5}{2},0).$"] ["question-2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7" :answer-field/id #uuid "edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7"] ["answer-5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f" :answer/id #uuid "5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f"] ["answer-5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f" :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}"] ["answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7" :answer-field/correct "answer-5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f"] ["answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7" :answer-field/choices "answer-5356afcd-b86a-5455-aebb-d397c1bba50f"] ["question-2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-edb8e55d-e68f-59da-af4c-bf5091ccb2d7"] [17592186068926 :knowledge-point/questions "question-2ac6642f-2218-5fe7-be53-d9c45b78af41"] ["question-44ed6b9e-67d9-570a-adb5-f3b8825b1118" :question/id #uuid "44ed6b9e-67d9-570a-adb5-f3b8825b1118"] ["question-44ed6b9e-67d9-570a-adb5-f3b8825b1118" :question/math-academy-id "q-167104"] ["question-44ed6b9e-67d9-570a-adb5-f3b8825b1118" :question/problem "Write the equation of $\overset{↔}{AB}$ in **standard form**.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ 2x+y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So, we are done!

["question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-167105"] ["question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa" :question/problem "Write the equation of the line that passes through the point $(4,0)$ and is parallel to $\overset{↔}{AB}.$

The slope-intercept form of the equation is $y\,=\,$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa" :question/worked-solution "Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line $\overset{↔}{AB},$ i.e.,

$$
m=-2.
$$

So, we want a line with the slope $m=-2$ that passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,0).$ 

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-2\cdot (x-4) \\ y & =-2x+8\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2" :answer-field/id #uuid "23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2"] ["answer-ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211" :answer/id #uuid "ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211"] ["answer-ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211" :answer/value "-2x+8"] ["answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2" :answer-field/correct "answer-ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211"] ["answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2" :answer-field/choices "answer-ea512d41-ab28-59ba-a04a-101b45b11211"] ["question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-23a2ac4b-2fc2-50ff-b99d-a884d3fa4ee2"] [17592186175910 :knowledge-point/questions "question-6b070545-3ae6-5e49-a6d2-101dac09a1fa"] ["question-c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f" :question/id #uuid "c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f"] ["question-c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-167106"] ["question-c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f" :question/problem "Write the equation of the line that passes through the point $(10,3)$ and is perpendicular to $\overset{↔}{AB}.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f" :question/worked-solution "Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other. Therefore, since $\overset{↔}{AB}$ has the slope $m=-2,$ our perpendicular line must have a slope of 

$$
{m}_{1}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, our perpendicular line has the slope ${m}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3).$ 

Finally, using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}_{1}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-10) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}x-5 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c6760dcc-4403-5b3c-b44a-9e304dd2dc4f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-852439a5-b0a0-5f09-92f8-0c58c72638c3" :answer-field/id #uuid left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{e}^{3e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=e,$ and the upper bound is $b=3e.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3e-e}{n}=\frac{2e}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{e}^{3e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(e+i\cdot \frac{2e}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(e+\frac{2ie}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{2ie}{n})\cdot \frac{2e}{n}].\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x,

$$
Δx=\frac{4-2}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

$$

:question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{1}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{1}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=4{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=4{x}^{3}$ and $b=3.$"] ["question-0eabe319-fbfe-5f66-832c-db699322266a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] III. $x \in (-1,4]$"] [17592186124285 :question/worked-solution "First, let's graph the given function. The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-2|-2$ can be obtained in the following way:  

1\. Take the curve $y=|x|.$

2\. Translate it by $2$ units to the right,  to get $y= |x-2|.$

3\. Finally, translate $y= |x-2|$ by $2$ units down to get $f(x)=|x-2|-2.$

![](images/60/60c2601abfd3c4034991408f47b75c8cf70a1bccb72f73b2f9624a52d0ed7b42.png)

Now, remember that a function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in(-\infty,2].$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/45/45b0cdd26280d9379a449af41edbc9e69dd9d76f3b4116d938fbe708c21f6f29.png)

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in(0,\infty)$ and $x \in (-1,4].$ On these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/55/55b8483c59362d3a59dfd269db74f2c5f17a97cee1f25c896ece16890d80bd42.png)

  

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."] ["question-0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc" :question/id #uuid "0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc"] ["question-0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-108578"] ["question-0fa77d6e-f50d-59b7-b662-8c42e4bce6dc" :question/problem "![](images/44/448ae88055ea0da5dd44fb3db608b5ac71dbd3709c88edd41440c15124d74eae.png)

["question-dd52658d-d0dc-5c1e-b084-552fde414f6a" :question/problem "Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-dd52658d-d0dc-5c1e-b084-552fde414f6a" :question/worked-solution "An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are elementary matrices."] ["question-dd52658d-d0dc-5c1e-b084-552fde414f6a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{1}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]

\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,{I}_{2}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[{I}_{2}\,|\,{E}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

- $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}$

First, note that we are given the length of the hypotenuse $\overset{―}{AB}$ and wish to find the length of the leg $\overset{―}{BC}$ adjacent to the given angle $∠B.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse is *cosine*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(m∠B) & =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}) & =\frac{BC}{12} \\ BC & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}).\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡({38}^{∘}) \\  & =12(0.788\,01…) \\  & =9.456\,12… \\  & ≈9.5,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."] ["question-3c476ad6-03e3-57c6-ac0c-7d3e461a358b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1b7b0522-84f1-5956-962e-86aea240df5c" :answer-field/id "question-db59e458-8e99-5a95-814f-8adc8a6a9836"] [17592186078725 :question/problem "A triangle $△LMN$ has $m∠L={90}^{∘},$ $m∠N={37}^{∘},$ and $LM=8.$ Find the length of $\overset{―}{LN}$ rounded to the nearest integer."] [17592186078725 :question/worked-solution "For an angle $\theta $ in a right triangle, the trigonometric ratios are as follows:

- $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}$

First, let's sketch the given triangle.

![](images/38/38dcba98867c158c671b35ec033fa1ec55c8cedc67466ebe981de9fbbae314e9.png)

Notice that we are given the length of the leg $\overset{―}{LM}$ opposite to the given angle $∠N$ and wish to find the length of the leg $\overset{―}{LN}$ adjacent$∠N.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite leg to the adjacent leg is *tangent*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠N) & =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘}) & =\frac{8}{LN} \\ LN\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘}) & =8 \\ LN & =\frac{8}{\operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =\frac{8}{\operatorname{tan}⁡({37}^{∘})} \\  & =\frac{8}{(0.753\,55…)} \\  & =10.616\,35… \\  & ≈11,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer."] [17592186078725 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186075226 :answer-field/correct 17592186075231] F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-5x, & x\in [-2,0) \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}, & x\in [0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-2,2).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |"] ["question-6acce05c-927e-54a3-ab7e-dea3332ed930" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-2,2).$ Its graph is shown below.

![](images/64/64b557365c3642ae7a4206794080804bf2bbccb07230dfa46a4f415570f85329.png)

- Statement II is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is $\text{true}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}-5x=-5(-2)=10
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}(2)^{2}=10.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{true}$ since statements I, II, and III are all true.

**Note:** The $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R$ has the graph shown below.

{x}^{3}∼{\pi }^{2}x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{{field-3}}\cdot {{field-4}}.
$$"] ["question-ed658204-766e-56cd-a12e-1cf2b14b40f7" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=\pi $ and we are already given the coefficients for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\pi }^{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-\pi ,\pi ).$ 
Therefore, the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $2.2.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*"] [17592186064473 :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =50,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.1+4\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5+0.4+0.3+0.8 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.2)-{2}^{2} \\  & =(0.5+0.8+0.9+3.2)-4 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2,\frac{1.4}{50}) \\  & ∼N(2,0.028).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2) & ≈P(Z>\frac{2.2-2}{\sqrt{0.028}}) \\  & =P(Z>1.20) \\  & =1-Φ(1.20).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2)=1-Φ(1.20).

["question-d6dbf98c-84c4-5c67-a15a-4f405cbbd0b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-41401"] ["question-d6dbf98c-84c4-5c67-a15a-4f405cbbd0b5" :question/problem "The height (in feet) and the average number of points scored per game (APG) of four players on a basketball team are shown in the following table. 

| Height $(x)$ | **$6$** | **$6.5$** | **$6.5$** | **$7$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| APG $(y)$ | $5$ | $8$ | $10$ | $10$ |

Find the line of the form $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, what will be the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft}?$

*Hint: You can use the fact that*

$$
({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}84.75 & -13 \\ -13 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{X}^{T}y=[\begin{aligned}33 \\ 217\end{aligned}],
$$

*where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector.*"] ["question-d6dbf98c-84c4-5c67-a15a-4f405cbbd0b5" :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 1 & 6.5 \\ 1 & 6.5 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8 \\ 10 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

 

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =[\begin{aligned}84.75 & -13 \\ -13 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}33 \\ 217\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-24.25 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=-24.25+5x.$ 

Finally, to predict the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft},$  we substitute $x=6.45$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-24.25+5(6.45) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, according to the model,  the average number of points scored per game by a player whose height is $6.45\,\text{ft}$ will be $8$  points per game."] ["question-d6dbf98c-84c4-5c67-a15a-4f405cbbd0b5" :question/problem "A physics experiment consists of a small object moving along a straight line. The following table contains data collected on the distance traveled by the object (in inches) during the first five seconds. 

| Time $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$5$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Distance $(y)$ | $8.6$ | $13.1$ | $24.6$ | $28.1$ | $38.6$ |

Find the line of the form $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, what distance will the object cover after $6$ seconds, assuming the trend continues? 

*Hint: You can use the fact that*

$$
({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{X}^{T}y=[\begin{aligned}113 \\ 414\end{aligned}],
$$

*where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector.*"] ["question-1515bb33-4938-5f32-8710-f2dc1f06ddad" :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8.6 \\ 13.1 \\ 24.6 \\ 28.1 \\ 38.6\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}113 \\ 414\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 7.5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=0.1+7.5x.$

Finally, to predict the distance the object will cover after $6$ seconds, we substitute $x=6$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.1+7.5(6) \\  & =45.1\end{aligned}
$$

So, according to the model, the object will cover a distance of $45.1$ inches in $6$ seconds.  

**Note**: Since we're extrapolating ($x=6$ is not within the range of the original set of $x$-values), our result *may* be unreliable."] ["question-1515bb33-4938-5f32-8710-f2dc1f06ddad" "answer-field-7cbcd786-caa3-5353-bd0b-1dabaa09f399"] [17592186133805 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1515bb33-4938-5f32-8710-f2dc1f06ddad"] [17592186135062 :tutorial/content "Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1}=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1}=15\end{aligned}
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

![](images/8b/8bacbea6990395351aecca8befe779358d57d50f8c14f865d73c2107688fa728.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0.1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$"] [17592186134029 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/id #uuid "d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046"] ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/math-academy-id "q-7002"] ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/problem "For the function $f(x)$ defined by $f(x)=2x-3,$ find ${f}^{-1}(x).$"] ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y=2x-3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x=2y-3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-3 \\ x+3 & =2y \\ \frac{x+3}{2} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x)$:

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+3}{2}
$$"] ["question-d76f6fd1-8c28-5a6f-b6d6-f8935ad11046" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-2df6be3a-0f6d-5096-bf4e-b8bfa2d2b0ec" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-adab6899-9f13-599d-9b9d-313f4a53055c" :question/problem "$$
|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 5 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 2 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}|
$$

Consider the above $4\times 4$ determinant. Which of the following $3\times 3$ determinants has the same value?

*Hint: Use elementary row operations to make the entries above ${a}_{44}$ equal to zero.*"] ["question-adab6899-9f13-599d-9b9d-313f4a53055c" :question/worked-solution "Let's make entries above ${a}_{44}=1$ equal to zero using elementary row operations.

Since adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another row (column) in a matrix does not change the value of its determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 5 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 2 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+3{R}_{4} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{4} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{4}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 14 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 9 & 3 & 10 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the result along the $4$th column, we get

$$

You should be able to reduce the given $4\times 4$ determinant to a $3\times 3$ determinant.*"] ["question-231b9e48-9ef0-506b-a5a1-fc73da681086" :question/worked-solution "Using elementary row operations, let's make entries below ${a}_{14}=1$ equal to zero.

Since adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another row (column) in a matrix does not change the value of its determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & -4 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & -5 & 2 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -13 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the result along the $4$th column, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -13 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+4}|\begin{aligned}6 & -13 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & 9 & -7\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}6 & -13 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & 9 & -7\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 6\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-5 & -1 \\ 9 & -7\end{aligned}| \\  & =-6(35-(-9)) \\  & =-264.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-231b9e48-9ef0-506b-a5a1-fc73da681086" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3af53959-1d8a-5698-92dc-98fa9d92ef56" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =3,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x\text{-axis}.$ Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move toward $\text{infinity}$ in the phase plane as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{3t} \\ y={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}

The point $P(\frac{6}{7},\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7})$ lies on the unit circle, as shown. What is $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ?$"] ["question-29930a9c-51d8-56d8-87b6-15535f5105d7" :question/worked-solution "![](images/fb/fb0da765a857607ce0c8f13690efaa2f0d504ccaa51899a23044ee4ed17f0aa5.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{6}{7}$ and $y=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{6}{7},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7}.
$$

Knowing that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we can calculate $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta :$

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{13}}{7})}{(\frac{6}{7})}=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{6}.

:question/problem "Given that $P(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $5,$ which of the following statements are always true?

I. $P(x)-4{x}^{6}$ is a polynomial

II. $4{x}^{6}\cdot P(x)$ is a polynomial

III. $\frac{4{x}^{6}}{P(x)}$ is a polynomial"] ["question-ceee5cde-40e3-565c-b032-fa1a9c5be489" :question/worked-solution "Let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Polynomials are closed under subtraction.

["question-a3aefa5f-7730-50af-bdda-78228d7a1e41" :question/problem "In a hardware store, there are three boxes containing light bulbs. Box $A$ contains $15$ bulbs, of which $2$ are defective. Box $B$ contains $10$ bulbs, of which $1$ is defective. And box $C$ contains $10$ light bulbs, of which $2$ are defective. A box is selected at random, and a bulb is randomly selected from the box. Find the probability that the bulb is defective."] ["question-a3aefa5f-7730-50af-bdda-78228d7a1e41" :question/worked-solution "Let $D$ be the event of selecting a defective bulb, and 

- let $A$ be the event that the bulb is from box $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the bulb is from box $B$

- let $C$ be the event that the bulb is from box $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space. 

To calculate the probability of selecting a defective bulb at random from one of the three boxes, we can use the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D\cap A)+P(D\cap B)+P(D\cap C) \\  & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since a box is selected at random, we have

$$
P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Since there are $2$ defective bulbs out of $15$  in box $A,$ $1$ defective bulb out of $10$ in box $B,$ and $2$  defective bulbs out of $10$ bulbs in box $C,$ we have 

$$
P(D|A)=\frac{2}{15},\,P(D|B)=\frac{1}{10},\,P(D|C)=\frac{2}{10}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability, the probability of selecting a defective bulb at random from one of the three boxes is 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C) \\  & =(\frac{2}{15})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{10})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{2}{10})(\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{45}+\frac{1}{30}+\frac{2}{30} \\  & =\frac{13}{90}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a3aefa5f-7730-50af-bdda-78228d7a1e41" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-be770eee-142d-5138-82b0-d774ea34700b" :answer-field/id #uuid from ranch $C$ is a dairy cow?"] ["question-87509e91-72b0-5f1f-83b2-ad41631e8459" :question/worked-solution "Let $D$ be the event that a selected cow is a dairy cow, and

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space.

To calculate the probability that the randomly selected cow is a dairy cow, we use the law of total probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D\cap A)+P(D\cap B)+P(D\cap C) \\  & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation. 

- Since $34%$ of all the rancher's cows are on ranch $A$, $36%$ are on ranch $B,$ and $30%$ are on ranch $C,$ we have

$$
P(A)=0.34,\,P(B)=0.36,\,P(C)=0.3.
$$

- Since $25%$ of all cows on ranch $A$ and $20%$ of all cows on ranch $B$ are dairy cows, we have 

$$
P(D|A)=0.25,\,P(D|B)=0.2.
$$

- Since the probability that a randomly selected cow from any of the three ranches is  a dairy cow is $37%,$ we have

$$
P(D)=0.37.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(D|C),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C) \\ 0.37 & =(0.25)(0.34)+(0.2)(0.36)+P(D|C)(0.3) \\ 0.37 & =0.085+0.072+0.3P(D|C) \\ 0.3P(D|C) & =0.213 \\ P(D|C) & =0.71\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected cow from ranch $C$ is a dairy cow is $71%.$"] ["question-87509e91-72b0-5f1f-83b2-ad41631e8459" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3,$ and its subset $B=\{a{t}^{3}+b{t}^{2}+ct\,|\,a,b,c\in Q\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$"] ["question-60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{3}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{1}t$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{3}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}t$ are two polynomials from $B,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{3}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{1}t)+({a}_{2}{t}^{3}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}t) \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{3}+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}){t}^{2}+({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})t,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $B$ since ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},\,{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}$ are in $Q.$ So, $B$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(t)={t}^{2}$ and $k=\sqrt{2},$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =\sqrt{2}{t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B,$ because $\sqrt{2}\notin Q.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only.""] ["question-60c155e6-f24c-5a27-86a4-e2d2fb148ceb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-6c7a58a4-6c9f-528f-bd18-00fe71c43a41" :question/math-academy-id "q-107100"] ["question-6c7a58a4-6c9f-528f-bd18-00fe71c43a41" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{4}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $4,$ and its subset $A$ containing all polynomials of the form $a{t}^{4}+b{t}^{2},$ with $a,b\in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${R}_{4}[t]$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{4}[t]$"] ["question-6c7a58a4-6c9f-528f-bd18-00fe71c43a41" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{4}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2}$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{4}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}$ are two polynomials from $A,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{4}+{b}_{1}{t}^{2})+({a}_{2}{t}^{4}+{b}_{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{4}+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(t)=a{t}^{4}+b{t}^{2}\in A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =k(a{t}^{4}+b{t}^{2}) \\  & =(ka){t}^{4}+(kb){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""] ["question-6c7a58a4-6c9f-528f-bd18-00fe71c43a41" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] </tbody></table>"] [17592186204581 :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {y}_{2} & {y}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}1\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\ 1+2+3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 & 3 \\ 42 & 24 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186204581 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e" :answer/id #uuid "dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e"] ["answer-dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e" :answer/value "7"] [17592186203420 :answer-field/correct "answer-dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e"] [17592186203420 :answer-field/choices "answer-dcc67051-2347-5c4e-9e43-c494abdd7e5e"] ["answer-316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33" :answer/id #uuid "316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33"] ["answer-316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33" :answer/value "4"] [17592186203419 :answer-field/correct "answer-316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33"] [17592186203419 :answer-field/choices "answer-316633d4-c832-597f-bfdd-ba8fe21eae33"] ["answer-d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb" :answer/id #uuid "d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb"] ["answer-d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb" :answer/value "3"] [17592186203422 :answer-field/correct "answer-d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb"] [17592186203422 :answer-field/choices "answer-d6616688-0122-57c7-8244-6a4ed78090eb"] ["answer-f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be" :answer/id #uuid "f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be"] ["answer-f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be" :answer/value "24"] [17592186203421 :answer-field/correct "answer-f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be"] [17592186203421 :answer-field/choices "answer-f5702173-007e-5e88-ab6b-3cfa857c23be"] [17592186204589 :question/problem "Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186204589 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722" :answer/id #uuid "6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722"] ["answer-6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722" :answer/value "2"] [17592186203456 :answer-field/correct "answer-6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722"] [17592186203456 :answer-field/choices "answer-6f15b05f-36f5-5ea3-9bed-f930f886c722"] ["answer-ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c" :answer/id #uuid "ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c"] ["answer-ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c" :answer/value "6"] [17592186203454 :answer-field/correct "answer-ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c"] [17592186203454 :answer-field/choices "answer-ec5a3336-3253-558e-8eea-a50f43e5289c"] ["answer-a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e" :answer/id #uuid "a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e"] ["answer-a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e" :answer/value "12"] [17592186203455 :answer-field/correct "answer-a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e"] [17592186203455 :answer-field/choices "answer-a6a5ce82-7ccb-54b4-abfb-a30641f2c77e"] ["question-9684ce08-aa53-5b58-9612-0d1c154cab40" :question/id #uuid "9684ce08-aa53-5b58-9612-0d1c154cab40"] ["question-9684ce08-aa53-5b58-9612-0d1c154cab40" :question/math-academy-id "q-269802"] ["question-9684ce08-aa53-5b58-9612-0d1c154cab40" :question/problem "Consider the functions $y(x)=Ax$ and $f(y)=By,$ where $x\in {R}^{3},y\in {R}^{2},$ and the matrices $A$ and $B$ are given by

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$

$$

:question/problem "Joseph is measuring the weight gain of his pet puppy by recording the following two numbers for different values of $t,$ where $t$ is the time, in days, since he started his observations:

- $W(t)$ - The puppy's weight, in kilograms

- $r(t)$ - the rate at which the puppy's weight is increasing.

What is the relationship between $W(t)$ and $r(t)?$"] ["question-99da720f-6132-59c4-9760-cafcb4cb789a" :question/worked-solution "The function $W(t)$ gives the weight of the puppy after $t$ days. Then,

$$
{W}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}W(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }W}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${W}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the weight of the puppy increases at time $t$, which is the same as $r(t).$ Therefore, the relationship between $W(t)$ and $r(t)$ is ${W}^{′}(t)=r(t).$"] :question/problem "$\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}=$"] ["question-343c6002-3a70-5903-a244-0acddb5859ce" :question/worked-solution "We can calculate $\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}$ using synthetic division.

For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5} & =\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3(x-\frac{5}{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}$, we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{4} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{5}{3} & 9 & 12 & 0 & 0 & -25 \\  & ↓ & 15 & 45 & 75 & 125 \\  & 9 & 27 & 45 & 75 & 100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})} & =\frac{1}{3}(9{x}^{3}+27{x}^{2}+45x+75+\frac{100}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, our final result is

$$
\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}=3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.
$$"] ["question-343c6002-3a70-5903-a244-0acddb5859ce" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a916e5ab-d2bf-5c35-99df-efcacc3f8e56" :answer-field/id #uuid "8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5"] ["question-8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5" :question/math-academy-id "q-343819"] ["question-8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{{field-2}}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$"] ["question-8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,+3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n}=0 \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the second equation, 

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6}.
$$

Substituting this into the third equation gives

$$
-(-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6})\frac{n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)} \\  & =-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$"] ["question-8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-819e15d7-2e20-52a4-83ba-4e170679fa89" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5"] ["question-336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/id #uuid "336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e"] ["question-336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-344058"] ["question-336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-3 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9})\frac{n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{9}\cdot (-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}) \\  & =\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-319f9cc5-6350-50bc-9ef5-9fc966e9afe8" :answer-field/id #uuid ${y}^{″}-9y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$"] [17592186222035 :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)-9({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
-{a}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)=\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"] [17592186222035 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-ec30d690-d89c-5e99-97e6-bdae59c5d3d2" :answer/id #uuid "ec30d690-d89c-5e99-97e6-bdae59c5d3d2"] ["question-f846bdbb-b4eb-53cc-9341-26d00f9d6239" :question/math-academy-id "q-343906"] ["question-f846bdbb-b4eb-53cc-9341-26d00f9d6239" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$"] ["question-f846bdbb-b4eb-53cc-9341-26d00f9d6239" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A=9 \\ 2\pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{9}{2\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{9x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$"] ["question-f846bdbb-b4eb-53cc-9341-26d00f9d6239" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8ce88b2e-b185-5d2e-8cfe-5be89cc0aa87" :answer-field/id #uuid Consider the data above and the matrices below. Find an expression for the vector of coefficients of the curve $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}+{\beta }_{3}{x}^{3}$ that best fits the data. 

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & {0}^{2} & {0}^{3} \\ 1 & 2 & {2}^{2} & {2}^{3} \\ 1 & 4 & {4}^{2} & {4}^{3} \\ 1 & 6 & {6}^{2} & {6}^{3} \\ 1 & 8 & {8}^{2} & {8}^{3}\end{aligned}],\,\beta =[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2} \\ {\beta }_{3}\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-789ea0d3-54ac-52af-9aa3-c806bd076e69" :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the curve 

$$
y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}+{\beta }_{3}{x}^{3}
$$

that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
X\beta =y,
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$"] ["question-789ea0d3-54ac-52af-9aa3-c806bd076e69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b5f5769d-1629-52ad-a8ed-38afe0f42079" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-1dfba625-81c0-581d-a463-4b6d422c9f73"] [17592186135063 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data $(x,y).$ We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. We call this process **polynomial regression**.

The following table gives the number of units $x$ (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing $x$ units:

| Goods $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Profit $(y)$ | $16$ | $11$ | $15$ | $18$ |

Suppose we want to find the quadratic function

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
$$

that best fits the given data points.

![](images/93/93fe1784b89ce4c892c84a03a0dc80909f16f46ac463c5cc30b40f869a7802bf.png)

Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+1{\beta }_{1}+{1}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=16 \\ {\beta }_{0}+2{\beta }_{1}+{2}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+3{\beta }_{1}+{3}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=15 \\ {\beta }_{0}+4{\beta }_{1}+{4}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=18\end{aligned}
$$

This system can be written using matrix notation as

![](images/72/729e20ddab6e49b109ebccbb049b1abb9ca2fc11003a9e7f4828bff305a283b4.svg)

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the curve that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}22.5 \\ -9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the quadratic curve of best fit (regression curve) is 

$$
y = 22.5 - 9x + 2x^2.
$$"] [17592186135144 :tutorial/content "In some cases, we might need to constrain the regression curve so that some of its coefficients equal zero. 

Consider the table below, which gives the number of units $x$ (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing $x$ units. 

| Goods $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |

It's known that the profit equals zero when the company does not produce any goods, so $y=0$ when $x=0.$ The company wishes to find a *quadratic* curve that best fits the data *subject to* the constraint that it should pass through the point $(0,0).$

So, our regression curve must pass through the point $(0,0).$ In other words, the $y$-intercept of the quadratic curve must be $0.$ Therefore, we want to find the quadratic function

$$
y = \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
$$

that best fits the given data points.

Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{1}+{1}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=2 \\ 2{\beta }_{1}+{2}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=5 \\ 3{\beta }_{1}+{3}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=8 \\ 4{\beta }_{1}+{4}^{2}{\beta }_{2}=18\end{aligned}
$$

This system can be written using matrix notation as

![](images/ed/ed2c245e39c03d6d60500866bba6daf37c4e86becb570720b3c6e65aad90720e.svg)

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector.

{{field-3}}"] ["question-92424f72-7efe-5e04-9bfc-7a9f038c16a4" :question/worked-solution "We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-2x)-3} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-2x)}\cdot {e}^{-3} \\ (x+1) & \ge (4-2x)\cdot \frac{1}{{e}^{3}} \\ {e}^{3}(x+1) & \ge 4-2x \\ x{e}^{3}+{e}^{3} & \ge 4-2x \\ {e}^{3}-4 & \ge -2x-x{e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3}-4 & \ge -x(2+{e}^{3}) \\ \frac{{e}^{3}-4}{2+{e}^{3}} & \ge -x \\ x & \ge \frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-1 \\ 4-2x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-1$ and $x<2,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,2)$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,2)=[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},2)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},2),$ which can also be written as 

$$
\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}}\le x<2.
$$"] ["question-92424f72-7efe-5e04-9bfc-7a9f038c16a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5858f7d1-e301-50d1-b011-9da4a3416c26" :answer-field/id #uuid Note that we can write a corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:
![](images/f9/f91ceb948ae8dadf7a0ce4750d28e6550a996ce7adeb13e63d6622d5a273625b.svg)"] ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/id #uuid "718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9"] ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-135486"] ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/problem "Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.7 \\ 0.9 & 0.3\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.35 \\ 0.25 & 0.65\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.7 \\ 0.9 & 0.3\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.1+0.9=1 \\ 0.7+0.3=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $V$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.35 \\ 0.25 & 0.65\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $W$  *not* a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries):

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ only.""] ["question-718b908f-f156-56c4-954e-a24b1b0d0bf9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9b9b2d59-8140-5362-8fc0-b70ab471b530" With that in mind, let's examine our vectors in turn.

$$

$$

"question-55574236-41f2-5d82-abc0-f140064784e6"] [17592186124769 :question/problem "Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.25 \\ 0.55 & 0.75\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$"] [17592186124769 :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $V$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.45 & 0.25 \\ 0.55 & 0.75\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.45+0.55=1 \\ 0.25+0.75=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $W$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$V$ only.""] [17592186124769 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186121211 :answer-field/correct 17592186121213] ["question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/id #uuid "7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c"] ["question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/math-academy-id "q-135564"] ["question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/problem "There are three supermarket chains in a particular city: chain $A,$ chain $B,$ and chain $C.$ A study has shown that, each month

- from the customers that prefer chain $A,$ $5%$ change to chain $B$ and $15%$ change to chain $C,$

- from the customers that prefer chain $B,$ $25%$ change to chain $A$ and $25%$ change to chain $C,$

- from the customers that prefer chain $C,$ $15%$ change to chain $A$ and $35%$ change to chain $B.$

The stochastic matrix that describes this situation is given below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & a & 0.15 \\ b & 0.5 & 0.35 \\ 0.15 & 0.25 & c\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/worked-solution "We are given the following situation for each month:

- From the customers that prefer chain $A,$ $5%$ change to chain $B$ and $15%$ change to chain $C.$ This implies that $80%$ of them continue to prefer chain $A.$

- From the customers that prefer chain $B,$ $25%$ change to chain $A$ and $25%$ change to chain $C.$ This implies that $50%$ of them continue to prefer chain $B.$

- From the customers that prefer chain $C,$ $15%$ change to chain $A$ and $35%$ change to chain $B.$ This implies that $50%$ of them continue to prefer chain $C.$

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" rowspan="3">To:</td>

<td align="center">$0.15$</td>

<td align="center">$0.05$</td>

We can write the corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.25 & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.5 & 0.35 \\ 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we have

$$
a+b+c=0.25+0.05+0.5=0.8.
$$"] ["question-7d2bfda5-1f22-5eca-90c5-42502b97859c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-87636227-a251-5be3-befa-08c44f225fa6" :answer-field/id #uuid Currently, $6\,000$ customers use flour $A,$ while $4\,000$ customers use flour $B.$ How many customers will use flour $A$ in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change."] ["question-34952883-ed67-58e1-83a4-6ee369a6dde8" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of flour is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6\,000 \\ 4\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(10\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{10\,000}[\begin{aligned}6\,000 \\ 4\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.42 \\ 0.58\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one month, $42%$ of customers will use flour $A.$ Computing $42%$ of $10\,000,$ we obtain

$$
10\,000\cdot 0.42=4\,200.
$$

Therefore, $4\,200$ customers will use flour $A$ in one month."] ["question-34952883-ed67-58e1-83a4-6ee369a6dde8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate]
