"answer-field-d3eedce2-2377-5540-8cff-1c60ab867920"] [17592186124545 :knowledge-point/questions "question-af97554b-6ce7-555f-8ebb-05f560ef6317"] [17592186125800 :tutorial/content "We can use repeated matrix multiplication to determine the state of a system given its initial state and some information about how one state transitions to the next state.

To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

This information can be represented using a diagram, like the one below.

![](images/ab/ab6b3cecac2af22b8665078db56c7daf492c0381434c9c88fe21f2630f743466.png)

We can also present this information as a table:

<table align="center" cellpadding="10" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td align="center" colspan="2">From:</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="60"><b>City</b></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="60"><b>Countryside</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" rowspan="2">To:</td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="60"><b>City</b></td>
<td align="center">$0.94$</td>
<td align="center">$0.03$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="60"><b>Countryside</b></td>
<td align="center">$0.06$</td>
<td align="center">$0.97$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>

We want to use this information to determine how the population will be distributed $n$ years after the study was carried out. 

First, let's turn this table into a matrix $P\mathbin{:}$

![](images/aa/aa1be872e6f5cdcd842a2f02074f1b9ddd7619697973a2cd06a05f9c1cf9ab75.svg) 

Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

- it is a square matrix

- the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$

- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

A square matrix with these properties is called a **stochastic matrix**.

Now suppose that, at the time of the study, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside. We can represent this **initial state** using a so-called **stochastic vector** $\mathbf x_0,$ given by

![](images/35/35a20015fc0e96a78ebf1ea2b8fa49721343279a39a35206d41c5ade0ac78ba8.svg)

Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals $1.$ Note that each column of $P$ is a stochastic vector.

Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

- To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product $P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}$
![](images/93/93e30410bcea9b657efe84dc9c32e5f8b3fd3cff159c41f0196547ac5119c766.svg)
The resulting vector 
![](images/4b/4b331a70fadd7c061d20b85bb6a7c144de91880f386691f498b1b417f65fa264.svg)
tells us that one year after the study, $66.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $33.3$% will live in the countryside.

- To model the distribution after $2$ years, we compute $P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}$
![](images/53/53c774ea2bf14c3f98927d468db9d872c90d11bb8a7ce56f70f611e55faffab8.svg)
The resulting vector 
![](images/36/363f748dfe8d79023473d0e3a83f331ec6a92a905ddcc9115b675362a6194f1b.svg)
tells us that two years after the study, $63.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $36.3$% will live in the countryside."] [17592186125801 :tutorial/content "Let's reconsider the population we looked at earlier, where the stochastic vector that represents the initial distribution of people between the city and the countryside is

![](images/a4/a423e2c13f55ff6af245ae6e51c7dfc6618d350f0e6de7ec813db176892be05c.svg)
and the yearly change in this distribution is represented by the stochastic matrix 

![](images/71/714196a216ec63873059d772ce8c548ea644825f62ea32a6047469eaf285a875.svg)

Earlier, we found that the population distribution after $1$ and $2$ years is given by the vectors $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2,$ 
 respectively, where

![](images/d0/d0b99c9251cef4d82dd48b71d2f4bfc1884f43439a516bd007a1b8ea903c65a5.svg)

and

![](images/48/48982abc258980890c8afd48b2949401e33e2401f8c692e5b1c65b3c4c68705d.svg)

The vectors $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ are called **state vectors**, and $\mathbf x_0$ is the **initial state**. 

To find the state vector corresponding to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

A sequence of stochastic vectors $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ related to a stochastic matrix $P$ in this way is called a **Markov chain**."] [17592186124711 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/id #uuid "24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5"] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-274506"] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{2}{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{5}{6}.
$$

If $v$ lies in the first quadrant, then $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=${{field-1}}."] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡v=1-{sin}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡v & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{11}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})+(-\frac{2}{3})(\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}}{18}-\frac{10}{18} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}-10}{18}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/id #uuid "82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3"] ["answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer/id #uuid "d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f"] ["answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f" :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{55}-10}{18}"] ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/correct "answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f"] ["answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3" :answer-field/choices "answer-d4a6ccf5-14ce-5806-ace1-7ca838a6fd7f"] ["question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-82fa694a-25f2-5e7d-ab30-eca894f443f3"] [17592186184142 :knowledge-point/questions "question-24a538ad-232b-5718-acdd-ce07c94cc6d5"] ["question-97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" :question/id #uuid "97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e"] ["question-97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-119317"] ["question-97834400-1835-5bc3-9180-5bacac383a8e" :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, we use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{4}{5}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{5}{13})(-\frac{3}{5})+(\frac{12}{13})(\frac{4}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{15}{65}+\frac{48}{65} \\  & =\frac{33}{65}\end{aligned}

$$

"question-bb1f9724-9227-5181-ae8d-25a299447d4f"] [17592186185347 :tutorial/content "We can compute trigonometric ratios using the sum and difference formulas for sine together with the Pythagorean identity.

Let's suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin v = \dfrac{3}{5}, \qquad \cos v = \dfrac{4}{5}, \qquad \sin u = -\dfrac{12}{13}.
$$

How can we find the value of $\sin\left(u - v\right)$ given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant? 

First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\sin(u-v) = \sin u \cos v- \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{v}$, $\cos{v}$, and $\sin{u}.$ To find the missing value of $\cos{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \cos^2 u = 1- \sin^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(-\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{12}^{2}}{{13}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{169}{169}-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{25}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{169}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have 

$$
\cos u= -\dfrac{5}{13}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{12}{13})(\frac{4}{5})-(-\frac{5}{13})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{48}{65}+\frac{15}{65} \\  & =-\frac{33}{65}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186184422 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0] [17592186158002 :question/problem "In a particular park, the smallest tree is $6$ meters tall, and the tallest tree $10$ meters tall. In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[6,10],$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{6+10}{2}=8
$$

["question-1818fb31-e6dd-51ed-98a5-48141bc40666" :question/math-academy-id "q-318203"] ["question-1818fb31-e6dd-51ed-98a5-48141bc40666" :question/problem "When a new app was first launched, it had $60$ downloads. An exponential model estimates that at the end of each day after launch, the number of downloads increased by $120%$ of the number of downloads at the end of the previous day.

Which of the following equations best represents this model, where $D$ is the estimated number of downloads $t$ days after the app was launched, and $t\le 7?$"] ["question-1818fb31-e6dd-51ed-98a5-48141bc40666" :question/worked-solution "The number of downloads $D(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $120%.$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=60$ is the total number of downloads initially

- $r=1.2$ is the growth rate ($120%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in days) after launch

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
D=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $D(t)$ is

$$
D=60\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
D(t)=60\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$"] ["question-1818fb31-e6dd-51ed-98a5-48141bc40666" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c306525f-8dcb-5d5f-ac56-1625bc0e3733" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\frac{1\times 9}{2\times 9}=\frac{9}{18}
$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "Solve the inequality $-\frac{y}{3}\le 3.$"] ["question-66604494-d5d9-5eb8-81e3-a76e00656f7f" :question/worked-solution "The variable $y$ is being *divided* by $3.$ To isolate $y$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-3.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{3}\,\, & \le \,\,3 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-3)\cdot 3 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,-9\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ (\cancel{-}3)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ 3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{3y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{\cancel{3}y}{\cancel{3}} & \ge -9 \\ y & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y\ge -9.$"] ["question-66604494-d5d9-5eb8-81e3-a76e00656f7f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4e4a26f0-ed0b-57e8-a627-d6b00292461a" use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}$ for $s>1.$"] [17592186368088 :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =L{7{t}^{2}}+L{5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =7L{{t}^{2}}+5L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}} \\ L{{t}^{4}} & =\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}}=\frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =7L{{t}^{2}}+5L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{120}{(s-1)^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>1.$"] [17592186161797 :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/44/44753acffd8b6384cd291f9b0758edd7676acb319caa22d5b07be36dcf72a5a6.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

- it is a square matrix

- the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$

- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

How can we find the value of $\sin\left(u - v\right)$ given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant?

$$
\sin(u-v) = \sin u \cos v- \cos u \sin v

We know the values of $\sin{v}$, $\cos{v}$, and $\sin{u}.$ To find the missing value of $\cos{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{169}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{13}.\end{aligned}

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/a4/a423ab56220e438fb849d2025ab53b99bb74ef598e16110c911d691680130527.png)

Consider the semicircle and constant vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the semicircle is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$
- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$
- ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works  against the particle for $x<0,$ while $F$  works with the particle for $x>0.$ 

![](images/cd/cd52e91c72d481980c9a48575da7ca3eaebd2ed27f96b1054cf5c1c5da1aa3d9.png)

 
By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $x<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x>0.$ So, 

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/a1/a1e8fa5262fc787b691b3753fc57ab39aceee7c57dbbe166c6da6f6effaf42dc.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186275256 :question/id #uuid "08ceb92c-03d7-50b0-a12d-3ba81bdd7b99" :question/math-academy-id "q-150011"} {:db/id 17592186414783 :question/id 17592186180720 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ is a smooth curve in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the line integral

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r
$$

represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along $C.$ Loosely speaking:

- if $W > 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *speed up* as it moves along $C,$ and

- if $W < 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *slow down* as it moves along $C.$

To understand this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the path $C$ defined by the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. 

![](images/2a/2a3b3896767e5f6beb4eec39f44afcc2387e178df0cec0ebbbdaa5e4cb68e964.png)

 

It's helpful to imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a uniform gravitational field near the earth's surface. 

Let's consider two examples.

- If a particle moves from $A$ to $B$ along the segment, it will pick up speed because it moves *with* the vector field:

![](images/0f/0f0bbc24f7ed26390643546bf578b88a879da58f56ac0b817159deeea25f164b.png)

 
Intuitively, this makes sense. We know from real-world experience that if we drop a pebble, its speed increases as it descends. 

Therefore,

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

- If a particle moves from $B$ to $A$ along the segment, it will slow down because it moves *against* the vector field:

![](images/2e/2eabe985ee8b360ef79841561547b2251a818e63e53e91785a83d0c2cf3609e3.png)

Again, this matches our intuition: If we toss a pebble into the air, its speed decreases as it ascends.

Therefore,

$$
W = \int\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e08c55c-9b68-57ce-97fe-81922244739a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5834 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2c33a62f-70ce-5226-b2d4-39e1df8540da" :step/math-academy-id 35733 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180502}} {:db/id 17592186180498 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179742 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179604 :question/id #uuid "d844a573-49a1-59c3-bec4-e409c486469d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9542"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d72127a-90d6-5f7e-bd87-75d03285a918" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050885}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180019} {:db/id 17592186180020} {:db/id 17592186259817} {:db/id 17592186259818} {:db/id 17592186259819} {:db/id 17592186259820} {:db/id 17592186259844} {:db/id 17592186275259} {:db/id 17592186414784} {:db/id 17592186414786} {:db/id 17592186535015} {:db/id 17592186535078}] :knowledge-point/title "Interpreting the Sign of a Line Integral Over a Non-Constant Vector Field"} :step/id #uuid "e76a04e3-a2f3-5a0a-9547-3a509b4d4d5c" :step/math-academy-id 35747} {:db/id 17592186180502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180723 :tutorial/content "In some situations, a particle's speed increases and then decreases (or vice-versa) as it moves along a curve in a vector field. 

Let's consider a particle moving from $A$ to $B$ along the arc of a semicircle centered at $O$ in a uniform gravitational field, as shown below.

![](images/46/466bd1716e626f6e3cc7859589974c27d49bdaa77bed9aa5813ef4bd9f3328e9.png)

 

Note that:

- as the particle moves from $A$ to $T,$ it works against $\mathbf F$ and slows down, and

- as the particle moves from $T$ to $B,$ it works with $\mathbf F$ and speeds up.

By symmetry, the contribution to $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ for $x <                   0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x > 0.$ So, 

$$
\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =     0.
$$

Intuitively, this means that the particle's speed is the same at the points $A$ and $B,$ and these are the points of maximum speed. 

Additionally, since $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ is decreasing as we move from $A$ to $T,$ the particle moves at its slowest speed at the point $T.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f659a6f3-f2aa-5170-a3d7-e5ba24fd59c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5843 :tutorial/title "Cases When a Particle Experiences Acceleration and Deceleration"} :step/id #uuid "dda3ff66-7674-5b97-99fb-85a94a2b066a" :step/math-academy-id 35802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180493}} {:db/id 17592186180503 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180724 :tutorial/content "Another noteworthy situation is when ![](images/c7/c75d4b37611dd632920692d430870b4d582fed06ac19178ccf69eb7c7dcb264a.svg) is perpendicular to ![](images/c0/c0c348883f19c18a48444415da35aeaa27f8a18606bf5955e34aec416e248cad.svg) at all points along ![](images/27/278f99df1e14fe0ebfb61bdb72262a62670dcaa60d322148bc3ee591b278ec2d.svg)

![](images/f3/f3f8b96e06c9e802e038130db69356924df9c9a385dc913e55cb5d9cc3a697b1.png)

 

Since the force ![](images/c7/c75d4b37611dd632920692d430870b4d582fed06ac19178ccf69eb7c7dcb264a.svg) acts perpendicular to the particle's motion as it moves from ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) to ![](images/65/65ada9c919fe5c4bee19fb4cafff28ed46a36bf6fc90b4cecf70e0fa02386ce0.svg) it neither helps nor hinders its motion. Therefore,

![](images/06/06b0f05fc417c4572bb7763607ef1d471efc1282067b22c372f23caba33fcb19.svg)

In particular, if ![](images/c0/c0c348883f19c18a48444415da35aeaa27f8a18606bf5955e34aec416e248cad.svg) is a level curve of a scalar field ![](images/bc/bc562d54615dad55d095db2afed7626f62ff7ebf0ab6c5d45471b77ac30b6398.svg) and ![](images/c5/c5b03af80a954012283edf6f027c02c7fe387d08ee6424e6b92186d580a65e7e.svg) then
![](images/b3/b3dddb4aa6f178a9ab5ec8245e4881b260d60cfba33123b56b8b5ea99cda95d8.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "13e79581-4a65-5db7-9362-f065ba606386" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5844 :tutorial/title "Cases When the Vector Field and Curve are Perpendicular"} :step/id #uuid "51bd906d-35f0-5627-ad2d-ac5987f58545" :step/math-academy-id 35803 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180498}}] :activity/title "Interpreting Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179848} {:db/id 17592186180497 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180720 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ is a smooth curve in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the line integral

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r
$$

represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along $C.$ Loosely speaking:

- if $W > 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *speed up* as it moves along $C,$ and

- if $W < 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *slow down* as it moves along $C.$

To understand this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the path $C$ defined by the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. 

![](images/2a/2a3b3896767e5f6beb4eec39f44afcc2387e178df0cec0ebbbdaa5e4cb68e964.png)

 

It's helpful to imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a uniform gravitational field near the earth's surface. 

Let's consider two examples.

- If a particle moves from $A$ to $B$ along the segment, it will pick up speed because it moves *with* the vector field:

![](images/0f/0f0bbc24f7ed26390643546bf578b88a879da58f56ac0b817159deeea25f164b.png)

 
Intuitively, this makes sense. We know from real-world experience that if we drop a pebble, its speed increases as it descends. 

Therefore,

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

- If a particle moves from $B$ to $A$ along the segment, it will slow down because it moves *against* the vector field:

![](images/2e/2eabe985ee8b360ef79841561547b2251a818e63e53e91785a83d0c2cf3609e3.png)

Again, this matches our intuition: If we toss a pebble into the air, its speed decreases as it ascends.

Therefore,

Recall that the line integral

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r
$$

represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along $C.$ Loosely speaking:

- if $W > 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *speed up* as it moves along $C,$ and

- if $W < 0,$ then $\mathbf F$ causes the particle to *slow down* as it moves along $C.$

To understand this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the path $C$ defined by the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. 

![](images/2a/2a3b3896767e5f6beb4eec39f44afcc2387e178df0cec0ebbbdaa5e4cb68e964.png)

 

It's helpful to imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a uniform gravitational field near the earth's surface. 

Let's consider two examples.

- If a particle moves from $A$ to $B$ along the segment, it will pick up speed because it moves *with* the vector field:

![](images/0f/0f0bbc24f7ed26390643546bf578b88a879da58f56ac0b817159deeea25f164b.png)

 
Intuitively, this makes sense. We know from real-world experience that if we drop a pebble, its speed increases as it descends. 

Therefore,

$$
W = \int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

- If a particle moves from $B$ to $A$ along the segment, it will slow down because it moves *against* the vector field:

![](images/2e/2eabe985ee8b360ef79841561547b2251a818e63e53e91785a83d0c2cf3609e3.png)

Again, this matches our intuition: If we toss a pebble into the air, its speed decreases as it ascends.

Therefore,

$$
W = \int\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e08c55c-9b68-57ce-97fe-81922244739a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5834 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180723 :tutorial/content "In some situations, a particle's speed increases and then decreases (or vice-versa) as it moves along a curve in a vector field. 

Let's consider a particle moving from $A$ to $B$ along the arc of a semicircle centered at $O$ in a uniform gravitational field, as shown below.

![](images/46/466bd1716e626f6e3cc7859589974c27d49bdaa77bed9aa5813ef4bd9f3328e9.png)

 

Note that:

- as the particle moves from $A$ to $T,$ it works against $\mathbf F$ and slows down, and

- as the particle moves from $T$ to $B,$ it works with $\mathbf F$ and speeds up.

By symmetry, the contribution to $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ for $x <                   0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x > 0.$ So, 

$$
\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =     0.
$$

Intuitively, this means that the particle's speed is the same at the points $A$ and $B,$ and these are the points of maximum speed. 

Additionally, since $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ is decreasing as we move from $A$ to $T,$ the particle moves at its slowest speed at the point $T.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f659a6f3-f2aa-5170-a3d7-e5ba24fd59c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5843 :tutorial/title "Cases When a Particle Experiences Acceleration and Deceleration"} :step/id #uuid "dda3ff66-7674-5b97-99fb-85a94a2b066a" :step/math-academy-id 35802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180493}} {:db/id 17592186180498 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179742 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179604 :question/id #uuid "d844a573-49a1-59c3-bec4-e409c486469d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9542"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d72127a-90d6-5f7e-bd87-75d03285a918" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050885}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180019} {:db/id 17592186180020} {:db/id 17592186259817} {:db/id 17592186259818} {:db/id 17592186259819} {:db/id 17592186259820} {:db/id 17592186259844} {:db/id 17592186275259} {:db/id 17592186414784} {:db/id 17592186414786} {:db/id 17592186535015} {:db/id 17592186535078}] :knowledge-point/title "Interpreting the Sign of a Line Integral Over a Non-Constant Vector Field"} :step/id #uuid "e76a04e3-a2f3-5a0a-9547-3a509b4d4d5c" :step/math-academy-id 35747} {:db/id 17592186180723 :tutorial/content "In some situations, a particle's speed increases and then decreases (or vice-versa) as it moves along a curve in a vector field.

17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =L\{5t\}+L\{3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}=\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$"} {:db/id 17592186222044 :question/id #uuid "94d7e94a-1d17-5470-a293-1353d69fb49f" :question/math-academy-id "q-89592" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4aca0833-9adf-5c73-a1ab-d07568183f99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(s+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{s-2}" :db/id 17592186355332} {:answer/id #uuid "8290279a-5ab8-57ac-9792-73f13640f201" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{s-2}" :db/id 17592186355812} {:answer/id #uuid "8f0198a4-4fab-5362-bb17-7ad99d588499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)(s-2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186355926} {:answer/id #uuid "91c23727-f24d-5c74-bf75-ea326ecfa263" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)^{2}(s-2)}" :db/id 17592186355953} {:answer/id #uuid "d05463d4-fa4b-567c-9712-d946fd6321f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186356485}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356485} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e1a231c-22ee-57a9-969d-ae5213d3dae3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356969}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that

:tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Suppose

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that

$$
F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.
$$

Comparing the two integrals, we see that

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).
$$

For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
s>s_0+a.
$$

This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).
$$

In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "23a4eff8-b2bf-51f0-87ea-b1466d7af3ca" :step/math-academy-id 600094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222358}} {:db/id 17592186222358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things:

- *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$.

- *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$.

To see this in action, consider the following example.

We are given that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.
$$

Suppose we want to compute

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.
$$

First, we identify the base transform:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}
$$

Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for

$$
s>2.
$$

This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by $e^{at}$ leads to a simple substitution $s:= s-a$, along with a corresponding shift in the domain." :tutorial/id #uuid first shifting theorem states that if

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),
$$

then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).
$$

This means the new Laplace transform is the original graph of $F$ evaluated at $s-a$.

So, the graph shift is:

- If $a>0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the right** by $a$ units.

- If $a<0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the left** by $|a|$ units.

For example, suppose $F(s)$ has the following graph:

![](images/45/45ce62c981e4c7853ef158046eb21fbc9c135f5fa0a8887d813a07594077c8ce.png)

Then the Laplace transform of $e^{-3t} f(t)$ is $F(s+3).$ Here, $a=-3$, so this corresponds to shifting the graph of $F(s)$ three units to the left:

![](images/b7/b75658824079fe90c9c4f43d4d37d355c95b845ebed3f11bdf751b52f8d34f55.png)

A useful self-check is that any horizontal features move the same way:

- vertical asymptotes shift left/right by the same amount,

"3f432000-4480-52b3-b24b-72186edeb9f6" :step/math-academy-id 600108 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222364}} {:db/id 17592186222364 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222520 :tutorial/content "Using the first shifting theorem, we can obtain new Laplace transforms from old ones without performing any additional integration.

If

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

The table below shows some general results we can obtain using the first shifting theorem.

| $f(t)$ | $F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}$ | Compare With |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $e^{at} t^n$ | $\dfrac{n!}{(s-a)^{n+1}}$ | $\mathcal L \{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ |
| $e^{at}\sin \omega t$ | $\dfrac{\omega}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |
| $e^{at}\cos \omega t$ | $\dfrac{s-a}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\cos\omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |

So, each new entry in our table is obtained by taking a known transform and replacing $s$ with $s-a$, and then shifting the domain accordingly." :tutorial/id #uuid "dbf3c06b-f0f4-528b-aff6-5b6adcae65b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14692 :tutorial/title "A Laplace Transforms Comparison Table"} :step/id #uuid "aa6dc187-37cc-58ad-bd19-cba1f304979e" :step/math-academy-id 600111}] :activity/title "The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221462} {:db/id 17592186222357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222476 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Suppose

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that

$$
F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.
$$

Comparing the two integrals, we see that

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).
$$

For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
s>s_0+a.
$$

This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).
$$

In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "23a4eff8-b2bf-51f0-87ea-b1466d7af3ca" :step/math-academy-id 600094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222358}} {:db/id 17592186222476 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. Suppose

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that

$$
F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.
$$

Comparing the two integrals, we see that

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).
$$

For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
s>s_0+a.
$$

This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).
$$

In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things:

- *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$.

- *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$.

To see this in action, consider the following example.

We are given that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.
$$

Suppose we want to compute

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.
$$

First, we identify the base transform:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}
$$

Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for

$$
s>2.
$$

This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by $e^{at}$ leads to a simple substitution $s:= s-a$, along with a corresponding shift in the domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "511f0e8e-f19d-5e1e-955e-97dbd8386ea2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14590 :tutorial/title "Using the First Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3390cec0-8a87-5c98-86f2-ba843c736c0d" :step/math-academy-id 600095 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222359}} {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{-9t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$" :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{-9t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $9$ units to the left."} :step/id #uuid "e19c971d-0087-5320-ade5-7561c8259640" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481699}} {:db/id 17592186481699 :step/content {:db/id 17592186445925 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5812230e-36ca-591f-b89d-48a8b7e1dcc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{7}{(s-5)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186445914} {:answer/id #uuid "83050161-c9bb-5cd0-b5d2-7a04f0e38764" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{s-3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186445916} {:answer/id #uuid "a6286f17-855d-5d36-bc99-ac311ecdbde2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186445918} {:answer/id #uuid "eb1cbeb1-e8a7-518d-a6fb-cbc0586e7fc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s+5)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186445920} {:answer/id #uuid "f81a2466-a55c-5f7e-b7c2-eccdac0d7ed6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{s-3}+\frac{14}{(s+5)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186445921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445918} :answer-field/id #uuid "cbbbb7ac-d5cd-51d2-b97c-84f0232078de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186445924}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "34e7ccd4-a685-5844-a89f-5c57b735778f" :question/math-academy-id "q-332187" :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}$ for $s>5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}\}+L\{7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>5.$"} :step/id #uuid "58a277dc-7f40-5be3-81ea-a2342d28f19a"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5812230e-36ca-591f-b89d-48a8b7e1dcc2" :answer/type {:db/id By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-9t}d(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

Now, recall that $D(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t=D(s+9),
$$

$$

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8828e2f6-2765-54b6-be68-2960b77fe33e" :question/math-academy-id "q-332127" :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{6t\}+L\{4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} :step/id #uuid "1ca3e022-cc39-56cd-87c5-f311545581d9"} {:db/id 17592186498616 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221931 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices "Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{2t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t=F(s-2),
$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2727354f-cd77-55e1-a1d0-cd9c6788d154" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498639}} {:db/id 17592186498627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498513 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17ddf7a6-02de-5357-a0f7-fda2afff17f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/97/97b2ac07998dea2ba0116ae4b1b26bccdc2c6b2a64d99836578c01d5502c61d2.png" :db/id 17592186497855} {:answer/id #uuid "385d8719-8052-5ba5-93c6-443dbaca8ec8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/60/6095f8d90e29e62054e66ce058aaf9ef8b592b61a991e7ce9d93b6759d330c7f.png" :db/id 17592186497923} {:answer/id #uuid "38be91b4-49a4-5c7a-9985-97b2fa85e3e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/fb/fb0bda88019114bf77d68c8c72d164bfa21abc1c10cf0fe52d72b53c1ddbe102.png" :db/id 17592186497924} {:answer/id #uuid "7370344f-b222-597a-9d15-849b3ab68fb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/ee/ee965e81bc2b44c9d00c08dcd4f227b76c927fb467921e2fac664834b6bb978a.png" :db/id 17592186498074} {:answer/id #uuid "9339d5e1-6245-5bf5-bba6-2750f42458db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/ba/ba6fb6239cc146b1fb5fc31300015984826e4ab1fe4061a0bd14ce3b2643569f.png" :db/id 17592186498134}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186497855} :answer-field/id #uuid "64110326-a77e-5f76-b890-3c31d6f5dae0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186498404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2ff7cb38-62cd-5c8f-a2e0-afb3c4fd3adf" :question/math-academy-id "q-332120" :question/problem "![](images/ba/ba6fb6239cc146b1fb5fc31300015984826e4ab1fe4061a0bd14ce3b2643569f.png)

$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{6t\}+L\{4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

"526e692c-07a8-5c67-8d8e-821cf2ff406c" :question/math-academy-id "q-331797" :question/problem "Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$

$$

where

s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} :step/id #uuid "cece9bbe-7f93-5417-a941-680f66b0cf57" :step/next {:db/id 17592186535136}} {:db/id 17592186535136 :step/content {:db/id 17592186535087 :question/math-academy-id "q-331796" :question/problem "Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d715b5d0-cb33-5478-a9fe-0e3da862463c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186535122}}] :activity/title "The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186534264} {:db/id 17592186535130 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222044 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4aca0833-9adf-5c73-a1ab-d07568183f99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(s+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{s-2}" :db/id 17592186355332} {:answer/id #uuid "8290279a-5ab8-57ac-9792-73f13640f201" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{s-2}" :db/id 17592186355812} {:answer/id #uuid "8f0198a4-4fab-5362-bb17-7ad99d588499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)(s-2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186355926} {:answer/id #uuid "91c23727-f24d-5c74-bf75-ea326ecfa263" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{(s+2)^{2}(s-2)}" :db/id 17592186355953} {:answer/id #uuid "d05463d4-fa4b-567c-9712-d946fd6321f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186356485}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356485} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e1a231c-22ee-57a9-969d-ae5213d3dae3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356969}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "94d7e94a-1d17-5470-a293-1353d69fb49f" :question/math-academy-id "q-89592" :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} :step/id #uuid "cece9bbe-7f93-5417-a941-680f66b0cf57" :step/next {:db/id 17592186535136}} {:db/id 17592186535120 :step/content {:db/id 17592186535049 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b2047a0-77e5-59eb-b2d8-c4830bf40585" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the left." :db/id 17592186534323} {:answer/id #uuid "5c3fa65d-99cc-5c77-bd71-1f41ffaf620f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $6$ horizontally." :db/id 17592186534451} {:answer/id #uuid "ab5d9892-a999-54fb-b2bc-6e3cfce7f088" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the right." :db/id 17592186534652} {:answer/id #uuid "b0c4c853-8f85-580a-b3fc-4912e7fb4cda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $6$ vertically." :db/id 17592186534659} {:answer/id #uuid "f45c8098-fbed-5d8d-a23a-ce5636def254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The Laplace transform is unchanged." :db/id 17592186534810}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186534652} :answer-field/id #uuid "07472d6e-7c20-5717-a8e5-c9592eadbbb0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186534831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a295f504-6868-5fd6-8219-b8135f071992" :question/math-academy-id "q-332061" :question/problem "Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{6t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$" :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if

"Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$" :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $5$ units to the right."} :step/id #uuid "b1d2ef25-b3ce-50d5-96e8-d900a85497fc" :step/next {:db/id By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{9t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Q(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t=Q(s-9),
$$

where 

$$
s-9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+9.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "470da428-0379-5a0d-992c-de8783330311" :step/next {:db/id 17592186549150}} {:db/id 17592186549098 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222042 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50798ffc-3732-5591-ba0b-04ece45c7da1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{3}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186548505} {:answer/id #uuid "5c5f41d3-f5c2-5c17-99da-23a331941594" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{4}}" :db/id 17592186548525} {:answer/id #uuid "83c7c20a-5a9a-5e9c-92d4-1db64ddad7aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186548607} {:answer/id #uuid "9a625c27-70a6-5cf6-bcf3-a7be0cbcc47f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{3}{(s-3)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186548661} {:answer/id #uuid "9fb78983-301f-5651-9fb7-1ab6e18840f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}" :db/id 17592186548667}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548667} :answer-field/id #uuid "657c492a-d1c0-573d-a492-e9c1d9f752bb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186220936}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "998b7976-7802-594e-8c46-4a5b40b28b4c" :question/math-academy-id "q-64298" :question/problem "Given that

$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =L\{5t\}+L\{3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}=\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$"} :step/id #uuid "517ae331-e78e-5e2c-9909-0a4fabd9ed67" :step/next {:db/id 17592186549104}} {:db/id 17592186549104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186390920 $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the graph of the Laplace transform $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\}?$" :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272180 :question/id #uuid "27d94b0d-b387-5e7f-9e04-38b9668fec27" :question/math-academy-id "q-140987"} {:db/id 17592186360530 :question/id #uuid - For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =1,\,-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}-1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}-(-3)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162653 :question/id #uuid "14118443-b386-51d2-bcd8-a6f6bd250385" :question/math-academy-id "q-95064" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162006 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables." :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}14 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}14-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 6-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +75 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =15,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=15,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-15I & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}-15\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-15I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}15 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364544 :question/id #uuid "a7869b9c-6fbb-54b1-92e1-8d96639ffbe6" :question/math-academy-id "q-95065"} {:db/id 17592186400902 :question/id #uuid $$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364551 :question/id #uuid "b9543a01-1e62-5371-b840-4c039e62087b" :question/math-academy-id "q-95104"} {:db/id 17592186364558 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 3126} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162854 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163229 :tutorial/content "Consider a quadratic form 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. As we know, any symmetric matrix can be orthogonally diagonalized as follows:

$$
D = P^T \! AP,
$$

where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix and $D$ is a diagonal matrix that contains eigenvalues of $A$ on the main diagonal. 

Now, substituting the change of variable $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}$ into our quadratic form, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}\,AP)y \\  & ={y}^{T}\,Dy,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives us a canonical form. 

As a result, using the orthogonal diagonalization of $A,$ we can find the canonical form of $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}.$

For example, let's find the canonical form of 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+4x_1x_2+x_2^2.
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 - y_2^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "26652f7d-7ad4-54a0-b4a6-5d9faafa8403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6a819afd-fa45-5c12-8319-bbdf2452f54b" :step/math-academy-id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162221} {:db/id 17592186162854 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163229 :tutorial/content "Consider a quadratic form 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. As we know, any symmetric matrix can be orthogonally diagonalized as follows:

$$
D = P^T \! AP,
$$

where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix and $D$ is a diagonal matrix that contains eigenvalues of $A$ on the main diagonal. 

Now, substituting the change of variable $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}$ into our quadratic form, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}\,AP)y \\  & ={y}^{T}\,Dy,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives us a canonical form. 

As a result, using the orthogonal diagonalization of $A,$ we can find the canonical form of $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}.$

For example, let's find the canonical form of 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+4x_1x_2+x_2^2.
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 - y_2^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "26652f7d-7ad4-54a0-b4a6-5d9faafa8403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6a819afd-fa45-5c12-8319-bbdf2452f54b" :step/math-academy-id 30542 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162892}} {:db/id 17592186163229 :tutorial/content "Consider a quadratic form

The straight line shown above intersects the $y$-axis when $y=5$ and intersects the $x$-axis when $x=7.$ Find its slope." :question/worked-solution "Note that the line passes through the points $(0,5)$ and $(7,0).$ So, we let $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,5)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(7,0),$ and compute the slope using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{0-5}{7-0} \\  & =\frac{-5}{7} \\  & =-\frac{5}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the line is $-\frac{5}{7}.$"} {:db/id 17592186503744 :question/id #uuid "d59c0884-c058-5785-9ee6-42436f91acb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-166754"} {:db/id 17592186518135 {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Determine the equation of the line that passes through the points $(2,7)$ and $(3,11).$" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{11-7}{3-2} \\  & =\frac{4}{1} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=4$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y=4x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x+b \\ 7 & =4(2)+b \\ 7 & =8+b \\ 7-8 & =b \\ -1 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

So the equation of the line is $y=4x-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186069510 :question/id #uuid "1bd9d0c4-d29b-5e58-82dc-7566e93760ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-72624"} {:db/id 17592186235491 :question/id #uuid "79269f91-5805-554e-93e4-b4f45ec65084" :question/math-academy-id "q-167792"} {:db/id 17592186492004 :question/id #uuid "2c3bccae-4e28-5fb1-b439-021959c48cae" :question/math-academy-id "q-177611"} {:db/id 17592186492040 :question/id #uuid "9fe1d449-6681-5500-8e11-aea191ceb681" :question/math-academy-id "q-177619"} {:db/id 17592186503720 :question/id #uuid "9be101d3-9545-55c8-953e-3e73d5bfedaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-6944" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33213927-0872-5481-b492-8c2a15d7bc5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=10x-33" :db/id 17592186503073} {:answer/id #uuid "3e07aaa1-5380-511b-82d1-705ddf05637f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=10x+7" :db/id 17592186503096} {:answer/id #uuid "a3fd756d-7353-5103-b953-d571e22e7381" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=10x+47" :db/id 17592186503312} {:answer/id #uuid "ca218148-c955-580f-8eb5-5479cf23735d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=10x+17" :db/id 17592186503386} {:answer/id #uuid "fb7e9268-f0e3-598c-acbf-cc02c162d4d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=10x-47" :db/id 17592186503502}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503073} :answer-field/id #uuid "806cc9db-3354-5070-98b7-05a7234f89ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503576}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Determine the equation of the line that passes through the points $(4,7)$ and $(5,17).$" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{17-7}{5-4} \\  & =\frac{10}{1} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=10$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y=10x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =10x+b \\ 7 & =10(4)+b \\ 7 & =40+b \\ 7-40 & =b \\ -33 & =b.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the line is $y=10x-33.$"} {:db/id 17592186523950 :question/id #uuid "4a3e6aca-bc4b-546e-bf1b-908fe05212b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-167071"} {:db/id 17592186068926 $$
