17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

For example, starting with the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix ![](images/09/09dfa5716dbd500a4684f62a5c409a392761e7546c7ac5e4b592133623552506.svg) we can apply a single elementary row operation to get any of the matrices below:

![](images/44/44bf82527f952ba4d01bbc16f0b81a47fe9e82f447a996f75bccef5171d92242.svg)

- $E_1$ is obtained from $I_2$ by applying the row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.$

- $E_2$ is obtained from $I_2$ by applying the row operation $R_1:=2R_1.$

- $E_3$ is obtained from $I_2$ by applying the row operation $R_2 := R_2 + (-7)R_1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "85735558-3e6a-5a6e-be0b-95227712e60a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3164 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ffae07b2-82f2-5c26-9de5-cb69f517ee2c" :step/math-academy-id 17220 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116125}} {:db/id 17592186116125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115243 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115072 :question/id #uuid "239ee94c-c3d9-5955-8cdd-afff77ec3279" :question/math-academy-id "e-4716"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "853a04b2-591a-51c2-b80f-73f559355d9f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048252} {:db/id 17592186050527}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115738} {:db/id 17592186115839} {:db/id 17592186265973} {:db/id 17592186299786} {:db/id 17592186329683} {:db/id 17592186400499} {:db/id 17592186400506} {:db/id 17592186436527} {:db/id 17592186436529}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying an Elementary 2x2 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "7e9e3e32-4737-52d8-8430-910568cdf491" :step/math-academy-id 17221 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116126}} {:db/id 17592186116126 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116496 :tutorial/content "Each elementary matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E$.
To illustrate, let's consider the matrix 

![](images/01/0144b651cc6eff46265156e1491f58aacfc167da6dce571dbf4a92c9d94e7177.svg)
To find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/fb/fbb291c4f2d7ccc79939cf9368579b07f6649709f123fb70a1383deefaec6fc1.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to the entire row (not only the left part):

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,{I}_{2}] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =[{I}_{2}\,|\,{E}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
![](images/1e/1e71a52dda452f98fa77c01117f40d055fa0661100a0e4ffc25147d9baefc0af.svg)

We can work out the inverse of all elementary $2 \times 2$ matrices in a similar way." :tutorial/id #uuid "24a632e9-4a94-5212-b848-8d4b4403d452" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3165 :tutorial/title "The 629} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186079491 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079639 :tutorial/content "Trigonometric ratios can be used to solve for a missing side of a right triangle if one side is known along with the measure of an acute angle. However, the question of which ratio to use depends on what side is given and what side is unknown. 

![](images/8b/8b123fed4a9a42ceb69f3a6ff68ed89f27ae42294137f0cd12a9232d329d77b0.png)

In the triangle above, we are given an angle $\theta = 42^\circ,$ and the length of the hypotenuse is given but the length of the side opposite is unknown.

So, we need to choose the trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite side to the hypotenuse. This is sine, and now we can just set up the ratio, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\  & =\frac{x}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we simply solve for the unknown value $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{x}{8} \\ x & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} \\  & =8(0.669\,13...) \\  & =5.353\,04... \\  & ≈5.4,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

Note that we used a calculator to evaluate $\sin(42^\circ).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e320c0f6-5f85-56c6-a082-c880c7e97433" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2449 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x \in [-2,2).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}.$
Determine whether each statement below is true or false.

I. $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in(-2,2).$

II. $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in(-2,2).$

III. $\lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x).$

IV. $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $\mathbb{R}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The function $F(x)$ is continuous on $x \in (-2,2).$ Its graph is shown below.

![](images/5c/5c1cc57825a318df088ac0bc28ffe75c21579c5fe007fbb52cf0710a1937dc1e.png)

- Statement II is true. The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x \in (-2,2).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} (-2x) = -2(-2) = 4
$$

and 

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} x^2 = (2)^2 = 4.
$$

So, $\lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x).$

- Statement IV is true since statements I, II, and III are all true.

**Note:** The $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ has the graph shown below.

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}x+1, & x\in [-2,0) \\ -2, & x\in [0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-2,2).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is $\text{false}.$ The function $F(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=0.$ Its graph is shown below.

![](images/7c/7cfd6da222fb36d06be1153ac0e398e567f8b9fb8cd1cd9e21f1bb35ed131f8d.png)

- Statement II is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-2,2).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is $\text{false}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}(x+1)=-2+1=-1
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-2)=-2.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}F(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{false}$ since statements I and III are false.

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x, & x\in [-3,0) \\ {x}^{2}, & x\in [0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-3,3).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-3,3)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-3,3)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-3,3).$ Its graph is shown below.

![](images/11/11f9718c9384ad2fea0bf3f5cc7da720559c512a5b3cebbc11ca966d5ec0f28b.png)

- Statement II is $\text{true}.$ The function $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-3,3).$ It consists of two smooth pieces.

- Statement III is $\text{false}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}2x=2(-3)=-6
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}{x}^{2}=(3)^{2}=9.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{false}$ since statement III is false.

**Note:** The $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R$ has the graph shown below.

![](images/68/689e50221843f953a679c91852b2cc11b4b89cb8aa86613be59fcec65ac75c43.svg)" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right).
$$

In our case, $L=5.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{107}{6}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{250(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^2}
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right)}.
$$

Now, notice that  

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-5,5),$

- continuous on $[-5,5),$ and

- satisfies $F(-5)=F(5),$ if we extend the value at $x=5$ using the formula $F(x)=\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-3.$

Therefore, the $10$-periodic extension $f$ is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{continuous} }$ and $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{piecewise smooth}}$
on $\mathbb{R},$ so we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186048813} {:db/id 17592186050789} {:db/id 17592186222027 :question/id #uuid "d5d0172c-6e34-5d1d-9e31-e326cbe0c123" :question/math-academy-id "q-341195" :knowledge-point/_questions $$
G(x)=-2{x}^{2}={\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x).$

The Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
-4x∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }{{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f$ is 
{{field-2}} 
on $R,$ we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term to get

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an odd function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=1$ and we are already given the coefficients ${b}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-1,1).$ 
Therefore, the $2$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186317390 :question/id #uuid "3b75f000-c288-5650-b319-990a54e2ce6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-343340"} {:db/id 17592186402263 :question/id #uuid "2602318d-f33f-5fd6-9721-6e9791bc0896" :topic/math-academy-id 6383} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222385 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222519 :tutorial/content "When a Fourier series represents a function $f$, it is often much easier to differentiate the series term-by-term than to recompute a brand-new Fourier series from scratch. 

However, term-by-term differentiation is only guaranteed to work when the underlying periodic function is sufficiently "well-behaved".

The theorem about **term-by-term differentiation of Fourier series** states the following:

Suppose that

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

is a $2L$-periodic function which is

- piecewise smooth, and

- continuous.

Then, the Fourier series of $f'(x)$ can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f'(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\dfrac{n\pi a_n}{L}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+\dfrac{n\pi b_n}{L}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

In other words, if $f(x)$ is the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ defined on $x \in [-L,L),$ then the Fourier series of $f'(x)$ can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of $f(x)$ provided that

- $F(x)$ is continuous on $x \in (-L,L),$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186222527 :tutorial/content "Term-by-term differentiation is a huge time-saver: it lets us obtain a Fourier series for $f'(x)$ without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch. 

But differentiation also tends to make Fourier series "less convergent", it "spends" one power of $n$. So, we need to be careful about what the differentiated series actually does.

In a $2L$-periodic Fourier series, differentiating 

$$
\cos\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right) \qquad \text{or} \qquad \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

introduces a factor of $\dfrac{n\pi}{L}$. So, very roughly,

$$
\big(\text{new coefficient size}\big) \approx n \cdot \big(\text{old coefficient size}\big).
$$

That means one level of coefficient decay is "used up" when we differentiate.

For example, consider the so-called *triangle wave* and *sawtooth wave*, the $2\pi$-periodic extensions from $x \in  [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ of the functions $y=|x|$ and $y=x,$ respectively. 

![](images/90/90341fcc0828ee1fbefa229a1dc8b0a55ebf5912cfaf934585c73dae5ab720d0.png)

Their Fourier series are the following:

$$
|x| \sim \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{\cos\!\big((2n-1)x\big)}{(2n-1)^2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x \sim 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx)
$$

The convergence of their corresponding derivatives is summarized in the table below.

| **Function Type** | **Continuity** | **Fourier Series Coefficient Decay** | **Derivative Series Convergence** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Triangle wave | Continuous | $O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)$ | Converges 
(to the average of slopes) |
| Sawtooth wave | Discontinuous | $O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)$ | Diverges |

Notice that:

- For the continuous and piecewise smooth *triangle wave*:

- The function has enough "smoothness" (continuity) that its Fourier coefficients decay quickly at a rate of $\sim \dfrac{1}{n^2}.$

- Differentiation "costs" one level of decay: 

$$
n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

Since the terms $\dfrac{1}{n}$ still approach $0,$ the series can converge. At the "corners," it settles on the average of the left- and right-hand slopes.

- For the discontinuous but piecewise smooth *sawtooth wave*:

- The function's jump discontinuities "use up" the smoothness budget. The coefficients decay only at a rate of $\sim \dfrac{1}{n}.$

- Differentiation cancels out the decay entirely: 

$$
n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n} = 1
$$

Since the terms of the series do not approach $0,$ the series fails the basic divergence test and does not converge." :tutorial/id #uuid "8eb8cb65-4c1f-5100-8e0e-28fa1bcfaf41" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14759 :tutorial/title "A Word on Convergence"} :step/id #uuid "409a0a22-bfc0-5edd-ba4e-495f349d4ac6" :step/math-academy-id 602019 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222389}} {:db/id 17592186222389 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222521 :tutorial/content "Just like differentiation, integration can also be applied directly to a Fourier series. This is often useful when we already know the Fourier series of $f(x)$ and want a series for an antiderivative of $f(x)$ without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch.

The theorem about **term-by-term integration of Fourier series** states the following:

Suppose that

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

is a $2L$-periodic function which is piecewise continuous. Then, an antiderivative $F(x)$, where $F'(x) = f(x)$, can be found by integrating the Fourier series of $f(x)$ term-by-term:

$$
F(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}x + C + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigg( \dfrac{a_n L}{n\pi}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)-\dfrac{b_n L}{n\pi}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg) \bigg)
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant of integration.

**Watch out!** Note the following caveats:

1\. The expression for the antiderivative $F(x)$ is not a Fourier series in the usual sense because it contains the linear term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}x.$

2\. Even if $f(x)$ is periodic, its antiderivative $F(x)$ is not necessarily periodic. In particular, if $a_0 \neq 0,$ then the term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}x$ grows without bound as $x$ increases.

If we want a periodic antiderivative, we typically need the average value of $f$ over one period to be $0$ (equivalently, $a_0=0$), so that the linear term disappears.

**Note:** Integration is generally "safer" than differentiation for Fourier series. Differentiation can slow convergence or even destroy it, whereas integration divides the $n$th coefficient by $n,$ which typically improves convergence.

Next, let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "87052b6b-4aae-58df-8271-019f0cb8fb55" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14708 :tutorial/title "Integrating Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "d66cfd7d-a10e-557e-b6f8-239debcedcac" :step/math-academy-id 602020 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222390}} {:db/id 17592186222390 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221451 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221202 :question/id #uuid "77c71e9d-c2a4-5a2c-9c67-a90e8913ba13" :question/math-academy-id "e-21856"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c1e01d04-6c13-52eb-a4b6-ad9a5cde8134" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050571}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222030} {:db/id 17592186222038} {:db/id 17592186317389} {:db/id 17592186317390} {:db/id 17592186402263} {:db/id 17592186425675} {:db/id 17592186425679} {:db/id 17592186425681}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating a Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "2dbaea0b-5765-5b39-b530-0a1d72db0b20" :step/math-academy-id 602021}] :activity/title "Differentiating and Integrating Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221474} {:db/id 17592186222385 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222519 :tutorial/content "When a Fourier series represents a function $f$, it is often much easier to differentiate the series term-by-term than to recompute a brand-new Fourier series from scratch.

$$

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-\pi ,\pi ),$

- continuous on $[-\pi ,\pi ),$ and

$$

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-5,5),$

- continuous on $[-5,5),$ and

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=5$ and we are already given the coefficients ${a}_{0}$ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼-\frac{5}{4}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{75(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-5,5),$

- continuous on $[-5,5),$ and

- satisfies $F(-5)=F(5),$ if we extend the value at $x=5$ using the formula $F(x)=-\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}+5.$

In cases where we wish to remove a radical from a denominator, we must **rationalize the denominator**.

If the denominator of an expression consists of two terms and includes one or more radicals, we rationalize it by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the **conjugate** of the denominator. 

To illustrate, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}
$$

 

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{2},$ we *flip the sign* between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is 

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{2}.
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we start by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1-\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{1-\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1\cdot (1-\sqrt{2})}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} &  \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the difference of squares formula:

$$
(a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Applying the difference of squares formula with $a=1, b=\sqrt 2$ to simplify the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{{1}^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{1-2} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{-1} & = \\ \sqrt{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2b34f4d4-8931-5c24-8872-dfa9420a1a87" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13463 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "57ebf44f-ed04-5203-ae79-eb57faf1422c" 17592186055764 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055933 :tutorial/content "When simplifying numerical expressions, it is generally preferable to avoid having radicals in the denominator. In cases where we wish to remove a radical from a denominator, we must **rationalize the denominator**.

If the denominator of an expression consists of two terms and includes one or more radicals, we rationalize it by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the **conjugate** of the denominator. 

To illustrate, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}
$$

 

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{2},$ we *flip the sign* between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is 

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{2}.
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we start by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1-\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{1-\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1\cdot (1-\sqrt{2})}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} &  \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the difference of squares formula:

$$
(a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Applying the difference of squares formula with $a=1, b=\sqrt 2$ to simplify the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{{1}^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{1-2} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{-1} & = \\ \sqrt{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2b34f4d4-8931-5c24-8872-dfa9420a1a87" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13463 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "57ebf44f-ed04-5203-ae79-eb57faf1422c" :step/math-academy-id 478487 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055765}} {:db/id 17592186055933 :tutorial/content "When simplifying numerical expressions, it is generally preferable to avoid having radicals in the denominator. "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{121}$ be a random sample of size $n=121$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =300$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =55.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $295.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1587\,$ | $\,0.1562\,$ | $\,0.1539\,$ |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1841\,$ | $\,0.1814\,$ | $\,0.1788\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.2119\,$ | $\,0.2090\,$ | $\,0.2061\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=121,\,\mu =300,\,\sigma =55.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(300,\frac{{55}^{2}}{121}) \\  & ∼N(300,25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<295).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =P(Z<\frac{295-300}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z<-\frac{5}{5}) \\  & =P(Z<-1) \\  & =Φ(-1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1)=0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =Φ(-1) \\  & =0.1587.\end{aligned}

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=108,\,\mu =20,\,\sigma =90.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(20,\frac{{90}^{2}}{108}) \\  & ∼N(20,75).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5) & =P(-5<\overset{―}{X}<5) \\  & =P(\frac{-5-20}{\sqrt{75}}<Z<\frac{5-20}{\sqrt{75}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}<Z<-\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.89<Z<-1.73) \\  & =P(Z<-1.73)-P(Z<-2.89) \\  & =Φ(-1.73)-Φ(-2.89).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.89)=0.0019, \\ Φ(-1.73)=0.0418.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5) & =Φ(-1.73)-Φ(-2.89) \\  & =0.0418-0.0019 \\  & =0.0399.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186507486 :question/id #uuid "b6fde37e-341a-51be-b26a-9707a878cfcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-143491" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2259ef19-beca-5d96-bf66-94592e4f2902" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7234" :db/id 17592186506749} {:answer/id #uuid "242a34c0-9396-511b-8301-8c26b4b1eab4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7198" :db/id 17592186506757} {:answer/id #uuid "2cd6880f-2bc7-53f5-a6a6-c57354d3847f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6521" :db/id 17592186506783} {:answer/id #uuid "4b9884b1-26c4-5e0f-8600-f24b14be3e54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7064" :db/id 17592186506856} {:answer/id #uuid "a9426178-4882-54e8-9402-ba02092dc4d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6893" :db/id 17592186507049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506856} :answer-field/id #uuid "6483a111-3bf1-5368-91c6-9ae9b785bfb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507299}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{126}$ be a random sample of size $n=126$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =5$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =84.$ Find an approximation for $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5).$

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=126,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =84.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{84}^{2}}{126}) \\  & ∼N(5,56).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<3.5) \\  & =1-P(-3.5<\overset{―}{X}<3.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-3.5-5}{\sqrt{56}}<Z<\frac{3.5-5}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & ≈1-P(-1.14<Z<-0.20) \\  & =1-(P(Z<-0.20)-P(Z<-1.14)) \\  & =1+Φ(-1.14)-Φ(-0.20).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.14)=0.1271, \\ Φ(-0.20)=0.4207.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5) & =1+Φ(-1.14)-Φ(-0.20) \\  & =1+0.1271-0.4207 \\  & =0.7064.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064314 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063914 :question/id #uuid "65a0be54-6801-5337-b68f-01c7049365cb" :question/math-academy-id "e-10088"} :knowledge-point/id Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n=30$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.2).$

*Hint: Two tables of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2389\,$ | $\,0.2358\,$ | $\,0.2327\,$ |
| $\,-0.6\,$ | $\,0.2709\,$ | $\,0.2676\,$ | $\,0.2643\,$ |
| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.3050\,$ | $\,0.3015\,$ | $\,0.2981\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=30,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-2\cdot 0.3+(-1)\cdot 0.2+0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.4 \\  & =-0.6-0.2+0+0.8 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-2)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.2+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.4)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(1.2+0.2+0+1.6)-0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{3}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.1).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.2) & =P(\overset{―}{X}<-0.2)+P(\overset{―}{X}>0.2) \\  & ≈P(Z<\frac{-0.2-0}{\sqrt{0.1}})+P(Z>\frac{0.2-0}{\sqrt{0.1}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.63)+P(Z>0.63) \\  & =P(Z<-0.63)+1-P(Z<0.63) \\  & =1+Φ(-0.63)-Φ(0.63).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.63)=0.2643.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, by the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\,Φ(0.63)=1-Φ(-0.63).
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=100,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+5\cdot 0.4+10\cdot 0.2+20\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0+2+2+4 \\  & =8,\end{aligned}

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{5}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{10}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{20}^{2}\cdot 0.2)-{8}^{2} \\  & =(0+10+20+80)-64 \\  & =46.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(8,\frac{46}{100}) \\  & ∼N(8,0.46).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=128,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+4\cdot 0.25+6\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.25 \\  & =0.4+1+0.6+2 \\  & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{6}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.25)-{4}^{2} \\  & =(0.4+4+3.6+16)-16 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(4,\frac{8}{128}) \\  & ∼N(4,0.0625).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & ≈-P(\frac{3.6-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}<Z<\frac{4.2-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}) \\  & ≈-P(-1.6<Z<0.8) \\  & =P(Z<0.8)-P(Z<-1.6) \\  & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.8)=0.7881, \\ Φ(-1.6)=0.0548.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6) \\  & =0.7881-0.0548 \\  & =0.7333.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186507433 :question/id #uuid "48e8571c-7a4d-574c-8be0-d4e37adb9dc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-143511" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "211e4a79-2ead-5c5a-917f-9ed87a5cf227" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.54)" :db/id 17592186506743} {:answer/id #uuid "266ad046-e761-524c-9ea8-8883d9273e98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.71)" :db/id 17592186506765} {:answer/id #uuid "5d0c91dd-c09a-5698-8506-c125cd149111" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.37)" :db/id 17592186506902} {:answer/id #uuid "5e829eb7-0b10-5408-a695-e14eed4c7ac0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.20)" :db/id 17592186506905} {:answer/id #uuid "caf99f16-626f-5c36-9a89-b64e0d85d6a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1)" :db/id 17592186507120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507120} :answer-field/id #uuid "c679502e-a36e-5bea-8114-62641a56a051" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507361}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=80,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-1\cdot 0.3+0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.3+0+0.1+0.3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-1)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(0.3+0+0.1+0.4)-0 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{0.8}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1) & ≈P(Z>\frac{0.1-0}{\sqrt{0.01}}) \\  & =P(Z>1) \\  & =1-Φ(1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=60,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.3+(-4)\cdot 0.3+(-2)\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-2.4-1.2-0.6+0.2 \\  & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-4)^{2} \\  & =(19.2+4.8+1.2+0.4)-16 \\  & =9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-4,\frac{9.6}{60}) \\  & ∼N(-4,0.16).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.5) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.5-(-4)}{\sqrt{0.16}}) \\  & =P(Z<-1.25) \\  & =Φ(-1.25).\end{aligned}

$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499451 :question/id #uuid "23386dfb-4266-50f7-b8bd-add2ea98080d" :question/math-academy-id "q-143499"} {:db/id 17592186499537 :question/id #uuid "cad4258a-bb8c-5f12-a390-574af230e1b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143509" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064315 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "327e406f-f432-5db4-a79f-80195c02cc96" :knowledge-point/title "Using the CLT With a Population Whose Probability Distribution Is Continuous"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3315a5cb-452e-528e-8eb5-78dbc3e12104" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.9992" :db/id 17592186498846} {:answer/id #uuid "6de957fe-2080-57db-b272-b3b2f6646ab1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.8845" :db/id 17592186498974} {:answer/id #uuid "77e88625-4c75-5215-8f5a-0c85b4e5a671" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.9123" :db/id 17592186498999} {:answer/id #uuid "a5f8b3c7-8fde-5c2f-927e-132d799da466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.8976" :db/id 17592186499091} {:answer/id #uuid "f7306d02-503e-55d9-b966-b99018652bee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.9576" :db/id 17592186499283}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3315a5cb-452e-528e-8eb5-78dbc3e12104" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.9992" :db/id 17592186498846} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d5ea7fd-d63e-51a1-9d3e-f96a0fcebecf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186499337}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n=30$ from a population with probability density function

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03,$ calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5} \\  & =0.8,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0.8,\frac{0.03}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0.8,0.001).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =P(Z>\frac{0.7-0.8}{\sqrt{0.001}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-3.16)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-3.16) & =1-P(Z<-3.16) \\  & =1-Φ(-3.16).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-3.16)=0.0008.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =1-Φ(-3.16) \\  & =1-0.0008 \\  & =0.9992.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499566 :question/id #uuid "fc097a1b-4231-5bd2-b0eb-22f13d9b5569" :question/math-academy-id "q-143501" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064315 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "327e406f-f432-5db4-a79f-80195c02cc96" :knowledge-point/title "Using the CLT With a Population Whose Probability Distribution Is Continuous"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ab06347-a361-5e1d-be5c-dba35197e7c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1314" :db/id 17592186498820} {:answer/id #uuid "407cfaea-b447-5e42-a30b-1d2cd829a0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1093" :db/id 17592186498878} {:answer/id #uuid "a63f4b53-b75c-5bc8-8070-14f83b495105" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.2641" :db/id 17592186499094} {:answer/id #uuid "c4ceab23-5225-54d0-8603-cea96aaf2b24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1562" :db/id 17592186499163} {:answer/id #uuid "cc3a2118-ab8a-5090-8fc2-f6b42b9b4b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1112" :db/id 17592186499180}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2ab06347-a361-5e1d-be5c-dba35197e7c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1314" :db/id 17592186498820} :answer-field/id #uuid "72921358-da9c-5842-82f0-b8015a6f19c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186499372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population with probability density function

\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2) & =Φ(-1.12) \\  & =0.1314.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 359} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065189 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065393 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a *normal* population $N(\mu,\sigma^2),$ then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with the following sampling distribution:

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i \sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

However, what if the sample were drawn from a population that is not normally distributed? What can we say about the sampling distribution of the sample mean in this case?

Ultimately, the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ depends on the population distribution. Unfortunately, no general result exists that tells us how $\overline{X}$ is distributed for an arbitrary population distribution. 

However, an important result, known as the **central limit theorem,** tells us that when the sample size $n$ is large, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is approximately normally distributed. Moreover, the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ for large $n$ *does not depend on the population distribution!* 

Let's state the theorem formally:

*Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as* 

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

In other words, as the sample size increases, the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal. 

Let's note a few points:

- We assume that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed, and they can have *any* probability distribution (discrete or continuous).

- The theorem is valid for *sufficiently large* $n.$ Typically, $n \geq 30$ is assumed to be sufficiently large, although this does vary. In general, the larger, the better!

- The CLT assumes that $\mu$ and $\sigma$ both exist. Surprisingly, this is not true for every probability distribution (e.g. the Cauchy distribution).

The central limit theorem is a crucial result in statistics and has far-reaching implications. Let's build some intuition around it." :tutorial/id #uuid "370857ad-bdaf-5274-993a-aeebe34e1c01" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5490 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Consider a random variable $X$ that follows a binomial distribution, where

$$
X \sim B(20,0.1).
$$

In this case, the parameters are $m=20$ and $p=0.1.$ Let's start by calculating the mean and the variance of $X\mathbin{:}$

- It can be shown that the mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & =mp \\  & =20\cdot 0.1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- It can also be shown that the variance $\sigma^2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =mp(1-p) \\  & =20\cdot 0.1\cdot 0.9 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

The probability mass function of our (discrete) binomial random variable for the first few values of $x$ is shown below.

![](images/44/4464e1b63865fad1e65a32657c5c3df8b227bfc53d22340219deeca63692bfbf.png)

To understand the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ for this population, suppose we conduct the following experiment:

1\. Pick a value for the sample size $n.$

2\. Using a computer, randomly generate $1\,000$ samples of size $n$ drawn from our binomial population.

3\. Calculate the sample mean for each sample.

4\. Create a histogram of the sample means to visualize the approximate sampling distribution.

5\. Repeat this process for increasing values of $n.$

Let's follow this procedure for samples sizes of $2,4$ and $9\mathbin{:}$

- First, let's consider samples of size $n=2.$ In this case

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}]=2, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \dfrac{1.8}{2} = 0.9.
$$

 
Next, generating $1\,000$ samples of size $n=2$ and calculating the corresponding sample mean for each sample, we can visualize the resulting distribution using a histogram similar to the one shown below.

![](images/25/25c6c71d77e8bd9bd3167fccaf8c8b3288d40fd552619960ae4bb925788f6eff.png)

Notice that since the sample size is very small, the distribution of the sample mean does not closely resemble the corresponding normal distribution.

- Next, we consider samples of size $n=4.$ In this case

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}]=2, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \dfrac{1.8}{4} = 0.45.
$$

 
Generating $1\,000$ samples of size $n=4,$ calculating the corresponding sample mean for each sample, and then drawing our histogram, we'll get something similar to the one shown below.

![](images/cd/cd3d94f0152c3bce6c380a6d4f463333a552241643232c5622b1d2c78bb23436.png)

Notice that the distribution of the sample mean is much closer to the corresponding normal distribution than the $n=2$ case.

- Finally, we consider samples of size $n=9.$ In this case

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}]=2, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \dfrac{1.8}{9} = 0.2.
$$

 
Generating $1\,000$ samples of size $n=9,$ calculating the sample mean for each sample, and then drawing our histogram, we'll get something similar to the one shown below.

![](images/ab/abdda642945400eeb8803abfa4775af59ad5815435a8367f56dc6be6d0c643ec.png)

Notice that the distribution of the sample mean is much closer to the corresponding normal distribution compared to the $n=2$ and $n=4$ cases.

As the sample size $n$ increases, the histograms become more and more similar to their corresponding normal distribution, and the standard error of the sample mean becomes smaller and smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "dc53f647-2007-5af6-865f-b0a2c9a4ae88" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6302 :tutorial/title "Visualizing the Convergence of the Sampling Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "c7a0a75b-0dee-5f38-ac9d-a2d9da89612d" :step/math-academy-id 38151 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065190}} {:db/id 17592186065216 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065399 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma,$ then for sufficiently large $n,$ 

$$
\overline{X}\approx N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We can rewrite the central limit in several different ways. Let's list some of the most common.

- One way of restating the central limit theorem is as follows:

$$
\overline{X} - \mu\approx N\!\left(0,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

This statement tells us that the deviation of $\overline{X}$ from the mean $\mu$ is (approximately) normally distributed with a mean of zero and a variance that's the same as $\overline{X}.$

- We can also write the central limit theorem as

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\approx N\!\left(0,1\right).
$$

This statement tells us that $z$-scoring the sample mean gives a random variable that (approximately) follows a standard normal distribution.

- Earlier, we saw that

$$
n\overline{X} \approx N\!\left(n\mu,n\sigma^2\right).
$$

If we $z$-score this result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{n\overset{―}{X}-n\mu }{\sqrt{n{\sigma }^{2}}} & =\frac{n(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )}{\sqrt{n}\sigma } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{n}(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )}{\sigma }\end{aligned}
$$

which means that we can express the central limit theorem in the following form:

$$
\dfrac{\sqrt{n}(\overline{X} - \mu) }{\sigma} \approx N(0,1)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f94f1f8-e852-58cb-989f-808d2596e3de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6305 :tutorial/title "Equivalent Forms of the Central Limit Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "c356540f-d332-5b32-9936-d8a253b82705" :step/math-academy-id 38174} {:db/id 17592186065217 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065400 :tutorial/content "Let's assume that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem states that, for sufficiently large $n,$ 

$$

$$

An important consequence of the central limit theorem is that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, then

$$
X =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).
$$

In other words, a sum of I.I.D random variables is approximately normally distributed. 

 To see why, note that if 

$$
\overline{X}  = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx N\!\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

 then the random variable

$$
X = n\overline{X} = \underbrace{\overline{X} + \overline{X}  + \cdots + \overline{X}}_{n\,\textrm{times}}
$$

 is a sum of $n$ (approximately) normally distributed random variables and is therefore normally distributed. Therefore, the mean and variance of $X$ are given by

$$
\textrm E[X] = n\cdot \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n^2\cdot \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = n\sigma^2.
$$

 Writing this in terms of $\overline{X},$ we have

$$
n\overline{X} \approx N\!\left(n\mu,n\sigma^2\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9393359e-791b-52d7-87c7-b7778d5fb7f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6515 :tutorial/title "Sums of I.I.D. In other words, as the sample size increases, the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal. 

Let's note a few points:

- We assume that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed, and they can have *any* probability distribution (discrete or continuous).

- The theorem is valid for *sufficiently large* $n.$ Typically, $n \geq 30$ is assumed to be sufficiently large, although this does vary. In general, the larger, the better!

- The CLT assumes that $\mu$ and $\sigma$ both exist. Surprisingly, this is not true for every probability distribution (e.g. the Cauchy distribution).

The central limit theorem is a crucial result in statistics and has far-reaching implications. :tutorial/content "Let's assume that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem states that, for sufficiently large $n,$ 

$$
\overline{X}\approx N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

An important consequence of the central limit theorem is that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, then

$$
X =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).
$$

In other words, a sum of I.I.D random variables is approximately normally distributed. 

 To see why, note that if 

$$
\overline{X}  = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx N\!\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

 then the random variable

$$
X = n\overline{X} = \underbrace{\overline{X} + \overline{X}  + \cdots + \overline{X}}_{n\,\textrm{times}}
$$

 is a sum of $n$ (approximately) normally distributed random variables and is therefore normally distributed. Therefore, the mean and variance of $X$ are given by

$$
\textrm E[X] = n\cdot \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n^2\cdot \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = n\sigma^2.
$$

 Writing this in terms of $\overline{X},$ we have

$$
n\overline{X} \approx N\!\left(n\mu,n\sigma^2\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9393359e-791b-52d7-87c7-b7778d5fb7f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6515 :tutorial/title "Sums of I.I.D. $$
\overline{X}\approx N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We can rewrite the central limit in several different ways. Let's list some of the most common.

- One way of restating the central limit theorem is as follows:

$$
\overline{X} - \mu\approx N\!\left(0,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

This statement tells us that the deviation of $\overline{X}$ from the mean $\mu$ is (approximately) normally distributed with a mean of zero and a variance that's the same as $\overline{X}.$

- We can also write the central limit theorem as

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\approx N\!\left(0,1\right).
$$

This statement tells us that $z$-scoring the sample mean gives a random variable that (approximately) follows a standard normal distribution.

- Earlier, we saw that

$$
n\overline{X} \approx N\!\left(n\mu,n\sigma^2\right).
$$

If we $z$-score this result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{n\overset{―}{X}-n\mu }{\sqrt{n{\sigma }^{2}}} & =\frac{n(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )}{\sqrt{n}\sigma } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{n}(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )}{\sigma }\end{aligned}
$$

which means that we can express the central limit theorem in the following form:

$$
\dfrac{\sqrt{n}(\overline{X} - \mu) }{\sigma} \approx N(0,1)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f94f1f8-e852-58cb-989f-808d2596e3de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6305 :tutorial/title "Equivalent Forms of the Central Limit Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "c356540f-d332-5b32-9936-d8a253b82705" :step/math-academy-id 38174} {:db/id 17592186065399 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma,$ then for sufficiently large $n,$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{84}$ be a random sample of size $n=84$ from a population with the probability mass function given above.  Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $1.75.$

*Hint: Two tables of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9861\,$ | $\,0.9864\,$ | $\,0.9868\,$ | $\,0.9871\,$ | $\,0.9875\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=84,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.3+3\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0+0.3+0.6+0.6 \\  & =1.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.2)-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =(0+0.3+1.2+1.8)-2.25 \\  & =1.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.5,\frac{1.05}{84}) \\  & ∼N(1.5,0.0125).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<1.75).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.75) & ≈P(Z<\frac{1.75-1.5}{\sqrt{0.0125}}) \\  & =P(Z<2.24) \\  & =Φ(2.24).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(2.24)=0.9875.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.75.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.5,\frac{0.75}{25}) \\  & ∼N(2.5,0.03).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2.4<\overset{―}{X}<2.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.4<\overset{―}{X}<2.7) & =P(\frac{2.4-2.5}{\sqrt{0.03}}<Z<\frac{2.7-2.5}{\sqrt{0.03}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.58<Z<1.15) \\  & =P(Z<1.15)-P(Z<-0.58) \\  & =Φ(1.15)-Φ(-0.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.15) & =0.8749, \\ Φ(-0.58) & =0.2810.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.4<\overset{―}{X}<2.7) & =Φ(1.15)-Φ(-0.58) \\  & =0.8749-0.2810 \\  & =0.5939.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "852d10ee-a259-5496-9a87-055b498422f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441387}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d98536d-9bc1-568b-8d9e-71026dbda70a" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{32}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2} \\  & =1.5,\end{aligned}

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15.$

$$

$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>1.29) & =1-P(Z<1.29) \\  & =1-Φ(1.29).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(1.29)=0.9015.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =1-Φ(1.29) \\  & =1-0.9015 \\  & =0.0985.\end{aligned}

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=65,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.1+(-6)\cdot 0.4+(-4)\cdot 0.4+(-2)\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.8-2.4-1.6-0.2 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.1+(-6)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-5)^{2} \\  & =(6.4+14.4+6.4+0.4)-25 \\  & =2.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{2.6}{65}) \\  & ∼N(-5,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.9-(-5)}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.5) \\  & =Φ(0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{116}$ be a random sample of size $n=116$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $3$ and $5.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=116,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.6+5\cdot 0.1+10\cdot 0.2+15\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+0.5+2+1.5 \\  & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.6+{5}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{10}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{15}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{4}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.5+20+22.5)-16 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(4,\frac{29}{116}) \\  & ∼N(4,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5) & ≈P(\frac{3-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{5-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-2<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5)=Φ(2)-Φ(-2).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca0175c6-365a-5159-8b93-9102cbcb7847" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484345}} {:db/id 17592186484352 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484253 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "40ba174f-6f4c-59fc-b3cb-137e1297aa50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5429" :db/id 17592186483689} {:answer/id #uuid "554630d6-0001-5d34-98b7-ae518e793543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6112" :db/id 17592186483721} {:answer/id #uuid "82de29c2-442b-50b3-b8a2-f2cef0536930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5678" :db/id 17592186483833} {:answer/id #uuid "da0abab7-344b-5db3-b96e-606236a85502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6601" :db/id 17592186484000} {:answer/id #uuid "e46f85da-0699-50b2-9c52-f46103534b9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7123" :db/id 17592186484019}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186484000} :answer-field/id #uuid "aa4e5556-e66f-5ee1-bddc-c98cca0920b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186484169}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "95a41c31-9a32-5733-b64d-135e1d1b45d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-143502" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n=30$ from a population with probability density function

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d0097ec8-75db-516a-b1e4-c90a66598b83" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484332}}] :activity/title "The Central Limit Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186483567} {:db/id 17592186484336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484259 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d40bd2c-dcd9-59ac-b0e2-c7d52d41a210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1539" :db/id 17592186483616} {:answer/id #uuid "1f98fc2b-1e1b-5ec3-bfa8-3c6f3b84ee29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1587" :db/id 17592186483618} {:answer/id #uuid "2d0c2446-935e-58d5-bb0b-b9f993444007" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1814" :db/id 17592186483643} {:answer/id #uuid "91359df8-d289-5d02-8538-3a34ade27caa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2061" :db/id 17592186483868} {:answer/id #uuid "b80bbc72-56db-5e70-9204-c74bdefa7b84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2119" :db/id 17592186483936}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186483618} :answer-field/id #uuid "cd48dcdf-ec5c-553b-93df-1ad0ce12e474" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186484179}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2c4c6dc-06db-5c59-88cb-4cad1074fe93" :question/math-academy-id "q-143480" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{121}$ be a random sample of size $n=121$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =300$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =55.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $295.$

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d0097ec8-75db-516a-b1e4-c90a66598b83" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484332}} {:db/id 17592186484345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484262 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e0e9d16-85d3-5733-86dd-b370bb650371" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1)" :db/id 17592186483617} {:answer/id #uuid "2218abf4-e023-5af3-b0eb-30e08e6ee534" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1)" :db/id 17592186483627} {:answer/id #uuid "7a9ebc6d-26da-5439-8344-0e789ccaddc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.5)" :db/id 17592186483815} {:answer/id #uuid "c7238fb6-2845-5bcb-8fb3-76e79b105b2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.2)" :db/id 17592186483960} {:answer/id #uuid "d30411eb-c7c7-50c0-be48-8d31e7a05041" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.5)" :db/id 17592186483990}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186483990} :answer-field/id #uuid "3fbc75be-8e9b-55b7-b598-a4421edd592d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186484109}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a7a75f10-4331-5d53-8955-dd0d91fe7458" :question/math-academy-id "q-143514" :question/problem "| $x$ | $-8$ | $-6$ | $-4$ | $-2$ |

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=80,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-1\cdot 0.3+0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.3+0+0.1+0.3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-1)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(0.3+0+0.1+0.4)-0 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{0.8}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1) & ≈P(Z>\frac{0.1-0}{\sqrt{0.01}}) \\  & =P(Z>1) \\  & =1-Φ(1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1)=1-Φ(1).

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=108,\,\mu =20,\,\sigma =90.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(20,\frac{{90}^{2}}{108}) \\  & ∼N(20,75).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5) & =P(-5<\overset{―}{X}<5) \\  & =P(\frac{-5-20}{\sqrt{75}}<Z<\frac{5-20}{\sqrt{75}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}<Z<-\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.89<Z<-1.73) \\  & =P(Z<-1.73)-P(Z<-2.89) \\  & =Φ(-1.73)-Φ(-2.89).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.89)=0.0019, \\ Φ(-1.73)=0.0418.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<5) & =Φ(-1.73)-Φ(-2.89) \\  & =0.0418-0.0019 \\  & =0.0399.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{0.6}{20}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.03).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<\overset{―}{X}<0.2) & =P(\frac{0-0}{\sqrt{0.03}}<Z<\frac{0.2-0}{\sqrt{0.03}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.15) \\  & =P(Z<1.15)-P(Z<0) \\  & =Φ(1.15)-Φ(0).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Φ(1.15)=0.8749,
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution, $Φ(0)=0.5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<\overset{―}{X}<0.2) & =Φ(1.15)-Φ(0) \\  & =0.8749-0.5 \\  & =0.3749\end{aligned}

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=126,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =84.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{84}^{2}}{126}) \\  & ∼N(5,56).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<3.5) \\  & =1-P(-3.5<\overset{―}{X}<3.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-3.5-5}{\sqrt{56}}<Z<\frac{3.5-5}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & ≈1-P(-1.14<Z<-0.20) \\  & =1-(P(Z<-0.20)-P(Z<-1.14)) \\  & =1+Φ(-1.14)-Φ(-0.20).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.14)=0.1271, \\ Φ(-0.20)=0.4207.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>3.5) & =1+Φ(-1.14)-Φ(-0.20) \\  & =1+0.1271-0.4207 \\  & =0.7064.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fe908c41-a001-5efb-a259-66897deb7943" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507575}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2259ef19-beca-5d96-bf66-94592e4f2902" :answer/type {:db/id Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{101}$ be a random sample of size $n=101$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $2.5$ and $3.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=101,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.7+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+1.4+0.4+0.8 \\  & =2.6,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{2.6}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.8+1.6+6.4)-6.76 \\  & =4.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.6,\frac{4.04}{101}) \\  & ∼N(2.6,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3) & ≈P(\frac{2.5-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}<Z<\frac{3-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(-0.5<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3)=Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "01fa0c05-b1ae-5422-bc1f-94b53ddae4b0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519636}} {:db/id 17592186519630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186427626 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0898778a-e9f2-5272-b446-decc5e417146" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0838" :db/id 17592186427595} {:answer/id #uuid "25c6b726-fd80-5fc4-87c6-1f8caae104bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0594" :db/id 17592186427596} {:answer/id #uuid "8d73d5cd-e782-589d-9c6e-6fdab9305338" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0681" :db/id 17592186427605} {:answer/id #uuid "b28f985b-b01a-5b8d-9f24-7716132f4a1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0606" :db/id 17592186427608} {:answer/id #uuid "f762fc2b-ccb2-5adb-bbf3-061f3f8eede8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0708" :db/id 17592186427617}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427617} :answer-field/id #uuid "31024a23-6322-5d05-b371-cb1388d4cd05" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9c900f37-300a-5da2-a8b6-a15d4ba96d8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-143524" :question/problem "| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ | $10$ | $20$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
