In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=65,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.1+(-6)\cdot 0.4+(-4)\cdot 0.4+(-2)\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.8-2.4-1.6-0.2 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.1+(-6)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-5)^{2} \\  & =(6.4+14.4+6.4+0.4)-25 \\  & =2.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{2.6}{65}) \\  & ∼N(-5,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.9-(-5)}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.5) \\  & =Φ(0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9f415f4c-b363-5f1a-bfb2-ee6ede551dd6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519659}} {:db/id 17592186519659 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064506 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9c5bf3b4-ed42-5eb0-ad5a-8ac0efb22629" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0985" :db/id 17592186061267} {:answer/id #uuid "d5d4ec58-1e94-5b26-987f-f90f2a1f6bca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1170" :db/id 17592186061268} {:answer/id #uuid "f23c9b14-6f45-5ea6-87c4-ad37be574c3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1003" :db/id 17592186061269} {:answer/id #uuid "030e07aa-4ecb-5bb4-bc80-5f5cbb2506a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0853" :db/id 17592186061270} {:answer/id #uuid "090ff02b-aeb9-5a1d-b36c-5054afc4b296" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1210" :db/id 17592186061271}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186061267} :answer-field/id #uuid "5cc45ee8-b0e6-5e8f-9a87-c2295533ec34" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186061266}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6df49040-5dbb-5927-a6aa-8f742c1a6cc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-143503" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}$ be a random sample of size $n=25$ from a population with probability density function

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{65}$ be a random sample of size $n=65$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $-4.9.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=65,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.1+(-6)\cdot 0.4+(-4)\cdot 0.4+(-2)\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.8-2.4-1.6-0.2 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.1+(-6)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-5)^{2} \\  & =(6.4+14.4+6.4+0.4)-25 \\  & =2.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{2.6}{65}) \\  & ∼N(-5,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.9-(-5)}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.5) \\  & =Φ(0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9)=Φ(0.5).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6267897a-1940-5884-b9bb-bc89d40bba6c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519630}} {:db/id 17592186519630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186427626 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0898778a-e9f2-5272-b446-decc5e417146" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0838" :db/id 17592186427595} {:answer/id #uuid "25c6b726-fd80-5fc4-87c6-1f8caae104bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0594" :db/id 17592186427596} {:answer/id #uuid "8d73d5cd-e782-589d-9c6e-6fdab9305338" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0681" :db/id 17592186427605} {:answer/id #uuid "b28f985b-b01a-5b8d-9f24-7716132f4a1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0606" :db/id 17592186427608} {:answer/id #uuid "f762fc2b-ccb2-5adb-bbf3-061f3f8eede8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0708" :db/id 17592186427617}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427617} :answer-field/id #uuid "31024a23-6322-5d05-b371-cb1388d4cd05" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9c900f37-300a-5da2-a8b6-a15d4ba96d8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-143524" :question/problem "| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ | $10$ | $20$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

- the sample size is 

$$
n=100,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.47)=0.0708.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<7) & =Φ(-1.47) \\  & =0.0708.\end{aligned}

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15,$ calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$

*Hint: Assume that the sample size is sufficiently large for the central limit theorem to be applied. A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ | $\,0.8810\,$ | $\,0.8830\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{32}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2} \\  & =1.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.5,\frac{0.15}{25}) \\  & ∼N(1.5,0.006).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =P(Z>\frac{1.6-1.5}{\sqrt{0.006}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.29)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>1.29) & =1-P(Z<1.29) \\  & =1-Φ(1.29).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(1.29)=0.9015.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =1-Φ(1.29) \\  & =1-0.9015 \\  & =0.0985.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b0db31b1-c295-5a9f-ba82-4934d9313b2e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519609}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186522819} :activity/id #uuid "8986df93-470d-5192-a0f6-95b5da54c771" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049014 :topic/id #uuid "d3c3f991-d569-536f-97fd-468824f21297" :topic/math-academy-id 359} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186522817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186519526 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "287f4c69-8bd4-5569-9333-3f219db98ca1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1)-Φ(-1.5)" :db/id 17592186519056} {:answer/id #uuid "38fb3acb-053d-552f-a825-7ddc2d36cb45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(2)-Φ(1)" :db/id 17592186519079} {:answer/id #uuid "728b0f84-6442-5c3f-96b2-7e64f3c56829" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1.5)-Φ(-1.5)" :db/id 17592186519168} {:answer/id #uuid "798138a1-9c96-5b5d-9bc0-6edae93977b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5)" :db/id 17592186519182} {:answer/id #uuid "f67a96ba-09f5-59df-948a-4c2d70d715d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1)-Φ(-1)" :db/id 17592186519397}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186519182} :answer-field/id #uuid "64ef3aa0-5b31-5f1c-8e8c-420a16ef0aa2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186519447}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1e9c32a8-c5ef-5dca-8493-0a63cb017fc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-143512" :question/problem "| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=101,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.7+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+1.4+0.4+0.8 \\  & =2.6,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{2.6}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.8+1.6+6.4)-6.76 \\  & =4.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.6,\frac{4.04}{101}) \\  & ∼N(2.6,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3) & ≈P(\frac{2.5-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}<Z<\frac{3-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(-0.5<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

$$

$$

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{101}$ be a random sample of size $n=101$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $2.5$ and $3.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=101,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.7+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+1.4+0.4+0.8 \\  & =2.6,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{2.6}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.8+1.6+6.4)-6.76 \\  & =4.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.6,\frac{4.04}{101}) \\  & ∼N(2.6,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3) & ≈P(\frac{2.5-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}<Z<\frac{3-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(-0.5<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3)=Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03b3cfb5-03c9-54cc-adb7-554c97f349a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186522878}} {:db/id 17592186522878 :step/content {:db/id 17592186522731 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "122e6ac5-9cff-55b6-b18d-000a481d0709" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-0.75)" :db/id 17592186522055} {:answer/id #uuid "2a41c234-f9c9-5382-8487-7886f440fe59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-0.5)" :db/id 17592186522115} {:answer/id #uuid "8465315b-a190-5203-b11a-3e21ec72ee2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-1.25)" :db/id 17592186522284} {:answer/id #uuid "a173100e-d855-5223-a3de-e706ed5de992" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-1)" :db/id 17592186522356} {:answer/id #uuid "a4cbe218-05ef-50ce-b350-172a085d5edd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-1.5)" :db/id 17592186522364}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186522284} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3d35207-52bf-5e87-8342-86fa07643744" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186522670}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "62924b2e-7117-58f6-a2b2-963583643766" :question/math-academy-id "q-143515" :question/problem "| $x$ | $-8$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $2$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=60,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.3+(-4)\cdot 0.3+(-2)\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-2.4-1.2-0.6+0.2 \\  & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-4)^{2} \\  & =(19.2+4.8+1.2+0.4)-16 \\  & =9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-4,\frac{9.6}{60}) \\  & ∼N(-4,0.16).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.5) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.5-(-4)}{\sqrt{0.16}}) \\  & =P(Z<-1.25) \\  & =Φ(-1.25).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.5)=Φ(-1.25).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cffb3e05-e1d3-55d2-9fb4-366dc20dfe0e"} {:db/id 17592186522894 :step/content {:db/id 17592186499537 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3315a5cb-452e-528e-8eb5-78dbc3e12104" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9992" :db/id 17592186498846} {:answer/id #uuid "6de957fe-2080-57db-b272-b3b2f6646ab1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8845" :db/id 17592186498974} {:answer/id #uuid "77e88625-4c75-5215-8f5a-0c85b4e5a671" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9123" :db/id 17592186498999} {:answer/id #uuid "a5f8b3c7-8fde-5c2f-927e-132d799da466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8976" :db/id 17592186499091} {:answer/id #uuid "f7306d02-503e-55d9-b966-b99018652bee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9576" :db/id 17592186499283}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498846} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d5ea7fd-d63e-51a1-9d3e-f96a0fcebecf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499337}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "cad4258a-bb8c-5f12-a390-574af230e1b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143509" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n=30$ from a population with probability density function

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03,$ calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5} \\  & =0.8,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0.8,\frac{0.03}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0.8,0.001).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =P(Z>\frac{0.7-0.8}{\sqrt{0.001}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-3.16)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-3.16) & =1-P(Z<-3.16) \\  & =1-Φ(-3.16).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-3.16)=0.0008.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =1-Φ(-3.16) \\  & =1-0.0008 \\  & =0.9992.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f80fbbff-d539-54c2-a972-4e6c9ba72aed" :step/next {:db/id 17592186522821}} {:db/id 17592186522821 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064507 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a341be9f-f5cb-56ef-a964-f9c027945b62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5352" :db/id 17592186061273} {:answer/id #uuid "d292bc3a-8208-5bf5-a235-4cb2c48daf77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5418" :db/id 17592186061274} {:answer/id #uuid "3c35e814-4cce-58ab-8005-ddcb9cd68208" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5286" :db/id 17592186061275} {:answer/id #uuid "57ac6be9-5847-5690-bf26-33234c5f0afe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5962" :db/id 17592186061276} {:answer/id #uuid "77c0132c-9add-590e-b595-23e65cc0a799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4778" :db/id 17592186061277}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186061275} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3c36985-e946-50fa-acb6-191dd6a15583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186061272}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7d145c65-2193-5d13-9b5d-a2fd49beb6b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143510" :question/problem "| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $2$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=30,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-2\cdot 0.3+(-1)\cdot 0.2+0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.4 \\  & =-0.6-0.2+0+0.8 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-2)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.2+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.4)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(1.2+0.2+0+1.6)-0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{3}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.2) & =P(\overset{―}{X}<-0.2)+P(\overset{―}{X}>0.2) \\  & ≈P(Z<\frac{-0.2-0}{\sqrt{0.1}})+P(Z>\frac{0.2-0}{\sqrt{0.1}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.63)+P(Z>0.63) \\  & =P(Z<-0.63)+1-P(Z<0.63) \\  & =1+Φ(-0.63)-Φ(0.63).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.63)=0.2643.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\,Φ(0.63)=1-Φ(-0.63).

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.2) & =1+Φ(-0.63)-Φ(0.63) \\  & =2Φ(-0.63) \\  & =2\cdot 0.2643 \\  & =0.5286.\end{aligned}

right triangle whose legs are both equal to $1,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a6d1e8bd928fe666859f7101be65819af5f16fe81df3900941650d279eecd496.png)

By considering either of the $45^\circ$ angles in this triangle, we find that

$$
\eqalign{
	\sin 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
	\cos 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{adj.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
	\tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{adj.}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1. 
}
$$

Isosceles right triangles are very common, so the values above occur a lot in trigonometry. It's a good idea to remember them." :tutorial/id #uuid "43cdd368-7207-5d18-8f22-5e384ebbc118" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2457 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "76d3dfad-1625-5612-88e9-44f6df730e85" :step/math-academy-id 453556 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084332}} {:db/id 17592186084332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083364 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082956 :question/id #uuid "58cfd10d-afd2-5678-a38a-e0fbc0221076" :question/math-academy-id "e-3272"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a622bad-6820-5e34-a347-890709103bc0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048121} {:db/id 17592186049915}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083629} {:db/id 17592186083644} {:db/id 17592186083829} {:db/id 17592186527953} {:db/id 17592186527959}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions With 45 Degree Angles"} :step/id #uuid "2f3823b3-f0cb-5b53-ab96-dc48e9c09690" :step/math-academy-id 453557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084333}} {:db/id 17592186084333 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084413 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle whose shortest leg has a length equal to $1,$ shown below.

![](images/67/679ce670484e57ba699030de4cf6d9ba52a5d6910d22b4beb2ad5d4e8ac4e0e0.png)

Now, we can calculate some trigonometric ratios without a calculator. Let's start with the $30^\circ$-angle. By the definition of sine, cosine, and tangent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{adj.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{adj.}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, by considering the $60^\circ$-angle, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{adj.}}{\text{hyp.}}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡{60}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opp.}}{\text{adj.}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}=\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d87688da-9a24-5f3e-9160-de9562217a11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2460 :tutorial/title "Trigonometric Ratios for 30-60-90 Triangles"} :step/id #uuid "60a44c52-c126-53ea-b949-1b44b8614b1c" :step/math-academy-id 453561 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084334}} {:db/id 17592186084334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083365 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082957 :question/id #uuid "b593adba-7766-5cce-b607-ae3f2ad24970" :question/math-academy-id "e-3275"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "462eeb28-d618-5c29-8568-186d63645f99" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048737}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083639} {:db/id 17592186083645} {:db/id 17592186083828} {:db/id 17592186527930} {:db/id 17592186527931}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions With 30 and 60 Degree Angles"} :step/id #uuid "bf2f2513-8031-5383-8527-049ce8fb6c88" :step/math-academy-id 453562 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084335}} {:db/id 17592186084335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084414 :tutorial/content "The values of the trigonometric ratios for $0^\circ$ angles are the following:

| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |
| $\cos \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $1$ |
| $\tan \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |

Why is this so? If we look at the right triangle below, we can imagine making the angle $\theta$ smaller by moving the vertex $C$ towards $A.$ 

![](images/9b/9bee0468c989067e12648e538788bcd8c7fb879e112000a942a1ee6f41d95c7d.png)

As the angle $\theta$ gets closer and closer to zero, the opposite side $AC$ also approaches zero. Also, the hypotenuse $BC$ and the adjacent side $AB$ become nearly the same length.

So, as $\theta$ approaches zero (which we can write as $\theta \rightarrow 0^\circ$) we have

$$
AC \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AB.
$$

 

Therefore, when $\theta = 0^\circ$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{BC}=0, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AB}{BC}=1, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{AB}=0.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d78c0611-a7ea-5bc0-830b-fb04311281da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2461 :tutorial/title "Special Values of the Zero Degree Angle"} :step/id #uuid "34c6a603-c08d-5f28-95f6-03d5cf07c17e" :step/math-academy-id 453566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084336}} {:db/id 17592186084336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083366 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082958 :question/id #uuid "0959222f-542e-5cea-b10a-fa3872c93571" :question/math-academy-id "e-3278"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "59c7be47-27c1-5300-8fd9-0e7d39e977d9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083630} {:db/id 17592186083652} {:db/id 17592186527940} {:db/id 17592186527990}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions With 0 Degree Angles"} :step/id #uuid "efdf3091-c5e4-5290-a97f-f9040128b097" :step/math-academy-id 453567 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084337}} {:db/id 17592186084337 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084415 :tutorial/content "The values of the trigonometric ratios for $90^\circ$ angles are the following:

| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin \left(90^\circ\right)$ | $1$ |
| $\cos \left(90^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |
| $\tan \left(90^\circ\right)$ | Undefined |

To understand where the values come from, this time, we can imagine increasing the value of the angle $\theta$ by moving the vertex $B$ towards $A.$ 

![](images/53/53d538ce2eca6af579b556bdac72d9fba9ba5e817de38ff73236a312b401c4cf.png)

As $B$ moves towards $A,$ the adjacent side $AB$ gets very close to zero, and the angle $\theta$ gets very close to $90^\circ.$ Also, the hypotenuse $BC$ and the opposite side $AC$ become nearly the same length.

So, as $\theta$ approaches $90^\circ$ (which we can write as $\theta \rightarrow 90^\circ$) we have

$$
AB \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AC.
$$

 

Therefore, when $\theta = 90^\circ,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{BC}=1, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AB}{BC}=0, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({90}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{AC}{0}=\text{undefined.}\end{aligned}

| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |
| $\cos \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $1$ |
| $\tan \left(0^\circ\right)$ | $0$ |

Why is this so? If we look at the right triangle below, we can imagine making the angle $\theta$ smaller by moving the vertex $C$ towards $A.$ 

![](images/9b/9bee0468c989067e12648e538788bcd8c7fb879e112000a942a1ee6f41d95c7d.png)

As the angle $\theta$ gets closer and closer to zero, the opposite side $AC$ also approaches zero. Also, the hypotenuse $BC$ and the adjacent side $AB$ become nearly the same length.

So, as $\theta$ approaches zero (which we can write as $\theta \rightarrow 0^\circ$) we have

$$
AC \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AB.
$$

 

Therefore, when $\theta = 0^\circ$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{BC}=0, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AB}{BC}=1, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({0}^{∘}) & =\frac{AC}{AB}=0.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d78c0611-a7ea-5bc0-830b-fb04311281da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2461 :tutorial/title "Special Values of the Zero Degree Angle"} :step/id #uuid "34c6a603-c08d-5f28-95f6-03d5cf07c17e" :step/math-academy-id 453566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084336}} {:db/id 17592186084414 :tutorial/content "The values of the trigonometric ratios for $0^\circ$ angles are the following:

Find the line of the form $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, how much will the spring stretch if we use an $8$-ounce mass, assuming that the trend continues?  

*Hint: You can use the fact that* 
![](images/40/400621e90f0419646dcd9e2b2e1bc31bc3cc280bef2be6c3d330c8b69308429c.png)

$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X^T} X )^{-1}$ and $X^T \mathbf{y}$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}23 & -6 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 38.2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.04 \\ 0.82\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y = 0.04+ 0.82x.$

Finally, to predict how much the spring will stretch if an $8$-ounce mass is hung from it,  we substitute $x=8$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.04+0.82(8) \\  & =6.6\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, according to the model, if an $8$ ounce mass is hung on the spring, the spring will stretch $6.6$ inches.

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A biologist has recorded data on a pine tree's age (in years) and height (in feet). This data is shown below. 

| Age $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Height $(y)$ | $1.2$ | $2.5$ | $3.6$ | $4.5$ |

Find the line of the form $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ that best fits the data above. According to the model, what will be the tree's height after $8$ years, assuming the trend continues?

*Hint: You can use the fact that*

$$
({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}15 & -5 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,{X}^{T}y=\begin{bmatrix}11.8 \\ 35\end{bmatrix},
$$

*where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector.*" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\hat{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1}\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1.2 \\ 2.5 \\ 3.6 \\ 4.5\end{bmatrix}}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\hat{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\hat{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}15 & -5 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}11.8 \\ 35\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 1.1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=0.2+1.1x.$

Finally, to predict the  height after $8$ years, we substitute $x=8$ into the equation of the line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.2+1.1(8) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, according to the model, the height of a pine tree that is $8$ years old will be $9$ feet. 

**Note**: Since we're extrapolating ($x=8$ is not within the range of the original set of $x$-values), our result *may* be unreliable."} {:db/id 17592186134362 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186134703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135062 :tutorial/content "Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1} &=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1} &=15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 100 \\ 1 & 110 \\ 1 & 120 \\ 1 & 130\end{bmatrix}
$$

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0.1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "49c9c3ab-40d7-5e87-934c-1c3fcd16b330" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3652 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0ac1d0c2-c862-5d00-b1e2-ce846fd9a9e9" :step/math-academy-id "af2c310b-8cc3-5365-a974-d47b29df8d67" :step/math-academy-id 37273 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134704}} {:db/id 17592186134888 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135142 :tutorial/content "Given a dataset of paired numerical observations $(x,y)$ and the corresponding linear regression model $\widehat{y} =f(x),$ the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-f(x) \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value. The residuals for the data set we considered earlier are shown below.

![](images/51/515aaaeef2f85bb131564b92bdaef9ef514d05c8028ae85382d231565d490665.png)

In the past, you may have seen that  calculating a regression line typically means finding a line where the sum of the squared residuals 

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2
$$

is as small as possible. 

Using matrix notation, the sum of the squared residuals can be viewed as 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2 = \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.
$$

Therefore, the condition that the sum of the squared residuals is minimized is equivalent to minimizing $\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.$ This, in turn, is equivalent to minimizing $\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|.$ 

Therefore, the problem of minimizing the squared residuals is equivalent to solving the least squares problem for $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eeb5c2f5-02c9-5579-97b5-0393df974a32" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6149 :tutorial/title "Least-Squares vs. Minimizing the Sum of the Squared Residuals"} :step/id #uuid "7c7f5aff-10ef-54b2-b0e0-98663daec8b4" :step/math-academy-id 37328}] :activity/title "Linear Regression With Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134029} {:db/id 17592186134703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135062 :tutorial/content "Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1} &=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1} &=15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 100 \\ 1 & 110 \\ 1 & 120 \\ 1 & 130\end{bmatrix}
$$

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0.1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "49c9c3ab-40d7-5e87-934c-1c3fcd16b330" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3652 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0ac1d0c2-c862-5d00-b1e2-ce846fd9a9e9" :step/math-academy-id 20307 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134886}} {:db/id 17592186135062 :tutorial/content "Consider the following data set:

"15cd299b-c720-5bf6-814c-2bef2c839e48" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Linear Function"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of $f(x) = 3x - 4.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow the four steps below.

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y.$

$$
y = 3x-4
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y.$

$$
x = 3y-4
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-4 \\ x+4 & =3y \\ \frac{x+4}{3} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x).$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac {x + 4} {3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078952 :question/id #uuid "08199b98-8c5c-53ed-84bc-457ce60e72a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-4671"} {:db/id 17592186079194 :question/id #uuid "a0dde42b-b841-57e9-9d97-196dbf9cc047" :question/math-academy-id "q-7028"} {:db/id 17592186244293 :question/id #uuid "d2752a39-bb48-5c81-8615-612461ddd179" :question/math-academy-id "q-109452"} {:db/id 17592186244294 :question/id #uuid "71df5b12-f6f0-5746-8bd0-d9b3ade2a868" :question/math-academy-id "q-109454"} {:db/id 17592186287940 :question/id #uuid "fb16746d-2b42-5efd-96a5-654615adefbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-19229"} {:db/id 17592186290357 :question/id #uuid "33d5b021-749e-5278-a7fc-314d6c4a5b27" :question/math-academy-id "q-218691" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186078415 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "15cd299b-c720-5bf6-814c-2bef2c839e48" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Linear Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "572579ea-d0b8-5c37-9948-6c0dd4599a42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7-x}{3}" :db/id 17592186288636}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "572579ea-d0b8-5c37-9948-6c0dd4599a42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7-x}{3}" :db/id 17592186288636} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4ae0a04-689d-5eb4-b3f7-68ce08afe4c5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186290152}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "If $f(x)=-3x+7$, then ${f}^{-1}(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y=-3x+7
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x=-3y+7
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3y+7 \\ 3y & =7-x \\ y & =\frac{7-x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x)$:

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{7-x}{3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338766 :question/id #uuid "188246c0-0b15-5b72-9a2a-49a34c61ebb1" :question/math-academy-id "q-7024"} {:db/id 17592186338768 :question/id #uuid "cbd9a061-09c2-52d4-9a2f-d9bac924c805" :question/math-academy-id "q-7026"} {:db/id 17592186078416 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078286 :question/id #uuid "096eb672-5a54-565f-91d7-1072e4ce7136" :question/math-academy-id "e-3970"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "40a70c8d-dc8e-52bd-a679-ffd6d1940451" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048274}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078875 :question/id #uuid "571a8cba-cfd8-52fd-9a68-e6aa48c003a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-35231"} {:db/id 17592186078876 :question/id #uuid "40530ca3-e238-5640-94b0-1433afa01d34" :question/math-academy-id "q-35310"} {:db/id 17592186244296 :question/id #uuid "e01590f9-0d58-5312-9091-24a6c6697fc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-109477"} {:db/id 17592186320960 :question/id #uuid "abfc488e-a974-5dbc-b40c-2f281295336b" :question/math-academy-id "q-35217"} {:db/id 17592186321090 :question/id #uuid "fc796b8b-9fd5-5962-9783-c6ca55e2aaea" :question/math-academy-id "q-35323"} {:db/id 17592186335911 :question/id #uuid "e65d22ca-217f-59b9-8247-2dc7f4907a4c" :question/math-academy-id "q-66876"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Function With a Parameter"} {:db/id 17592186078286 :question/id #uuid "096eb672-5a54-565f-91d7-1072e4ce7136" :question/math-academy-id "e-3970" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078416 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "40a70c8d-dc8e-52bd-a679-ffd6d1940451" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Function With a Parameter"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = bx-5,$ where $b$ is a constant." :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow the four steps below.

$$

$$

:tutorial/content "Suppose that we have the function $f(x) = 3x-9,$ and we wish to find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x).$ There's a simple technique that often works. The technique is described below in four steps.

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y.$

$$
y = 3x-9
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y.$

$$
x = 3y-9
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-9 \\ x+9 & =3y \\ \frac{x+9}{3} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x).$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x+9}{3}
$$

To verify that this is really the inverse of $f,$ we can check that

$$
(f\circ f^{-1})(x) = (f^{-1}\circ f)(x) = x.
$$

First, we check that $(f^{-1}\circ f)(x)=x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}∘f)(x) & ={f}^{-1}(f(x)) \\  & =\frac{f(x)+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{(3x-9)+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{3x}{3} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

So we've shown that $(f^{-1}\circ f)(x) = x.$ Using the same technique, we can verify that $(f \circ f^{-1})(x)=x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘{f}^{-1})(x) & =f({f}^{-1}(x)) \\  & =3{f}^{-1}(x)-9 \\  & =3(\frac{x+9}{3})-9 \\  & =x+9-9 \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $(f\circ f^{-1})(x) = (f^{-1}\circ f)(x) = x,$ we can be sure that we've found the correct inverse function." :tutorial/id #uuid "ce8a9de8-7b0b-574a-a238-b0d5a9df195d" $$

Expanding the result along the $3$rd row, we get

$$

column) containing all zeros except for one entry. Then, we can use a Laplace expansion across that row (or column) to compute the determinant.

Let's demonstrate this method on the matrix $A$ below.

![](images/37/37946204f088b803603ba8adc3f93494e1d49fbe59d9c0925347675311b23e5d.svg)

Notice that we can make entries to the right of $a_{21}=1$ equal to zero using elementary *column* operations.

Since adding a multiple of one column to another column in a matrix does not change the value of its determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 8 & 14 & 17\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{2}:={C}_{2}+(-2){C}_{1} \\ {C}_{3}:={C}_{3}+(-3){C}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -5 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & -2 & -7\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the result along the $2$nd row, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -5 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & -2 & -7\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ -2 & -7\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(21-10) \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4a9a955-bf0a-5e47-973a-fa7d6e4191be" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3240 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5e9a2059-bb14-516d-a920-81186f0ec60f" :step/math-academy-id $$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}9 & 3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:={C}_{1}+(-3){C}_{2} \\ {C}_{3}:={C}_{3}+(-2){C}_{2} \\ {C}_{4}:={C}_{4}+{C}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 & 3 \\ 8 & -2 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the result along the $1$st row, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 & 3 \\ 8 & -2 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}4 & 5 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3|\begin{aligned}4 & 5 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}

"$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-2y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$
that represents the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

![](images/69/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

![](images/28/28d8900ae13325f715af9679fdeab6f26645e322ea0df016618826a5b3dee328.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f7b031de-59cf-53fe-be90-ac3711677246" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14570 :tutorial/title "Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "75bd8867-e725-5442-988b-67f110d201f4" :step/math-academy-id 588337 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167864}} {:db/id 17592186167864 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168006 :tutorial/content "Consider the following system of linear differential equations: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is ![](images/23/23616d197363a3fd8ad4689a0b1e547c7b1044e0929cfd96add65a26e940731f.svg) The vector ![](images/3e/3e434cc0b5ca5d288695abb58500e8f4ca6be0c0cf2ecb5200d03f5fbcf522c2.svg) is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](images/0f/0f7c56980abff1ad84ca69aa98730bca2988cf5430f181f69d191f1e3c28eff0.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/c9/c9d65d3792c7cced40b86834fbd66769daa714ed58ffcde025cb956763c2c670.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/98/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](images/61/6170eec4537e26afef2a794426b4f5231b0f4366c21b8860c332f1ec7573b96a.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/4f/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/28/28d8900ae13325f715af9679fdeab6f26645e322ea0df016618826a5b3dee328.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is ![](images/23/23616d197363a3fd8ad4689a0b1e547c7b1044e0929cfd96add65a26e940731f.svg) The vector ![](images/3e/3e434cc0b5ca5d288695abb58500e8f4ca6be0c0cf2ecb5200d03f5fbcf522c2.svg) is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](images/0f/0f7c56980abff1ad84ca69aa98730bca2988cf5430f181f69d191f1e3c28eff0.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/c9/c9d65d3792c7cced40b86834fbd66769daa714ed58ffcde025cb956763c2c670.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/98/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

![](images/61/6170eec4537e26afef2a794426b4f5231b0f4366c21b8860c332f1ec7573b96a.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

![](images/4f/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$
that represents the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

$$

${e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$
that represents the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

![](images/bc/bca60509a15e4d32d06d96c7cf5eac65a00b4e5cb72242152dd998b933209d7d.png)

Notice that

- the $x$-coordinate of $P$ coincides with the cosine of the angle $\theta,$ and

- the $y$-coordinate coincides with the sine of the angle $\theta.$

So, we have

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

![](images/3d/3d51ca417ba4f6f62bd3e5db5997842d0671f18920a7de70578146a49de79ec3.png)

To prove that $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta,$ let's examine the triangle that's formed by $\overline{OP}$ and the $x$-axis.

![](images/53/53d84bedcddcb484bc613a2f01e002afe16b614daa909ff744195bcc45464472.png)

  

Notice that: 

- The hypotenuse has length $1$ since it is a radius of the unit circle.

- The adjacent and opposite sides have lengths $x$ and $y,$ respectively.

Therefore, using the definitions of $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{1} = x, \qquad  \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{1} = y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e7838544-050b-5270-a16a-1679e3489a02" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2494 :tutorial/title "A Proof of the Unit Circle Property"} :step/id #uuid "8eef6615-9b8a-526e-9e9e-25070edfdad2" :step/math-academy-id 453948 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055709}} {:db/id 17592186055709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054717 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054515 :question/id #uuid "59696ddf-7aa4-561a-ac77-2216038294b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-3346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "568011de-56c0-55f4-95ec-0a426cbf6b67" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049794}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055185} {:db/id 17592186055446} {:db/id 17592186534980}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "9d51bf5e-1d13-5f8d-9fd6-c02b852842c4" :step/math-academy-id 453949 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055710}} {:db/id 17592186055710 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054718 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054517 :question/id #uuid "acb093c8-daa1-5eee-8678-e985fb9dfd71" :question/math-academy-id "e-3348"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8487f45b-a734-5375-abc2-5a347d49587c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050928} {:db/id 17592186051029}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055169} {:db/id 17592186055449} {:db/id 17592186534971} {:db/id 17592186534982}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "a21ae939-d688-510c-9d02-aec18c105046" :step/math-academy-id 453952 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055711}} {:db/id 17592186055711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055963 :tutorial/content "To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.
$$

To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

![](images/99/99b51d7d25a266dbfda7839be6bafc335b181ecd6dc74224fcb0557180f872aa.png)

For this particular triangle, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}.
$$

When we take $\sin\theta$ and divide it by $\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{y}{z}÷\frac{x}{z} \\  & =\frac{y}{z}\cdot \frac{z}{x} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot z}{x\cdot z} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot \cancel{z}}{x\cdot \cancel{z}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that $\tan\theta$ is well-defined.

Finally, since $\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta},$ it immediately follows that

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a17ae159-de66-547d-8e9a-2190b512ab3c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2725 :tutorial/title "The Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent"} :step/id #uuid "68735c4a-f7f9-5265-80af-ded103195f00" :step/math-academy-id 453955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055712}} {:db/id 17592186055712 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054719 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054516 :question/id #uuid "ee188df6-0ef5-5819-8fd9-77d48e8a5dce" :question/math-academy-id "e-3347"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a4297b-016b-5182-bf4f-cd2b64a23c41" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055186} {:db/id 17592186055448} {:db/id 17592186410425} {:db/id 17592186534990} {:db/id 17592186535064}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Central Angle Given a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "8e354a30-502e-5775-810b-ba93046cedfb" :step/math-academy-id 453956}] :activity/title "Properties of the Unit Circle in the First Quadrant" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054870} {:db/id 17592186055706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055959 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ in the first quadrant, measured in the usual way.

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.
$$

To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

![](images/99/99b51d7d25a266dbfda7839be6bafc335b181ecd6dc74224fcb0557180f872aa.png)

For this particular triangle, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}.
$$

When we take $\sin\theta$ and divide it by $\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{y}{z}÷\frac{x}{z} \\  & =\frac{y}{z}\cdot \frac{z}{x} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot z}{x\cdot z} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot \cancel{z}}{x\cdot \cancel{z}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that $\tan\theta$ is well-defined.

Finally, since $\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta},$ it immediately follows that

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a17ae159-de66-547d-8e9a-2190b512ab3c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2725 :tutorial/title "The Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent"} :step/id #uuid "68735c4a-f7f9-5265-80af-ded103195f00" :step/math-academy-id 453955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055712}} {:db/id 17592186055963 :tutorial/content "To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1810} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121054 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the shortest distance between the point $P(3,0,-2)$ and the plane $\Pi$ that is given by the equation 

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\langle 2 , 3 , 1 \rangle ) \cdot \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle = 0.
$$

 

First, note that $\mathbf{n} = \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle$ is a vector that's normal to the plane.

![](images/7b/7b2dfcd87c1f5e4e2c2b1a0b9a7f73899772e33e1020465b2b38d1b2de29a66c.png)

Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(2,3,1)$. Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,1⟩-⟨3,0,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,3,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The shortest distance $d$ from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane, as shown below.

![](images/26/26e494eef47db4dba3ac36dfa96c7e9a9d191321b22bb82874f3e74bbd7116ef.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 4+3\cdot 4+3\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4+12+6|}{\sqrt{16+16+4}} \\  & =\frac{|14|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is $\dfrac{7}{3}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "224c4104-9097-5a92-9c37-5d0fe22171a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3261 :question/math-academy-id "q-129166" :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,3,-6)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $-x+2y+2z=8.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-2$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2y+2z & =8 \\ -1(-2)+2(1)+2z & =8 \\ 2z & =4 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-2,1,2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,1,2⟩-⟨-2,3,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-1,2,2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|0\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot 2+8\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|0-4+16|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\  & =\frac{|12|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{12}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14537fa3-6b22-5ad7-8a11-c7c69ec06d24"} {:db/id 17592186476984 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262941 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "129b0757-3ac6-5753-b6e3-478a8023eb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186260037} {:answer/id #uuid "4de222b6-19ed-5d3c-a87c-f1b937df4849" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186260536} {:answer/id #uuid "65ac176a-0b06-5588-9781-22d9e0435725" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186260758} {:answer/id #uuid "816e3b5d-f9fa-5bd9-b29d-3f7e216e3a23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261004} {:answer/id #uuid "df122527-7c53-5616-83fd-4d0c7dd7847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261846}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260536} :answer-field/id #uuid "ffc75d90-c023-5fb9-a940-576505f511c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0498861d-e4e1-5581-aee5-353d6a78f4f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-129102" :question/problem "Given that $Q(4,-2,8)$ lies on the plane $Π:r\cdot ⟨-3,6,2⟩=-8$, find the shortest distance from $P(3,-4,2)$ to $Π.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find

Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-4y+4z & =16 \\ -2(2)-4(3)+4z & =16 \\ 4z & =32 \\ z & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,8)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,8⟩-⟨-1,11,10⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-8,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,-4,4⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

:step/content {:db/id 17592186093471 :tutorial/content "Consider the following polynomials:

$$
P(x) = 2x^{\color{blue}4} - 3x + 1, \qquad
Q(x) = -6x^{\color{red}3} + 5x^2 + x
$$

Notice that these polynomials have degrees $4$ and $3,$ respectively. We write this as

$$
\textrm{deg}(P) = {\color{blue}4}, \qquad
\textrm{deg}(Q) = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Furthermore, 

- the leading term in $P(x)$ is $2x^{\color{blue}4},$ and

- the leading term in $Q(x)$ is $-6x^{\color{red}3}$

As a result, the leading term in the product $P \cdot Q$ equals the product of the leading terms of $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
2x^{\color{blue}4} \cdot (-6x^{\color{red}3}) = -12x^{{\color{blue}4}+{\color{red}3}} = -12x^{\color{purple}7}
$$

Therefore, the degree of $P \cdot Q$ must be ${\color{purple}{7}}.$

We have the following general rule:

*The degree of the product of two polynomials equals the sum of the degrees of these polynomials:* 

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \cdot Q) = \textrm{deg}(P) + \textrm{deg}(Q)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60187490-7cd6-566d-ab45-128e2c4f81c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6201 :tutorial/title "The Degree of a Product of Two Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f1dac5f5-12ea-56be-8067-1b9f815159f5" :step/math-academy-id 37591 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093196}} {:db/id 17592186093196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092312 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186092159 :question/id #uuid "d0f6fda4-4083-5541-8f0e-9a61f740ba8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9981"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f497212-3946-51e1-9c39-45284ab55da6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048406} {:db/id 17592186049729}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092555} {:db/id 17592186092711} {:db/id 17592186272251} {:db/id 17592186292688} {:db/id 17592186294932} {:db/id 17592186294933} {:db/id 17592186329775} {:db/id 17592186385158} {:db/id 17592186435057} {:db/id 17592186435059} {:db/id 17592186524975} {:db/id 17592186525010}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Degree of a Product of Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "7e843dd4-2f8a-5237-87b2-28b5a09adb3d" :step/math-academy-id 37594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093197}} {:db/id 17592186093197 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093472 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the degree of the sum and difference of two polynomials $P$ and $Q.$ 

First, let's suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have *different* degrees. In this case, the degree of the sum or difference equals the largest of the two degrees. We write

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \pm Q) = \max \big\{ \textrm{deg}(P), \textrm{deg}(Q) \big\},
$$

 
where the $\textrm{max}$ function simply returns the largest element of the set.

For example, suppose that $\textrm{deg}(P) = 5$ and $\textrm{deg}(Q) = 2.$ Then,

$$
\textrm{deg}(P + Q) = \max \big\{ 5, 2 \big\} = 5.
$$

 

To see why this is true, note that the leading term of $P$ contains an $x^5,$ and the leading term of $Q$ has an $x^2.$ When we add the two polynomials, no term of $Q$ could cancel out the leading term of $P.$ So the sum of the polynomials must have degree $5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fae91d47-b786-5c2f-9a29-dfb06624930f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6202 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 1"} :step/id #uuid "82947aff-7f67-51bc-9a88-6e5d204e1c08" :step/math-academy-id 37596 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093199}} {:db/id 17592186093198 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093473 :tutorial/content "Polynomials are also closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but not closed under division.

To illustrate, let's consider the following two polynomials:

$$
P(x) = x+1, \qquad Q(x) = x^2
$$

- When we *add* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P+Q & =(x+1)+({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *subtract* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P-Q & =(x+1)-({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1-{x}^{2} \\  & =-{x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *multiply* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P\cdot Q & =(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}) \\  & =x\cdot {x}^{2}+1\cdot {x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}

a \cdot b = 3\cdot 2 = 6\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

$$

We say the integers are **closed** under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but **not closed** under division.

$$

which is an integer." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7d0a253-b58a-5205-b05d-d5d2f1d49f6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1593 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "90c92812-0369-53f2-8139-3a602c9d8ddf" :step/math-academy-id 4197 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093198}} {:db/id 17592186093195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093471 :tutorial/content "Consider the following polynomials:

$$
P(x) = 2x^{\color{blue}4} - 3x + 1, \qquad
Q(x) = -6x^{\color{red}3} + 5x^2 + x
$$

Notice that these polynomials have degrees $4$ and $3,$ respectively. We write this as

$$
\textrm{deg}(P) = {\color{blue}4}, \qquad
\textrm{deg}(Q) = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Furthermore, 

- the leading term in $P(x)$ is $2x^{\color{blue}4},$ and

- the leading term in $Q(x)$ is $-6x^{\color{red}3}$

As a result, the leading term in the product $P \cdot Q$ equals the product of the leading terms of $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
2x^{\color{blue}4} \cdot (-6x^{\color{red}3}) = -12x^{{\color{blue}4}+{\color{red}3}} = -12x^{\color{purple}7}
$$

Therefore, the degree of $P \cdot Q$ must be ${\color{purple}{7}}.$

We have the following general rule:

*The degree of the product of two polynomials equals the sum of the degrees of these polynomials:* 

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \cdot Q) = \textrm{deg}(P) + \textrm{deg}(Q)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60187490-7cd6-566d-ab45-128e2c4f81c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6201 :tutorial/title "The Degree of a Product of Two Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f1dac5f5-12ea-56be-8067-1b9f815159f5" :step/math-academy-id 37591 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093196}} {:db/id 17592186093471 :tutorial/content "Consider the following polynomials:

First, let's suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have *different* degrees. In this case, the degree of the sum or difference equals the largest of the two degrees. We write

where the $\textrm{max}$ function simply returns the largest element of the set.

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
