$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=4 \\ \pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{4}{\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{4x}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e364e0b-e003-503e-aadb-895d96ad9926" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507557}} {:db/id 17592186507540 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507450 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d7f8754-41a4-514c-86d1-d5647b54333b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{98\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186506703} {:answer/id #uuid "a564bbb9-af52-596a-bcf1-bb101438423e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507039} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e53c4f-ca05-5e48-9e4b-fba6af34790c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507136} {:answer/id #uuid "e6ebfba2-6c04-5678-a8f3-079e02b2c158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{n(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507136} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8a63a77-7e75-5948-b4a4-f7660df42d29" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186507393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "776f8284-bdba-5ab6-8f5c-16f7e1be5e32" :question/math-academy-id "q-343877" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+49y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+49({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "29506e54-5d8b-54a1-b9a6-9e847bc7683d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507552}} {:db/id 17592186507552 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507448 :question/answer-fields $$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=4 \\ \pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{4}{\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{4x}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e364e0b-e003-503e-aadb-895d96ad9926" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507557}} {:db/id 17592186507557 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507508 :question/answer-fields $$
{y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)

$$
\omega =\sqrt{9{\pi }^{2}}=3\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=3\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))+x(-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x):$

$$
[-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\pi A &=0 \\ 6\pi B &=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{54\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+1)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5d1812d8-39e4-5dd4-b731-c6eb976d76d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343896" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}):$

$$
[-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\pi }{3}A &=0 \\ \frac{2\pi }{3}B &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{3}{2\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})-6(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))=6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-6\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-6)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})=6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=6 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-6) &=\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {b}_{n} &=\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9099693d-f185-5899-981c-a69e22a33e27" :step/next {:db/id 17592186513000}} {:db/id 17592186513019 :step/content {:db/id 17592186512930 :question/answer-fields in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$

$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2} &=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, for ${b}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15} \\  & =\frac{n\pi }{15}\cdot \frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)} \\  & =\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b98de4ab-a079-5d39-b165-ba7998caa236" :question/math-academy-id "q-343834" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{{field-2}}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2} &=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15})\frac{n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}
$$

Therefore, for ${b}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15} \\  & =\frac{n\pi }{15}\cdot \frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)} \\  & =\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d60f6806-c6cb-503b-a2c8-fff99cda0786" :step/next {:db/id 17592186513002}} {:db/id 17592186512998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317451 :question/answer-fields differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

$$

$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=0 \\ \pi B &=6\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

}^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}):$

$$
[-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\pi }{3}A &=0 \\ \frac{2\pi }{3}B &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{3}{2\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8730a614-36f9-5c60-80e1-eac2fd3a8305" :step/next {:db/id 17592186512998}} {:db/id 17592186513002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186368337 :question/answer-fields $$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=6 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-6) &=\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {b}_{n} &=\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=0 \\ 3\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{27\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function.

$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A &=0 \\ 2\pi B &=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{8\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{x}{8\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=0 \\ 3\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{27\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-343886" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-10y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-10(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=10 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)=\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a80e8457-da19-59dc-ac4a-260518248f13" :step/next {:db/id 17592186525075}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "344d0e42-cd70-5ad8-90fc-7db764816086" :answer/type {:db/id $$
X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y},

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186134706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135063 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data $(x,y).$ We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. We call this process **polynomial regression**.

The following table gives the number of units $x$ (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing $x$ units:

| Goods $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Profit $(y)$ | $16$ | $11$ | $15$ | $18$ |

Suppose we want to find the quadratic function

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
$$

that best fits the given data points.

![](images/93/93fe1784b89ce4c892c84a03a0dc80909f16f46ac463c5cc30b40f869a7802bf.png)

In particular, this would mean that the sum of the squared residuals [math]\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2[/math] must be as small as possible.

Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+1{\beta }_{1}+{1}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=16 \\ {\beta }_{0}+2{\beta }_{1}+{2}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+3{\beta }_{1}+{3}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=15 \\ {\beta }_{0}+4{\beta }_{1}+{4}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=18\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system can be written using matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & {1}^{2} \\ 1 & 2 & {2}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & {3}^{2} \\ 1 & 4 & {4}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

Now, using the matrix notation, the sum of the squared residuals can be viewed as 

\[
\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2 = \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.
\]

Thus, the condition that this sum must be minimized is equivalent to minimizing [math]\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2[/math] or, which is the same, minimizing [math]\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|.[/math]

Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the curve that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=\begin{bmatrix}22.5 \\ -9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the quadratic curve of best fit (regression curve) is 

$$
y = 22.5 - 9x + 2x^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a9d76d67-952b-5a5c-8891-757974db3a7f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3654 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5282b6c3-a052-5524-8cfc-ee4738c1759c" :step/math-academy-id Consider the table below, which gives the number of units $x$ (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing $x$ units. 

| Goods $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Profit $(y)$ | $2$ | $5$ | $8$ | $18$ |

It's known that the profit equals zero when the company does not produce any goods, so $y=0$ when $x=0.$ The company wishes to find a *quadratic* curve that best fits the data *subject to* the constraint that it should pass through the point $(0,0).$

So, our regression curve must pass through the point $(0,0).$ In other words, the $y$-intercept of the quadratic curve must be $0.$ Therefore, we want to find the quadratic function

$$
y = \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
$$

that best fits the given data points.

$$

$$

This system can be written using matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & {1}^{2} \\ 2 & {2}^{2} \\ 3 & {3}^{2} \\ 4 & {4}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

The rest of the arguments are the same as before. Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "34af7736-1458-54b5-b831-80b4e22a03b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6152 :tutorial/title "Regression Curves Containing Zero Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "e556ba45-b685-5183-8ad9-099c86720b9b" :step/math-academy-id 37335 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134707}}] :activity/title "Polynomial Regression With Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134030} {:db/id 17592186134706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135063 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data $(x,y).$ We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. The following table gives the number of units $x$ (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing $x$ units:

| Goods $(x)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Profit $(y)$ | $16$ | $11$ | $15$ | $18$ |

Suppose we want to find the quadratic function

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
$$

that best fits the given data points.

![](images/93/93fe1784b89ce4c892c84a03a0dc80909f16f46ac463c5cc30b40f869a7802bf.png)

In particular, this would mean that the sum of the squared residuals [math]\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2[/math] must be as small as possible.

Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+1{\beta }_{1}+{1}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=16 \\ {\beta }_{0}+2{\beta }_{1}+{2}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+3{\beta }_{1}+{3}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=15 \\ {\beta }_{0}+4{\beta }_{1}+{4}^{2}{\beta }_{2} &=18\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system can be written using matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & {1}^{2} \\ 1 & 2 & {2}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & {3}^{2} \\ 1 & 4 & {4}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

Now, using the matrix notation, the sum of the squared residuals can be viewed as 

\[
\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2 = \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.
\]

Thus, the condition that this sum must be minimized is equivalent to minimizing [math]\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2[/math] or, which is the same, minimizing [math]\| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|.[/math]

Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0, \beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the curve that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=\begin{bmatrix}22.5 \\ -9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the quadratic curve of best fit (regression curve) is 

$$
y = 22.5 - 9x + 2x^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a9d76d67-952b-5a5c-8891-757974db3a7f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3654 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186134708 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133807 $$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector.

:question/problem "Solve the inequality $\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+4\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+4 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x-2 & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x & \ge {e}^{-6}+2 \\ x & \ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-2>0\,⇒\,x>2
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}.$"} {:db/id 17592186354622 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}\cdot {e}^{-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ (x+2){e}^{-5} & \ge 3x \\ x+2 & \ge 3{e}^{5}x \\ 2 & \ge (3{e}^{5}-1)x \\ \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1} & \ge x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-2 \\ 3x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-2$ and $x>0,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty )$ and $(0,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]\cap (-2,\infty )\cap (0,\infty )=(0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
[1,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,2)\cap (-9,\infty )=[1,2)
$$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186158511 :tutorial/content "When we have a logarithm in an inequality with base $n > 1,$ we can use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $n.$

However, there is a catch: when we solve the resulting inequality, we must remember to remove extraneous solutions. We can do this by keeping only the solutions that are in the domain of the original logarithm.

For example, to solve the inequality

$$
\log_2 (x-1) < 4,
$$

we write each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x-1)} & <{2}^{4} \\ x-1 & <16 \\ x & <17.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-1 > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x > 1
$$

Our solution is $x < 17,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty, 17).$ But the domain of the logarithm is $x > 1,$ which can be expressed as $(1, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty, 17) \cap (1, \infty) = (1, 17)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \in (1,17),$ which can also be written as $1 < x < 17.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f8d2a28-784d-5ec0-b07f-a448d69b2d84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4665 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "142b0985-c893-5e26-8280-c0fd12dc1d25" :step/math-academy-id 28779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158195}} {:db/id 17592186158189 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158512 :tutorial/content "When we have two logarithms in an inequality, we can use the same solution procedure as before: we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of the base of the logarithm.

Just remember that we still need to remove extraneous solutions. We can do this by keeping only the solutions that are in the domains of *all* the logarithms in the original inequality." :tutorial/id #uuid "f55c2fc8-9543-526f-8a35-04ec05516471" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4666 :tutorial/title "Inequalities with Two Logarithms"} :step/id #uuid "c03fa6f8-ecd2-5532-ba6b-8afcdc3c4e6c" :step/math-academy-id 28780 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158184}} {:db/id 17592186158195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158515 :tutorial/content "We're allowed to use each side of an inequality as the exponent of a number $n>1.$ But why are we allowed to do this?

The reason is that this operation preserves the ordering of numbers. That is to say, if $a < b$ and $n>1,$ then $n^a < n^b.$

To see this concretely, consider the following order of numbers:

$$
-2 < -1 < 0 < 0.5 < 1 < 2 < 3
$$

If we raise $2$ to the power of these numbers, the results stay in the same order:

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dcec0706-6439-5e82-9c77-13f295dd1282" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4669 :tutorial/title "The Reason Why We Can Use Each Side as an Exponent"} :step/id #uuid "b51e214c-047d-565f-97e8-cdc1afe0b904" :step/math-academy-id 28788 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158183}}] :activity/title "Solving Inequalities Involving Logarithmic Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157503} {:db/id 17592186158188 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158511 :tutorial/content "When we have a logarithm in an inequality with base $n > 1,$ we can use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $n.$

- from the tenants using provider $A,$ $80%$ swap to provider $B$ and $10%$ swap to provider $C,$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We are given the following situation for each year:

- From the tenants using provider $B,$ $25%$ swap to provider $A$ and $25%$ swap to provider $C.$ This implies that $50%$ of them continue using provider $B.$

- From the tenants using provider $C,$ $70%$ swap to provider $A$ and $10%$ swap to provider $B.$ This implies that $20%$ of them continue using provider $C.$

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Provider A** | **Provider B** | **Provider C** |
| To: | **Provider A** | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.7$ |

| **Provider C** | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.2$ |  |

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 & 0.25 & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.25 & 0.2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
a+b+c=0.25+0.1+0.1=0.45.

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0},\,{x}_{2}=P{x}_{1}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.5 \\ 0.8 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.7 \\ 0.3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.29 \\ 0.71\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, after the second step, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.5 \\ 0.8 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.29 \\ 0.71\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.413 \\ 0.587\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

![](images/70/70ee929c71d89a443d3ea0efc39ed225f344685059b86a04285a118a476da0f8.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $\bf{U}$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 & 0 \\ 1.2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Matrix $\bf{V}$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}0.35 & 0.95 \\ 0.65 & 0.05\end{bmatrix}\,\begin{aligned}0.35+0.65=1 \\ 0.95+0.05=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $\bf{W}$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its third column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.4 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\bf{V}$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186048896} {:db/id 17592186124768 :question/id #uuid "6d6371d4-1a60-5526-b7b1-69a38ead3549" :question/math-academy-id "q-109881" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124614 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66b24a98-c641-5e08-8bec-30f221d1bb22" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "029787b4-76ef-5324-83eb-649b506a66cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$u$, $v$, and $w$" :db/id 17592186244331} {:answer/id #uuid "1bc43066-87ae-5d14-b7df-35e4b5a96b4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$u$ and $v$ only" :db/id 17592186244559} {:answer/id #uuid "1f880ee7-2dae-5e94-a00e-cf7ea06127d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$v$ only" :db/id 17592186244592} {:answer/id #uuid "47d8a976-4e1b-5d5c-9400-17de622336ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$u$ only" :db/id 17592186244953} {:answer/id #uuid "66317c76-eb73-56c5-a0e6-948b81d5904d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$u$ and $w$ only" :db/id 17592186245215}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "47d8a976-4e1b-5d5c-9400-17de622336ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$u$ only" :db/id 17592186244953} :answer-field/id #uuid "8587d707-0f0d-5a40-a9a9-e5a919395461" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186246777}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following are stochastic vectors?

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 0 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix},\,v=\begin{bmatrix}-0.45 \\ 1.55\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our vectors in turn.

- Vector $u$ is a stochastic vector. Indeed, 

- its entries are all nonnegative, and

- the entries add up to one:

$$
0.5+0+0.5=1
$$

- Vector $v$ is *not* a stochastic vector since it contains negative entries.

- Vector $w$ is *not* a stochastic vector since the entries do not add up to one:

$$
0+0=0\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$u$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186124769 :question/id #uuid "8d2f0627-b325-5745-b223-6d5747b6cfb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-109882" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124614 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66b24a98-c641-5e08-8bec-30f221d1bb22" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b14b2aa6-e2b0-5c7b-9b5e-bff935134b81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U$ and $V$ only" :db/id 17592186121212} {:answer/id #uuid "ce803d77-1449-5c03-be82-10019ec069fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ only" :db/id 17592186121213} {:answer/id #uuid "da0f9182-973c-5ad4-8864-b3f5bfe87290" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U$, $V$, and $W$" :db/id 17592186121214} {:answer/id #uuid "220b5ad9-a6a4-53ed-82b9-92706d35035d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/id 17592186121215} {:answer/id #uuid "5a819f20-4b26-5673-9f89-915cc0e71698" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/id 17592186121216}] :answer-field/id #uuid "28b7af88-7cb5-53b2-af84-a7246e3059bd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186121211}] :question/problem "Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

17592186125443 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125800 :tutorial/content "We can use repeated matrix multiplication to determine the state of a system given its initial state and some information about how one state transitions to the next state.

To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

This information can be represented using a diagram, like the one below.

![](images/ab/ab6b3cecac2af22b8665078db56c7daf492c0381434c9c88fe21f2630f743466.png)

We can also present this information as a table:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **City** | **Countryside** |
| To: | **City** | $0.94$ | $0.03$ |
| **Countryside** | $0.06$ | $0.97$ |  |

We want to use this information to determine how the population will be distributed $n$ years after the study was carried out. 

First, let's turn this table into a matrix $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

- it is a square matrix

- the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$

- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

A square matrix with these properties is called a **stochastic matrix**.

Now suppose that, at the time of the study, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside. We can represent this **initial state** using a so-called **stochastic vector** $\mathbf x_0,$ given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.70 \\ 0.30\end{bmatrix}
$$

Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals $1.$ Note that each column of $P$ is a stochastic vector.

Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

- To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product $P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

The resulting vector 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{bmatrix}
$$

tells us that one year after the study, $66.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $33.3$% will live in the countryside.

- To model the distribution after $2$ years, we compute $P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

The resulting vector 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.637 \\ 0.363\end{bmatrix}
$$

tells us that two years after the study, $63.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $36.3$% will live in the countryside." :tutorial/id #uuid "0d87aed7-76da-5126-8eee-f38ced9a46f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3645 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4f00b242-2400-5948-9531-618af1db558d" :step/math-academy-id 20288 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125564}} {:db/id 17592186125444 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124544 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124353 :question/id #uuid "e8f30d47-bfd2-50ea-b2ad-d474e2a58d29" :question/math-academy-id "e-5598"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abbdd778-7ace-5539-9d6f-cdf01804b237" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124912} {:db/id 17592186124913} {:db/id 17592186269082} {:db/id 17592186269083} {:db/id 17592186269084} {:db/id 17592186378678} {:db/id 17592186400730} {:db/id 17592186402468}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data"} :step/id #uuid "2ccc7d00-22a8-5d1a-a0d0-a3e6b10db6f5" :step/math-academy-id 20289 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125445}} {:db/id 17592186125445 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125801 :tutorial/content "Let's reconsider the population we looked at earlier, where the stochastic vector that represents the initial distribution of people between the city and the countryside is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.70 \\ 0.30\end{bmatrix}
$$

and the yearly change in this distribution is represented by the stochastic matrix 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

Earlier, we found that the population distribution after $1$ and $2$ years is given by the vectors $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2,$ 
 respectively, where

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ are called **state vectors**, and $\mathbf x_0$ is the **initial state**. 

To find the state vector corresponding to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

A sequence of stochastic vectors $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots$ related to a stochastic matrix $P$ in this way is called a **Markov chain**." :tutorial/id #uuid To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

- it is a square matrix

- the sum of the entries in each column equals $1$

- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

A square matrix with these properties is called a **stochastic matrix**.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.70 \\ 0.30\end{bmatrix}
$$

Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals $1.$ Note that each column of $P$ is a stochastic vector.

Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{bmatrix}
$$

tells us that one year after the study, $66.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $33.3$% will live in the countryside.

- To model the distribution after $2$ years, we compute $P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{bmatrix}
$$

The resulting vector 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0.637 \\ 0.363\end{bmatrix}
$$

tells us that two years after the study, $63.7$% of the population will live in the city, and $36.3$% will live in the countryside." :tutorial/id #uuid "0d87aed7-76da-5126-8eee-f38ced9a46f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3645 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124614 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124425 :question/id #uuid "25622a0e-3e5b-5f09-bef6-afaa30d153d3" :question/math-academy-id "e-9162"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66b24a98-c641-5e08-8bec-30f221d1bb22" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048896}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124768} {:db/id 17592186124769} {:db/id 17592186269070} {:db/id 17592186269071} {:db/id 17592186269072} {:db/id 17592186269073} {:db/id 17592186378671}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "d7e8a13c-5f02-5712-9c41-daa1892a5092" :step/math-academy-id 34164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125444}} {:db/id 17592186125444 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124544 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124353 :question/id #uuid "e8f30d47-bfd2-50ea-b2ad-d474e2a58d29" :question/math-academy-id "e-5598"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abbdd778-7ace-5539-9d6f-cdf01804b237" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124912} {:db/id 17592186124913} {:db/id 17592186269082} {:db/id 17592186269083} {:db/id 17592186269084} {:db/id 17592186378678} {:db/id 17592186400730} {:db/id 17592186402468}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data"} :step/id #uuid "2ccc7d00-22a8-5d1a-a0d0-a3e6b10db6f5" :step/math-academy-id 20289 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125445}} {:db/id 17592186125445 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125801 :tutorial/content "Let's reconsider the population we looked at earlier, where the stochastic vector that represents the initial distribution of people between the city and the countryside is

"3155a85f-7bd8-584c-a5ae-e2e18dd60cd2" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Sine of a Composite Angle Using Angles in the First Quadrant"}] :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin u = \dfrac{3}{4}, \qquad \cos u =  -\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}, \qquad \cos v = \dfrac{4}{5}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\sin\left(u + v\right) = \dfrac{a- b\sqrt 7}{20},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\sin(u+v) = \sin u \cos v+ \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{u},$ $\cos{u},$ and $\cos{v}.$ To find the missing value of $\sin{v},$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 v + \cos^2 v= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin^2 v = 1- \cos^2 v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{4}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{25}{25}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{25-16}{25} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\sin v= \dfrac{3}{5}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{4}{5})+(-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =\frac{12}{20}-\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{20} \\  & =\frac{12-3\sqrt{7}}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=12, b=3,$ and $a+b = 15.$"} {:db/id 17592186049059} {:db/id 17592186049773} {:db/id 17592186184824 :question/id #uuid "95046840-9961-5e1f-b439-f27000cbde20" :question/math-academy-id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{2}{7},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a-b\sqrt{55}}{42},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{11})^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36-11}{36} \\  & =\frac{25}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{5}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})+(\frac{5}{6})(\frac{2}{7}) \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{55}}{42}+\frac{10}{42} \\  & =\frac{10-3\sqrt{55}}{42}\end{aligned}
$$

together with the Pythagorean identity.

Let's suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin v = \dfrac{3}{5}, \qquad \cos v = \dfrac{4}{5}, \qquad \sin u = -\dfrac{12}{13}.
$$

How can we find the value of $\sin\left(u - v\right)$ given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant? 

First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\sin(u-v) = \sin u \cos v- \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{v}$, $\cos{v}$, and $\sin{u}.$ To find the missing value of $\cos{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \cos^2 u = 1- \sin^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}u & =1-{sin}^{2}u \\  & =1-{(-\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{12}^{2}}{{13}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{169}{169}-\frac{144}{169} \\  & =\frac{25}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{169}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have 

$$
\cos u= -\dfrac{5}{13}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}u\operatorname{cos}v-\operatorname{cos}u\operatorname{sin}v \\  & =(-\frac{12}{13})(\frac{4}{5})-(-\frac{5}{13})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{48}{65}+\frac{15}{65} \\  & =-\frac{33}{65}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "699a9021-a261-5b19-b767-75fd52b030bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6203 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "28ed07fc-351f-5531-9103-a17479e1cce6" :step/math-academy-id 37604 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184892}} {:db/id 17592186185018 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184226 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184132 :question/id #uuid "06df772e-eb43-55e8-9ede-3fc2f7ae291d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9984"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "99d7256f-6130-52b4-8188-3b1388c63f2b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048461}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184453} {:db/id 17592186184825} {:db/id 17592186275148} {:db/id 17592186292747} {:db/id 17592186302292}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Sine of a Composite Angle Using Angles in the Second, Third, or Fourth Quadrants"} :step/id #uuid "2c891011-e58f-5ba0-8625-0854ca6c6fa3" :step/math-academy-id 37605}] :activity/title "Calculating Trigonometric Ratios Using the Sum Formula for Sine" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184422} {:db/id 17592186185017 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185347 :tutorial/content "We can compute trigonometric ratios using the sum and difference formulas for sine together with the Pythagorean identity.

:tutorial/content "In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$ is uniformly distributed, then $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/93/93894f939fa0ef715ee6ab6c225f456972b746184673df0b8d8312656727d793.svg)

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution: 

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/fd/fd37b3e19aad197ebb7eeabad00fca068455eed8da462a12630134cd7980941e.svg)

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean waiting time is $10$ minutes." :tutorial/id #uuid "1087e8f4-f648-5237-8623-0c17d0025548" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4980 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "440a6b0e-f841-5fce-a0bd-4e3697ea4ea3" :step/math-academy-id 31001 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158259}} {:db/id 17592186158262 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157377 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157197 :question/id #uuid "2ab8efcd-495b-5ed4-a6be-e3d24d046fe1" :question/math-academy-id "e-8307"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "610bddb6-0731-53d1-9fcf-ab202d4cf151" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186158003} {:db/id 17592186158009} {:db/id 17592186525004} {:db/id 17592186525027} {:db/id 17592186525029} {:db/id 17592186525066}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Variance in Context"} :step/id #uuid "f455aacf-dfe4-59fa-854e-a6aac8ae7a22" :step/math-academy-id 31002}] :activity/title "Modeling With Continuous Uniform Distributions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157536} {:db/id 17592186158261 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158542 :tutorial/content "In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$ is uniformly distributed, then $X$ has the following probability density function:

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution: 

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/fd/fd37b3e19aad197ebb7eeabad00fca068455eed8da462a12630134cd7980941e.svg)

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean waiting time is $10$ minutes." :tutorial/id #uuid "1087e8f4-f648-5237-8623-0c17d0025548" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4980 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has at most two non-negative distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186496298 :question/id #uuid "afa39ae4-c580-535b-a23d-346f2dd8aacb" :question/math-academy-id "q-139495"} {:db/id 17592186543482 First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ 16-2\lambda -8\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -10) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{10} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=0\end{aligned}
