of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :tutorial/id #uuid "6230f35e-b526-5e84-be30-86c8cdcbd301" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "65534646-ddcd-5bd8-a87f-2133012193c1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508123}} {:db/id 17592186508145 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184877 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7d4ed93-75bb-5db0-9900-2362979d6c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4,\,3,\,0" :db/id 17592186404734} {:answer/id #uuid "aac056f1-2c7a-51fc-b3b8-c7516856527b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404735} {:answer/id #uuid "2ef4562a-20e9-5af5-80a4-ced17b367b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404736} {:answer/id #uuid "fd4157e7-a2cf-562a-af6a-fea80f5a7f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16,\,9,\,0" :db/id 17592186404737} {:answer/id #uuid "95d80c78-37a1-5b82-8b12-a47780191024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9,\,4,\,0" :db/id 17592186404738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404735} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce3dc232-fc1d-50e4-99b4-15ed1b8fa187" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404733}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9152817-159b-5a54-868d-fe52d19640cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-94981" :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "65534646-ddcd-5bd8-a87f-2133012193c1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508123}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a11d8c53-0d85-5382-8004-1a8f6e94884d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508139}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186509031} :activity/id #uuid "25c36865-a3f4-539d-ab87-b42995a49a22" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049462 :topic/id #uuid "f7488799-2322-5ff9-8065-6852954f5eb5" :topic/math-academy-id 3819} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186509001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186493969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08b31b5f-4d45-56bb-9d27-10f181056843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186493405} {:answer/id #uuid "1f5ebfbd-349c-5710-ab1d-bffdb6d4d025" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493445} {:answer/id #uuid "21c0505d-1159-59fb-ba8b-2bd5ac4199de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493447} {:answer/id #uuid "94c66a12-70a7-529f-ba21-ac7f034b13c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493623} {:answer/id #uuid "e4ada2c6-ebf0-5d58-9a21-8f0d7d2bddb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493447} :answer-field/id #uuid "6457d0d0-1968-5324-849a-7bcaae3a3d7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/math-academy-id "q-95286" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $6\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 9$ matrix $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has at most two non-negative distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

$$

$$

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

operation, which is *dividing* by $-9.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9a\,\, & \le \,\,-54 \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-54}{-9} \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-9$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-9a}{-9} & \ge 6 \\ \frac{\cancel{-9}a}{\cancel{-9}} & \ge 6 \\ a & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution "The variable $x$ is being *divided* by $2.$ To isolate $x$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{2}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-2)\cdot 4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -8.$"} {:db/id 17592186055025 :question/id #uuid "869b6bf9-10ab-5912-8b31-dc87d982f2a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-154018"} {:db/id 17592186489193 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}-24\,\, & >(-6)\cdot (-\frac{z}{6}) \\ -24 & >(\cancel{-}6)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{z}{6}) \\ -24 & >6\cdot \frac{z}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $6$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}-24 & >6\cdot \frac{z}{6} \\ -24 & >\frac{6z}{6} \\ -24 & >\frac{\cancel{6}z}{\cancel{6}} \\ -24 & >z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side:

$$
z<-24
$$

- If $|5-x|=5-x,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5-x| & =6 \\ 5-x & =6 \\ -x & =1 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|5-x| & =6 \\ -(5-x) & =6 \\ -5+x & =6 \\ x & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Find the measure of angle $B$ given that $m∠A=m∠C.$" :question/worked-solution "Using $m∠A=m∠C,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A & =m∠C \\ 3z+{20}^{∘} & =4z \\ z & ={20}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, substituting $z={20}^{∘}$ in the expression for $m∠C,$ we get

$$
m∠C=4({20}^{∘})={80}^{∘}.
$$

Now, we can find $m∠B$ using the fact that the internal angles of any triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2\cdot {80}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+{160}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048201} {:db/id 17592186048236} {:db/id 17592186049223} {:db/id 17592186050160} {:db/id 17592186050410} {:db/id 17592186050174 :topic/id #uuid The number of subscribers increased by $35%$ per year until $2005.$ How many cell-phone subscribers were there in $2005?$" :question/worked-solution "The number of subscribers $y(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $35%.$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
y=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

We have:

- $a=5\,000$ is the initial number of subscribers.

- $r=0.35$ is the growth rate ($35%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in years.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5\,000\cdot (1+0.35)^{t} \\  & =5\,000\cdot (1.35)^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the expression for the number of subscribers after $15$ years, we get

$$
y(15)=5,000\cdot (1.35)^{15}≈450\,792.
$$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
y=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

We have:

- $a=50$ dollars is the original price of the watch.

- $r=0.08$ is the growth rate ($8%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in decades.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =50\cdot (1+0.08)^{t} \\  & =50\cdot (1.08)^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the function at $t=3$ gives the value of the watch after $3$ decades.

$$
y(3)=50\cdot (1.08)^{3}≈63
$$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=50$ is the total number of views initially

- $r=1.2$ is the growth rate ($120%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in hours) after the video was posted

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
V=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $V(t)$ is

$$
V=50\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
V(t)=50\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$

To find the total number of views after $3$ hours, we evaluate the above for $t=3:$

$$
V(3)=50\cdot (2.2)^{3}≈532
$$

Therefore, the estimated number of views after $3$ hours is $532.$"} {:db/id 17592186500323 :question/id #uuid "7b3a2ac3-80ac-548f-ab31-d1de79eaa643" :question/math-academy-id "q-318202" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "421513ab-7ba9-53ad-8cc4-202843fff382" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499779} {:answer/id #uuid "49751aae-f779-5ca6-9b9e-7a8ffe15ccc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (2.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499793} {:answer/id #uuid "77ce4af4-fcc6-55af-ac0a-de8056e6b319" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (3.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499875} {:answer/id #uuid "961d3d8b-abcf-51c0-a2d4-4c9ea00eafc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (0.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499947} {:answer/id #uuid "fffde48d-2021-53c1-b6ab-24b4f090abde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (19)^{t}" :db/id 17592186500177}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499793} :answer-field/id #uuid "8f647258-0007-5333-ac78-26a8426f4858" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "When a new article was first published on a news website, it had $40$ views. 17592186069797 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069942 :tutorial/content "To find the **cube root** of a number $x$, we must ask ourselves, "what number *cubed* equals $x$?"

For example, the cube root of $8$ is $2$ since 

$$
2^3 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8,
$$

and the cube root of $-8$ is $-2$ since

$$
(-2)^3 = (-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8.
$$

In general, the cube root of $x^3$ is $x.$

Like the square root, the cube root is signified by a radical symbol, but it also has a little $3$ next to it, i.e., $\sqrt[3\!\phantom{p}]{\phantom{2}}.$ Using this notation, we can express the above statements mathematically:

- "The cube root of $8$ is $2$" can be expressed as $\sqrt[3]{8}=2.$

- "The cube root of $-8$ is $-2$" can be expressed as  $\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2.$

- "The cube root of $x^3$ is $x$" can be expressed as  $\sqrt[3]{x^3}=x.$

**Note:** For square roots, we have $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|,$ but for cube roots, we have $\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x.$ No absolute value is needed for cube roots, because

- the cube root of a positive number is a positive number, and

- the cube root of a negative number is a negative number." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad1bc727-9054-5115-83f0-a82aa24dc35e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1605 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7e24a880-f9da-5e1e-b0bf-5bb2128d72a1" :step/math-academy-id 4295 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069798}} {:db/id 17592186069798 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068850 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068467 :question/id #uuid "2ca53a08-7b11-552c-983f-96e7a392156c" :question/math-academy-id "e-1357"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "942732a6-ca14-5b61-b8fb-ab9ef81610cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049843}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069210} {:db/id 17592186069418} {:db/id 17592186484217} {:db/id 17592186484252} {:db/id 17592186547039}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Cube Root of a Monomial"} :step/id #uuid "eea06921-8121-51a7-86ad-15824cc00550" :step/math-academy-id 4296 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069719}} {:db/id 17592186069799 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068851 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068468 :question/id #uuid "c52719a7-544b-5844-b716-9b9d2999c028" :question/math-academy-id "e-1358"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "11c07788-b01d-5788-b2f1-0a027ea53cb2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069424} {:db/id 17592186069426} {:db/id 17592186484266} {:db/id 17592186484297} {:db/id 17592186499461}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Cube Root of a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "f7015e37-4cd2-5ffb-814e-264ca9a0b345" :step/math-academy-id 4299}] :activity/title "The Cube Root of a Perfect Cube With Algebraic Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068929} {:db/id 17592186069797 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069942 :tutorial/content "To find the **cube root** of a number $x$, we must ask ourselves, "what number *cubed* equals $x$?"

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069592 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070024 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to solve equations that contain absolute value expressions.

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
|x+1| = 4
$$

For this equation to be true, either the *positive or negative* of the expression inside the absolute value must equal the right-hand side. That is,

$$
x+1 = 4 \qquad\qquad \text{ or } \qquad\qquad -(x+1)=4.
$$

So, let's solve these two equations:

- First, we solve the equation $x+1 = 4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =4 \\ x+1-1 & =4-1 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we solve the equation $-(x+1) = 4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-(x+1) & =4 \\ -x-1 & =4 \\ -x-1+1 & =4+1 \\ -x & =5 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original absolute value equation are $x={\color{blue}3}$ and $x={\color{red}{-5}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35d16431-4611-59fc-8888-c1db1a7b9902" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0212403d-0f66-5be5-8ebb-0dcacbe7f08f" :step/math-academy-id 143132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069593}} {:db/id 17592186069593 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070025 :tutorial/content "So, we've seen that the solutions to the equation 

$$
|x+1| = 4
$$

are $x={\color{blue}3}$ and $x={\color{red}{-5}}.$ 

We can verify that these solutions are correct by substituting them back into the original equation and checking we get a true statement:

- Substituting $x={\color{blue}3}$ into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1| & =4 \\ |3+1| & =4 \\ |4| & =4 \\ 4 & =4.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x={\color{blue}3}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.

- Substituting $x={\color{red}-5}$ into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1| & =4 \\ |-5+1| & =4 \\ |-4| & =4 \\ 4 & =4.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x={\color{red}-5}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.

lesson, we'll learn how to solve equations that contain absolute value expressions.

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
|x+1| = 4
$$

For this equation to be true, either the *positive or negative* of the expression inside the absolute value must equal the right-hand side. That is,

$$
x+1 = 4 \qquad\qquad \text{ or } \qquad\qquad -(x+1)=4.
$$

So, let's solve these two equations:

- First, we solve the equation $x+1 = 4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =4 \\ x+1-1 & =4-1 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we solve the equation $-(x+1) = 4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-(x+1) & =4 \\ -x-1 & =4 \\ -x-1+1 & =4+1 \\ -x & =5 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original absolute value equation are $x={\color{blue}3}$ and $x={\color{red}{-5}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35d16431-4611-59fc-8888-c1db1a7b9902" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0212403d-0f66-5be5-8ebb-0dcacbe7f08f" :step/math-academy-id 143132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069593}} {:db/id 17592186070024 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to solve equations that contain absolute value expressions.

If the deer population doubles every year, can we find a function that gives the number of deer after $t$ years? 

First, let's write down what we know:

- $a = 120$ is the **initial number** of deer

- $b =2$ is the **growth factor** (equal to $2$ because the number of deer doubles every year)

- $t=$ the time (in years)

We let $y(t)$ be the number of deer in the reserve after $t$ years.  The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = ab^t.
$$

Substituting our values for $a$ and $b,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 120\cdot 2^t.
$$

We can use this formula to find the number of deer in the reserve for any value of $t \geq 0.$ For example, to find the number of deer after $3$ years, we substitute $t=3$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =120\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =120\cdot 8 \\  & =960\end{aligned}
$$

So there will be $960$ deer after $3$ years.

Finally, notice that substituting $t=0$ into the formula gives the initial number of deer:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =120\cdot {2}^{0} \\  & =120\cdot 1 \\  & =120\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ed1b9eba-931a-5908-99c6-58b738afef7d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1937 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "642a7826-566a-5e56-b810-cb6fb7d5fa0c" :step/math-academy-id 531824 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148357}} {:db/id 17592186148357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147473 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147198 :question/id #uuid "7e261e75-a3ec-59cf-a7b7-ad935cb4e55d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1987"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "80c3fbf3-5165-510f-b130-d216d5c8aa19" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049619} {:db/id 17592186050886}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147898} {:db/id 17592186147910} {:db/id 17592186489214} {:db/id 17592186489253}] :knowledge-point/title "Modeling Exponential Growth Using a Growth Factor"} :step/id #uuid "c0ba8192-ba62-514c-b119-d4b80274d19c" :step/math-academy-id 531825 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148358}} {:db/id 17592186148358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148683 :tutorial/content "When dealing with exponential growth, it's more common to be given a **growth rate** instead of a growth factor. A growth rate is usually expressed as a percent.

For example, suppose that an investor invests $\[math]500$ dollars in the shares of some high-growth companies. It's expected that the investment will grow by $35\%$ each year. Can we write a function that describes the value of the investment after $t$ years? 

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=\[/math]500$ is the **initial value** of the investment

- $r = 0.35$ is the **growth rate** (this is simply $35\%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t$ is the time (in years)

Let $y(t)$ be the value of the investment after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y = a(1+r)^t.
$$

Substituting in our values for $a$ and $r,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 500(1+0.35)^t.
$$

Simplifying the above, we arrive at

$$
y(t) = 500(1.35)^t.
$$

When creating exponential growth functions, the key takeaway is this:

- If you're given a **growth rate** $r$ (usually expressed as a percent), then use the formula $y = a(1+r)^t.$

- If you're given a **growth factor** $b,$ then use the formula $y = ab^t.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65e48fd4-d6c3-5e02-aad1-9a8dae46b0bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1936 :tutorial/title "Modeling Round your answer to the nearest dollar." :question/worked-solution "The price of the watch $y(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $8%.$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
y=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

We have:

- $a=50$ dollars is the original price of the watch.

- $r=0.08$ is the growth rate ($8%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in decades.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =50\cdot (1+0.08)^{t} \\  & =50\cdot (1.08)^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the function at $t=3$ gives the value of the watch after $3$ decades.

$$
y(3)=50\cdot (1.08)^{3}≈63
$$

Therefore, the value of the watch after $3$ decades will be approximately $$63.$"} :step/id #uuid "d0fc5aff-4ed7-58b6-9140-1572b6374187" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500427}} {:db/id 17592186500427 :step/content {:db/id 17592186500311 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6885483a-aa71-5fea-be44-2ce9914f562d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "86" :db/id 17592186499854} {:answer/id #uuid "99d3b702-8f26-5fec-864d-fc1d46d65b97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "700" :db/id 17592186499952} {:answer/id #uuid "a54c4dd1-562b-5848-ac11-19e631519c9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "532" :db/id 17592186499977} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6b2e34-5b0d-511b-9c71-0da9a7de6e76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "246" :db/id 17592186499993} {:answer/id #uuid "be53aed4-2603-538a-bb13-6ffecb59a0fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "198" :db/id 17592186500043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499977} :answer-field/id #uuid "1232ee90-f900-5499-a331-ceb50d527115" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500188}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "50e1b98c-c8a1-53cf-8367-e3764f5a2f08" :question/math-academy-id "q-317613" :question/problem "A video was posted on a streaming platform with $50$ initial views. $$
V=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

$$
V=50\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
V(t)=50\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$

To find the total number of views after $3$ hours, we evaluate the above for $t=3:$

$$
V(3)=50\cdot (2.2)^{3}≈532
$$

x^{2} - 4 &=  \\

:question/problem "Factor the expression $16{a}^{2}-81.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the expression as a difference of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{a}^{2}-81 & =(4a)^{2}-{9}^{2}\end{aligned}

:step/content {:db/id 17592186069927 :tutorial/content "To simplify a rational expression, we cancel out the largest common factor from the numerator and denominator. To do this, we sometimes need to factor the numerator and denominator before canceling.

For example, suppose that we wish to simplify $\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}.$ To do this, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any factors that they have in common.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}
		&=\dfrac {4(x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac {2 \cdot 2 \cdot (x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]		
		&=\dfrac {\cancel{2} \cdot 2(x - 3)} {\cancel{2}(5x + 2)}\[5pt]	
		&=\dfrac {2(x - 3)} {5x + 2}
	}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "332f534f-811e-5c03-8393-560134dd4ea8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1370 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "818bd86a-fb35-5a26-8a36-9ee10c0aa1c5" :step/math-academy-id For example, suppose that we wish to simplify $\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}.$ To do this, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any factors that they have in common.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}
		&=\dfrac {4(x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac {2 \cdot 2 \cdot (x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]		
		&=\dfrac {\cancel{2} \cdot 2(x - 3)} {\cancel{2}(5x + 2)}\[5pt]	
		&=\dfrac {2(x - 3)} {5x + 2}
	}

$$
\dfrac{{\color{red}x-1}}{{\color{blue}2}} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}2x-1}}{{\color{red}5}},
$$

then we can eliminate the rational expressions by applying **cross-multiplication**:

- we cross-multiply the left-hand side numerator $({\color{red}x-1})$ with the right-hand side denominator $({\color{red}5}),$ and

- we cross-multiply the left-hand side denominator $({\color{blue}2})$ with the right-hand side numerator $({\color{blue}2x-1}).$

Doing this, we get the following equation:

$$
({\color{red}x-1}) \cdot ({\color{red}5}) = ({\color{blue}2}) \cdot ({\color{blue}2x - 1})
$$

After we've cross-multiplied, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ 5x-5 & =4x-2 \\ 5x-5+5 & =4x-2+5 \\ 5x & =4x+3 \\ 5x-4x & =4x+3-4x \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Cross-multiplication might seem magical, but it is really just a shortcut for multiplying both sides of the equation by each denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{2} & =\frac{2x-1}{5} \\ 2\cdot \frac{x-1}{2} & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \frac{x-1}{\cancel{2}} & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ x-1 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ (x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5}\cdot 5 \\ (x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{\cancel{5}}\cdot \cancel{5} \\ (x-1)\cdot (5) & =(2)\cdot (2x-1)\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99ff1453-e12b-518f-94b1-9baf8ee914e6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8174 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "62154097-0663-58a8-8dfe-b1f260a5583e" :step/math-academy-id 175966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111527}} {:db/id 17592186111527 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110619 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110320 :question/id #uuid "7df7a073-8131-5732-b353-f89484052e38" :question/math-academy-id "e-13077"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3ff2f965-b406-5c9a-bd41-73ccdce951eb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048760}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110932} {:db/id 17592186111181} {:db/id 17592186111182} {:db/id 17592186488259} {:db/id 17592186488277} {:db/id 17592186497364}] :knowledge-point/title "Cross-Multiplying with One Binomial"} :step/id #uuid "79e64205-d43a-5719-a973-65d5eb873b04" :step/math-academy-id 175967 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111528}} {:db/id 17592186111528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110620 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110321 :question/id #uuid "4041cf6f-61b8-5794-9988-436722985bcd" :question/math-academy-id "e-13078"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e880edeb-82ad-5943-a846-dc3246e3e3bd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050908}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110933} {:db/id 17592186111155} {:db/id 17592186488196} {:db/id 17592186488233} {:db/id 17592186497390}] :knowledge-point/title "Cross-Multiplying with Two Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "39ea7244-0ca1-52cc-9e51-81973115c977" :step/math-academy-id 175971 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111529}} {:db/id 17592186111529 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111912 :tutorial/content "Consider the following equation:

- the angles $\angle{A}$, $\angle{B}$ and $\angle{C}$ formed by the sides are called the **interior angles** of the triangle.

To denote a triangle, we use the symbol $\boldsymbol{\triangle}$ and list its vertices (in any order). So, the above diagram shows us 

$$

$$

$$
x + 4 < 7
$$

To **solve** this inequality, we need to isolate the variable $x$ on one side.

Inequalities are just like equations because they can be solved using the addition and multiplication principles.

So, to solve this inequality, we subtract $4$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & <7 \\ x+4-4 & <7-4 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3.$ This tells us that any value of $x$ smaller than $3$ satisfies the original inequality.

However, there is one additional rule that we need to remember when solving inequalities:

*When multiplying or dividing both sides by a **negative number**, we flip the inequality sign.*

When we "flip the inequality sign," we switch the direction of the inequality symbol. For example:

- "$\color{blue}<$" becomes "$\color{red}>$" and vice versa

- "$\color{blue}\leq$" becomes "$\color{red}\geq$" and vice versa

To illustrate, consider the following inequality:

$$
- 3x \gt 9
$$

We can solve this inequality using the multiplication principle. However, when we divide both sides by $-3,$ we have to flip the inequality sign. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x\,\, & >\,\,9 \\ \frac{-3x}{-3}\,\, & <\,\,\frac{9}{-3} \\ \frac{-3x}{-3}\,\, & <\,\,-3 \\ \frac{\cancel{-3}x}{\cancel{-3}}\,\, & <\,\,-3 \\ x\,\, & <\,\,-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \lt -3.$

We'll discuss why we need to flip the inequality sign at the end of the lesson. Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y\,\, & >\,\,18 \\ \frac{-2y}{-2}\,\, & <\,\,\frac{18}{-2} \\ \frac{-2y}{-2}\,\, & <\,\,-9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

:question/worked-solution "The variable $x$ is being *divided* by $2.$ To isolate $x$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{2}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-2)\cdot 4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -8.$"} :step/id #uuid "b48eede8-bb40-5e1b-981b-25334c7cacd0"} {:db/id 17592186536965 :step/content {:db/id 17592186536866 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "360ebf0c-440b-5b80-aa5d-f220ea76cfe8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge 3" :db/id 17592186536367} {:answer/id #uuid "60e57476-d7c3-5931-afaa-b90f394b253b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le -3" :db/id 17592186536450} {:answer/id #uuid "6395e4d6-160c-524d-bea0-39d0f0cb0acb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge 11" :db/id 17592186536454} {:answer/id #uuid "6e12aa20-0d6e-5360-a6c8-7346274c8177" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge -3" :db/id 17592186536468} {:answer/id #uuid "a9e80f2e-a321-5d67-acf6-345376f7ea8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le 3" :db/id 17592186536554}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186536468} :answer-field/id #uuid "e410432f-86a4-50ea-8294-40d4d0eeeb2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186536794}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a6005239-b6a4-5801-8173-53f2d74d92ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-153600" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $4\le x+7.$" :question/worked-solution "To isolate $x,$ we need to perform the *opposite* of *adding* $7,$ which is *subtracting* $7.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}

$$
\left(a^m\right)^n = a^{mn}
$$

For example,

$$
\eqalign{
		\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \
				5^{2 \cdot 3} &= \
				5^6.
	}
$$

To see why the power rule for exponents is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way:

$$
\eqalign{
\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \[5pt]
	\underbrace{5^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 5^2}_{3\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
(5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) &= \[5pt]
	\underbrace{5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5}_{6\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
	5^6
}
$$

The power rule for exponents is just a shortcut for the process above." :tutorial/id #uuid "1a2e18f4-6996-52a0-95eb-77abb10d0e77" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1480 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d4e0fa30-ed7c-5ef6-9aaa-10d6ba2f9c05" :step/math-academy-id 3529 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065196}} {:db/id 17592186065196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064301 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063922 :question/id #uuid "a023e3eb-38bb-52ed-ae06-26ccdcd8fbf6" :question/math-academy-id "e-1076"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e463f04c-3ec1-5b0b-99a4-c286cf0f2d23" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050697} {:db/id 17592186051009}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064680} {:db/id 17592186064917} {:db/id 17592186485550}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Power Rule with Positive Exponents"} :step/id #uuid "57c38b87-4e15-573a-960c-a61055841b16" :step/math-academy-id 3530 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065197}} {:db/id 17592186065197 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064302 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063923 :question/id #uuid "bc3b926b-dc98-5c74-8fc6-32075763059c" :question/math-academy-id "e-1077"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5abe4cbe-7495-5723-88cd-f97796f8ef49" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064690} {:db/id 17592186064918} {:db/id 17592186485517} {:db/id 17592186485563} {:db/id 17592186544867} {:db/id 17592186544871}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Power Rule with Negative Exponents"} :step/id #uuid "94008045-7999-599a-b725-36201f5023db" :step/math-academy-id 3532 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065198}} {:db/id 17592186065198 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065339 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to remove the radical term in an expression like $\sqrt{x^{3}}.$ To do this, we first convert the radical to a fractional exponent:

$$
\sqrt{x^{3}}= \left(x^{3}\right)^{1/2}
$$

Then, we can apply the power rule and multiply the fractional exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({x}^{3})}^{1/2} & = \\ {x}^{(3)\cdot (1/2)} & = \\ {x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\sqrt{x^{3}} = x^{3/2},
$$

and in general,

$$
\sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{m/n}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "40488864-6672-59b7-9ac6-79903856b484" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1481 :tutorial/title "The Power Rule With Fractional Exponents"} :step/id #uuid "19a0572e-4edb-579e-b72d-fdc1fefe72ca" :step/math-academy-id 3536 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065199}} {:db/id 17592186065199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064303 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063924 :question/id #uuid "f61d95d1-9761-53c3-bfb3-699bdcf6467a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1079"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0b64073e-4aa0-551c-b914-98420b0be338" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050894}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064715} {:db/id 17592186064919} {:db/id 17592186485536} {:db/id 17592186485539} {:db/id 17592186544852}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Power Rule with Fractional Exponents"} :step/id #uuid "d556d6dc-07a0-5db1-b5db-945a6a81b5eb" :step/math-academy-id 3537 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065200}} {:db/id 17592186065200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064304 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063925 :question/id #uuid "bdb00b27-cb4d-5713-98c1-d4aa2eaa4643" :question/math-academy-id "e-1080"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "acc85958-ad98-5ce2-912c-e2ba70d025ca" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049729}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064750} {:db/id 17592186064920} {:db/id 17592186233088} {:db/id 17592186485504} {:db/id 17592186485511} {:db/id 17592186544805}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Challenging Expressions Using the Power Rule"} :step/id #uuid "7aabc08d-413a-5e15-8a0e-170869a0198c" :step/math-academy-id 3539}] :activity/title "The Power Rule for Exponents With Algebraic Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064449} {:db/id 17592186065195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065338 :tutorial/content "The **power rule for exponents** states that a power raised to another power is equal to the product of the two powers:

17592186075012 :tutorial/content "Recall that the product rule for radicals states that

$$
\sqrt{a\cdot b} = \sqrt{a}\cdot \sqrt{b}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are nonnegative numbers. 

We can use the product rule for radicals to simplify some expressions. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4af2af2e-0f81-5094-adf6-2ede72a493d2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5995 :tutorial/title "The Product Rule for Radicals"} :step/id #uuid "d050b8f3-0cc1-593c-8200-076f5b4f824f" :step/math-academy-id 36619 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074726}} {:db/id 17592186074728 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075013 :tutorial/content "We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
4\sqrt[3]2 - 6\sqrt[3] 2
$$

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\sqrt[3]{2}-6\sqrt[3]{2} & = \\ (4-6)\sqrt[3]{2} & = \\ -2\sqrt[3]{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

 

As with square roots, we *cannot* combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
3\sqrt[3] 2 + \sqrt[3] 5
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt[3] 2$ and $\sqrt[3] 5.$

Finally, it is not possible to combine square root and cube root terms -- not even if the numbers under the radical symbol are the same! For example, the expression

$$
4\sqrt 2 + \sqrt[3] 2
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt 2$ and $\sqrt[3] 2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "32078f96-6eaf-57d2-bc71-8af8495d5d6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5996 :tutorial/title "Simplifying Expressions With Cube Roots"} :step/id #uuid "f9fded71-c2d5-5d66-9f13-5b0253efd6ff" :step/math-academy-id 36620 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074725}} {:db/id 17592186074751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074948 :tutorial/content "When dealing with sums of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same number under the square root symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
2\sqrt 5 + 4\sqrt 5
$$

Remember that $2\sqrt 5$ and $4\sqrt 5$ mean $2\cdot\sqrt 5$ and $4\cdot\sqrt 5,$ respectively. 

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}+4\sqrt{5} & = \\ (2+4)\sqrt{5} & = \\ 6\sqrt{5} & \end{aligned}
$$

 

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{7} & = \\ 2\sqrt{7}-1\cdot \sqrt{7} & = \\ (2-1)\sqrt{7} & = \\ 1\cdot \sqrt{7} & = \\ \sqrt{7}. & \end{aligned}
$$

 

However, we *cannot* combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
2\sqrt 3 + \sqrt 5
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt 3$ and $\sqrt 5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9aa49408-30d5-57b5-8dff-ec1744f9fc6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1609 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "38f3ace0-f394-598e-8dad-37fefda9d86e" :step/math-academy-id 4327 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074752}} {:db/id 17592186074752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073806 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073464 :question/id #uuid "cf793c45-6c89-50c8-bb28-d066d2b8342a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1370"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2d8a8280-5248-57e4-a5ed-14e281f3db77" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050404}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074147} {:db/id 17592186074186} {:db/id 17592186485495} {:db/id 17592186485554}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Square Root Expressions"} :step/id #uuid "459089fc-d278-5487-bc0b-e4cd6237c142" :step/math-academy-id 4328 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074727}}] :activity/title "Adding and Subtracting Radicals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073921} {:db/id 17592186074751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074948 :tutorial/content "When dealing with sums of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same number under the square root symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt 2$ and $\sqrt[3] 2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "32078f96-6eaf-57d2-bc71-8af8495d5d6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5996 :tutorial/title "Simplifying Expressions With Cube Roots"} {:db/id 17592186074948 :tutorial/content "When dealing with sums of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same number under the square root symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
2\sqrt 5 + 4\sqrt 5
$$

Remember that $2\sqrt 5$ and $4\sqrt 5$ mean $2\cdot\sqrt 5$ and $4\cdot\sqrt 5,$ respectively. 

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}+4\sqrt{5} & = \\ (2+4)\sqrt{5} & = \\ 6\sqrt{5} & \end{aligned}
$$

 

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{7} & = \\ 2\sqrt{7}-1\cdot \sqrt{7} & = \\ (2-1)\sqrt{7} & = \\ 1\cdot \sqrt{7} & = \\ \sqrt{7}. & \end{aligned}
$$

 

However, we *cannot* combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
2\sqrt 3 + \sqrt 5
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt 3$ and $\sqrt 5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9aa49408-30d5-57b5-8dff-ec1744f9fc6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1609 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073806 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073464 :question/id #uuid "cf793c45-6c89-50c8-bb28-d066d2b8342a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1370"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2d8a8280-5248-57e4-a5ed-14e281f3db77" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050404}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074147} {:db/id 17592186074186} {:db/id 17592186485495} {:db/id 17592186485554}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Square Root Expressions"} :step/id #uuid "459089fc-d278-5487-bc0b-e4cd6237c142" :step/math-academy-id 4328 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074727}} {:activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186489345} :activity/id #uuid "f5d315b3-1937-5219-9b02-93324c4b74bb" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186408188 :topic/id #uuid "24a28f9b-1f4f-5349-9353-6e0a556259c4" :topic/math-academy-id 7011} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186489298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186489387 :tutorial/content "It's convenient to use the following special **bar-notation** to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely:

This is an example of a **repeating decimal** - a decimal in which the digits after the decimal point continue forever in a *repeating pattern*." :tutorial/id #uuid "b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15177 :tutorial/title "Repeating Decimals"} {:db/id 17592186489385 :tutorial/content "A rational number can have a decimal representation that either *ends* or *repeats*.

In this lesson, we will see how to convert rational numbers written as fractions into decimals using *long division*. 
We begin with examples where the decimal terminates. 

Let's convert $\dfrac{7}{2}$ into a decimal using long division.

To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator:

$$
7 \div 2
$$

We proceed using long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0\mathbin{:}$

for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Suppose

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that

$$
F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.
$$

Comparing the two integrals, we see that

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).
$$

For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
s>s_0+a.
$$

This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).
$$

In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." 17592186045417] [17592186222476 1065 14326 17592186045417] [17592186222476 1066 #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" 17592186045417] [17592186222476 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186222508 1064 "Recall that the first shifting theorem states that if

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),
$$

then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).
$$

This means the new Laplace transform is the original graph of $F$ evaluated at $s-a$.

So, the graph shift is:

- If $a>0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the right** by $a$ units.

- If $a<0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the left** by $|a|$ units.

For example, suppose $F(s)$ has the following graph:

![](images/45/45ce62c981e4c7853ef158046eb21fbc9c135f5fa0a8887d813a07594077c8ce.png)

Then the Laplace transform of $e^{-3t} f(t)$ is $F(s+3).$ Here, $a=-3$, so this corresponds to shifting the graph of $F(s)$ three units to the left:

![](images/b7/b75658824079fe90c9c4f43d4d37d355c95b845ebed3f11bdf751b52f8d34f55.png)

A useful self-check is that any horizontal features move the same way:

- vertical asymptotes shift left/right by the same amount,

- intercepts and key points shift left/right by the same amount." 17592186045417] [17592186222508 1065 14589 17592186045417] [17592186222508 1066 #uuid "db14b380-2e8e-5007-a9ad-722a83b574ae" 17592186045417] [17592186222508 1067 "Graph Shifting" 17592186045417] [17592186222509 1064 "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things:

- *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$.

- *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$.

To see this in action, consider the following example.

We are given that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.
$$

Suppose we want to compute

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.
$$

First, we identify the base transform:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}
$$

Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for

$$
s>2.
$$

17592186045417] [17592186055942 1064 "The **Cartesian coordinate system** (or **Cartesian plane**) is a grid that we can use to understand where certain objects lie, similar to a map. This grid looks as follows:

![](images/fd/fd702a53ff1127a2432cbdd9a3c7057a08c73ac7a086454c066fa2c96bea7974.png)

It consists of a horizontal number line called the **$x$-axis** and a vertical number line called the **$y$-axis**.

The **origin** is the location where the $x$ and $y$ axes meet and is given the symbol $O.$" 17592186045417] [17592186055942 1065 1431 17592186045417] [17592186055942 1066 #uuid "dacc8373-6186-517b-bba8-ec1729732e4d" 17592186045417] [17592186055942 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186055943 1064 "Every location on the Cartesian plane is called a **point**. Every point is identified using an $x$**-coordinate** and a $y$**-coordinate**. Together, points are expressed using an **ordered pair** of **coordinates** $(x,y).$

For example, we can mark (or **plot**) the point $A$ with coordinates $({\color{red}{3}},{\color{blue}{2}})$ by starting from $O$ and then traveling $\color{red}3$ units towards the right, followed $\color{blue}2$ units up.

![](images/c1/c1ef61dedbbcc6eedcd125c2c62cdfbaa4d9b9a12f10181714b51c060a059fd3.png)

We say that

- the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $3$,

- the $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $2$,

- the $xy$-coordinates (or just "the coordinates") of $A$ are $(3,2).$

The letter $A$ is just a label for our point. It's usually a good idea to label points!" 17592186045417] [17592186055943 1065 1432 17592186045417] [17592186055943 1066 #uuid "9e7847c5-757a-5cb8-b947-9c7d806b5dc5" 17592186045417] [17592186055943 1067 "Coordinates and Ordered Pairs" 17592186045417] [17592186055957 1064 "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

![](images/f1/f1eeb7f3bc0ab8b39e9dc7127d76a32f1dd130d380748fedc6e11b967f3878ed.png)

We plot an ordered pair $({\color{red}x},{\color{blue}y})$ similar to before, but if the number is negative, we reverse the direction. So, starting at the origin:

- if the first number is positive, move that number of places *right* along the $\color{red}x$-axis. If its negative, move *left*.

- if the second number is positive, move that number of places *up* along the $\color{blue}y$-axis. If its negative, move *down*.

To demonstrate, let's find the coordinates of the point $Q$ above.

To find the coordinates of $Q,$ we start at the origin, move $\color{red}3$ units *left*, and then $\color{blue}2$ units *down*. 

![](images/b4/b4f58f0c1ad6dc2936ed1b24c844fa82c1b1d5ec10c80e14c6a43f6f4eaf5544.png)

Since we move left, the $\color{red}x$-coordinate is negative, and since we move down, the $\color{blue}y$-coordinate is negative.

Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $({\color{red}{-3}},{\color{blue}{-2}}).$" 17592186045417] [17592186055957 1065 2092 17592186045417] [17592186055957 1066 #uuid "7383452c-9470-5f05-b206-dffbb84808dd" 17592186045417] [17592186055957 1067 "Extending the Coordinate Plane to Negative Numbers" 17592186045417] [17592186055958 1064 "The axes split the coordinate plane into four parts, called **quadrants**.

![](images/93/938125e855fcb96f743c01f2a00d289ef13e0601772bab56cf0f255e9adf4dcd.png)

Going counter-clockwise, it's common to call

- the top-right quadrant the first quadrant (I),

- the top-left is the second quadrant (II),

- the bottom-left is the third quadrant (III),

- and and bottom-right is the fourth quadrant (IV).

To remember the order of the quadrants, it's helpful to think about writing the letter "C" in the graph:

![](images/1e/1ef91f2bc25ea8b887ec449d2dafe2eaf6a157733e7bc50e4480280df8190728.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186055958 1065 2097 17592186045417] [17592186055958 1066 #uuid "8a1e27dd-9f87-5adf-b0c6-f0f6cd7e2aac" 17592186045417] [17592186055958 1067 "Quadrants in the Coordinate Plane" 17592186045417] [17592186056014 1064 "Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the **horizontal line** that passes through the point $(0,3)$, as shown below:

Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. To formally define a distance between two points $x$ and $y$, we use a **metric function** or **distance function**. This is a rule $d(x, y)$ that assigns a non-negative number to each pair of points, representing how far apart they are.

A valid distance function must satisfy these four properties:

- *Identity*:

$$
d(x, x) = 0
$$

- *Positivity*:

$$
d(x, y) > 0 \quad \text{if} \quad x \ne y
$$

- *Symmetry*:

$$
d(x, y) = d(y, x)
$$

- *Triangle inequality*:

$$
d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z)
$$

These conditions ensure the function behaves like a meaningful measure of distance.

Let’s consider some widely used concrete examples of metrics." 17592186045417] [17592186158439 1065 10854 17592186045417] [17592186158439 1066 #uuid "0f37d7d5-bb53-5b03-a189-fb4bdba4b82e" 17592186045417] [17592186158439 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186158440 1064 "We’ve seen how both Euclidean and Manhattan distances can be written in terms of vector norms. These are actually special cases of a more general formula known as the **Minkowski distance**.

Given a fixed value $p \ge 1$, the Minkowski distance between two points $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in $N$-dimensional space is defined as

$$
d_p(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N |a_i - b_i|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
$$

The corresponding **Minkowski norm** is given by

$$
\| \mathbf{v} \|_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N |v_i|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
$$

The parameter $p$ determines how differences in individual coordinates contribute to the total distance:

- **$p=1$** (Manhattan): All differences are summed equally.

- **$p=2$** (Euclidean): Larger differences have more weight due to squaring.

- **$p \to \infty$**: The distance is determined entirely by the single largest coordinate difference.

Let’s compute an example to see how this works in practice.

Suppose $\mathbf{a} = [1,\ 2,\ 3]^T$ and $\mathbf{b} = [4,\ 0,\ 6]^T$. Let's compute their Minkowski distance using $p = 5$.

$$

As $p$ increases, the smaller components contribute less and less to the overall value. The norm becomes increasingly influenced by the largest coordinate, in this case, $3.$

Let’s now understand why this happens more formally. Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is a nonzero vector, and that one of its entries is strictly larger than all the others. Let $j$ be the index where $|v_j| > |v_i|$ for every $i \ne j$.

Our goal is to understand the behavior of the norm as $p \to \infty{:}$

$$
\lim_{p \to \infty} \|\mathbf{v}\|_p = \lim_{p \to \infty} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N |v_i|^p \right)^{1/p}
$$

To simplify this expression, we factor out $|v_j|^p$ from the sum inside

$$
\lim_{p \to \infty} \|\mathbf{v}\|_p = \lim_{p \to \infty} |v_j| \left(1 + \sum_{i \ne j} \left( \frac{|v_i|}{|v_j|} \right)^p \right)^{1/p}.
$$

Since $|v_j|$ is the largest component, each ratio $\dfrac{|v_i|}{|v_j|}$ is a number less than $1.$ When we raise numbers less than $1$ to larger and larger powers, they shrink toward zero.

That leaves us with

$$
\lim_{p \to \infty} \|\mathbf{v}\|_p = |v_j| \cdot 1 = |v_j|.
$$

This motivates the definition of the **Chebyshev norm** (also called the **max norm** or $L^\infty$ norm) as

$$
\|\mathbf{v}\|_\infty = \max\left( |v_1|,\ |v_2|,\ \ldots,\ |v_N| \right).
$$

It simply picks out the largest absolute value among the components of $\mathbf{v}$.

Using this norm, we define the **Chebyshev distance** between two points $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ as

$$
d_\infty(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \max\left( |a_1 - b_1|,\ |a_2 - b_2|,\ \ldots,\ |a_N - b_N| \right).
$$

This distance reflects the largest difference across coordinates. It’s especially useful in situations where we care about the worst-case difference in any direction.

In the triangle above, we are given an angle $\theta = 42^\circ,$ and the length of the hypotenuse is given but the length of the side opposite is unknown.

So, we need to choose the trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite side to the hypotenuse. This is sine, and now we can just set up the ratio, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\  & =\frac{x}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we simply solve for the unknown value $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{x}{8} \\ x & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} \\  & =8(0.669\,13...) \\  & =5.353\,04... \\  & ≈5.4,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

The theorem about **term-by-term differentiation of Fourier series** states the following:

Suppose that

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)

- piecewise smooth, and

- continuous.

Then, the Fourier series of $f'(x)$ can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f'(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\dfrac{n\pi a_n}{L}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+\dfrac{n\pi b_n}{L}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

- $F(x)$ is continuous on $x \in (-L,L),$

- $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x \in (-L,L),$ and

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -L^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to L^-} F(x).$

**Note:** The constant term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}$ disappears after differentiating, since $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\!\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)=0.$

The theorem about **term-by-term integration of Fourier series** states the following:

Suppose that

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

is a $2L$-periodic function which is piecewise continuous. Then, an antiderivative $F(x)$, where $F'(x) = f(x)$, can be found by integrating the Fourier series of $f(x)$ term-by-term:

$$
F(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}x + C + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigg( \dfrac{a_n L}{n\pi}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)-\dfrac{b_n L}{n\pi}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg) \bigg)
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant of integration.

1\. The expression for the antiderivative $F(x)$ is not a Fourier series in the usual sense because it contains the linear term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}x.$

2\. Even if $f(x)$ is periodic, its antiderivative $F(x)$ is not necessarily periodic. In particular, if $a_0 \neq 0,$ then the term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}x$ grows without bound as $x$ increases.

If we want a periodic antiderivative, we typically need the average value of $f$ over one period to be $0$ (equivalently, $a_0=0$), so that the linear term disappears.

**Note:** Integration is generally "safer" than differentiation for Fourier series. Differentiation can slow convergence or even destroy it, whereas integration divides the $n$th coefficient by $n,$ which typically improves convergence.

In a $2L$-periodic Fourier series, differentiating 

$$

introduces a factor of $\dfrac{n\pi}{L}$. So, very roughly,

$$
\big(\text{new coefficient size}\big) \approx n \cdot \big(\text{old coefficient size}\big).
$$

That means one level of coefficient decay is "used up" when we differentiate.

For example, consider the so-called *triangle wave* and *sawtooth wave*, the $2\pi$-periodic extensions from $x \in  [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ of the functions $y=|x|$ and $y=x,$ respectively.

Their Fourier series are the following:

$$
|x| \sim \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{\cos\!\big((2n-1)x\big)}{(2n-1)^2}

x \sim 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx)
$$

| **Function Type** | **Continuity** | **Fourier Series Coefficient Decay** | **Derivative Series Convergence** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Triangle wave | Continuous | $O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)$ | Converges 
(to the average of slopes) |
| Sawtooth wave | Discontinuous | $O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)$ | Diverges |

- The function has enough "smoothness" (continuity) that its Fourier coefficients decay quickly at a rate of $\sim \dfrac{1}{n^2}.$

- Differentiation "costs" one level of decay: 

$$
n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{n}

Since the terms $\dfrac{1}{n}$ still approach $0,$ the series can converge. At the "corners," it settles on the average of the left- and right-hand slopes.

- For the discontinuous but piecewise smooth *sawtooth wave*:

- The function's jump discontinuities "use up" the smoothness budget. The coefficients decay only at a rate of $\sim \dfrac{1}{n}.$

- Differentiation cancels out the decay entirely: 

$$
n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n} = 1

"When simplifying numerical expressions, it is generally preferable to avoid having radicals in the denominator. In cases where we wish to remove a radical from a denominator, we must **rationalize the denominator**.

If the denominator of an expression consists of two terms and includes one or more radicals, we rationalize it by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the **conjugate** of the denominator. 

To illustrate, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}
$$

 

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{2},$ we *flip the sign* between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is 

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{2}.
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we start by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1-\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{1-\sqrt{2}} & = \\ \frac{1\cdot (1-\sqrt{2})}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} &  \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})} & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the difference of squares formula:

$$
(a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

However, what if the sample were drawn from a population that is not normally distributed? What can we say about the sampling distribution of the sample mean in this case?

Ultimately, the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ depends on the population distribution. Unfortunately, no general result exists that tells us how $\overline{X}$ is distributed for an arbitrary population distribution. 

However, an important result, known as the **central limit theorem,** tells us that when the sample size $n$ is large, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is approximately normally distributed. Moreover, the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ for large $n$ *does not depend on the population distribution!*

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

In other words, as the sample size increases, the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal.

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1} &=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1} &=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1} &=15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 100 \\ 1 & 110 \\ 1 & 120 \\ 1 & 130\end{bmatrix}
$$

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0.1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.

"Suppose that we have the function $f(x) = 3x-9,$ and we wish to find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x).$ There's a simple technique that often works. The technique is described below in four steps.

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y.$

$$
y = 3x-9
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y.$

$$
x = 3y-9
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-9 \\ x+9 & =3y \\ \frac{x+9}{3} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x).$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x+9}{3}
$$

To verify that this is really the inverse of $f,$ we can check that

$$
(f\circ f^{-1})(x) = (f^{-1}\circ f)(x) = x.
$$

First, we check that $(f^{-1}\circ f)(x)=x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}∘f)(x) & ={f}^{-1}(f(x)) \\  & =\frac{f(x)+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{(3x-9)+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{3x}{3} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

So we've shown that $(f^{-1}\circ f)(x) = x.$ Using the same technique, we can verify that $(f \circ f^{-1})(x)=x\mathbin{:}$

$$

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

$B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3,$ exist within a sample space $\mathcal S$ such that 

- $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ are *mutually exclusive*, and

- the events $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ cover the *entire* sample space.

When these two conditions are satisfied, we say that $\mathcal S$ is the **disjoint union** of  $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3,$ and we write 
 

$$
\mathcal S = B_1 \sqcup B_2 \sqcup B_3.
$$

A diagram of this situation is shown below. Notice that $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ cover the entire diagram but do not overlap.

![](images/f5/f5f9f04eb6affb9dca1f7d4e7d66d76c4d520cbf66db93db60639ce896fb19af.png)

 

Now suppose that we wish to compute the probability of an event $A$ that lies within $\mathcal S.$ Let's draw this event on our diagram and label its intersections with $B_1, B_2, B_3\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ed/ed6568369a3af39cf1f6ecd5cb481de20d6c31bbce0fa1be54eb9ae0ab4e7f20.png)

 

The **law of total probability** can be deduced from this diagram. It states that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+P(A\cap {B}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider a disjoint union of $\mathcal S$ consisting of three events. However, it should be noted that the law of total probability can be extended to an arbitrary number of events, that is

$$

selection of objects in which order does *not* matter. Two selections of the same items are always counted as the same selections, even if the items are in a different order.

For example, suppose we have $5$ books but can only take $3$ of them on a trip. How many combinations are there? In other words, how many ways can we take $3$ of the books?

First, recall that the total number of ways of selecting $3$ books from $5$ (where order matters) is given by the permutation ${}_5P_3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{5}{P}_{3} & =\frac{5!}{(5-3)!} \\  & =\frac{5!}{2!} \\  & =60\end{aligned}
$$

However, the permutation calculation ${}_5P_3$ assumes that order of selection matters, but in our problem order is not important. Regardless of the order in which we choose the books, the chosen books are coming with us on the trip and the rest of the books will be left behind.

So, we must divide by the number of ways to order the $3$ books that we selected, which is $3!.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{}_{5}{P}_{3}}{3!} & =\frac{60}{3!} \\  & =\frac{60}{6} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there are $10$ ways that we can take $3$ of the books with us." 17592186045417] [17592186084449 1065 3684 17592186045417] [17592186084449 1066 #uuid "4e5b5b6a-e449-5f00-9d3a-db539975a666" 17592186045417] [17592186084449 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186084450 1064 "In general, the number of unique combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula
